body.translated_text:
Composed by the illustrious <s>Arcaṭa</s>
|| <s>Hetubinduṭīkā</s> (Commentary on the Drop of Reason) ||
|| Homage to the Omniscient One ||
Auspicious invocation through salutation to <s>Jina</s>.

children.text: yaḥ sañjātamahākṛpo vyasaninaṃ trātuṃ samagraṃ janam,
children.translated_text: He who, having arisen with great compassion, [seeks] to save all beings afflicted [by suffering],
having accumulated the vast cause consisting of merit and knowledge, [his] fatigue dispelled,
who has ascended the mountain of the arising of the purest wisdom that pervades all objects of knowledge —
that sun among <s>Jinas</s>, destroyer of the densest darkness in the world — Him I salute with bowed head. || 1 ||

body.translated_text: <s>puṇya</s>- : <s>prastuta</s>-
Declaration that <s>Dharmakīrti</s>'s words are supremely delightful.
For it is better to re-chew what has been [already] chewed by <s>Dharmakīrti</s>,
even among things already masticated;

body.text: niṣpīḍitā'pi mṛdvī[kā mādhuryaṃ hi jahā]ti kim ? || 2 ||
body.translated_text: does a grape, even when squeezed, ever abandon its sweetness? || 2 ||
<s>carciteṣv api carvanam</s> — T.
Having declared his own humility, a promise to expound the treatise.

children.translated_text: Where is His profound speech, whose intellect weighed the whole world on the scale of reasoning, alone?

children.text: jayet tasya kva gambhīrā giro 'haṃ jaḍadhīḥ kva ca ? || 3 ||
children.translated_text: And where am I, of dull understanding? || 3 ||

body.text:
tathāpi mandamatayaḥ santi matto ['pi kecana |
  yānuddiśya] mayāpy eṣa hetubindur vibhajyate || 4 ||[ādivākyasya prayojanaprakaṭanam | ]

children.translated_text: 'Regarding that which is imperceptible' (<s>parokṣe</s>) —

children.text:
-- [Tt. 355b.] ty ādinā prakaraṇārambhe prayojanam āha | tac ca[3]śrotṛjanapravṛtty artham itikecit |
  tad ukta[m --
children.translated_text:
— [Tt. 355b.] By [this word] beginning with this, he states the purpose at the commencement of the treatise. And that [purpose], according to some, is for the sake of prompting the audience's engagement.
As it has been stated —
For any treatise whatsoever, or indeed any action,
so long as its purpose is not stated, who would take it up?

children.text:
iti | tad ayuktam[4]| yato 'sya prakaraṇasyedaṃ prayojanam iti [pradarśane prayo]janaviśeṣaṃ prati upāyatāṃ prakaraṇasya niścityānupāye
{p. 2.1} pravṛttyasambhavāt prekṣāvatāṃ tadarthitayā[5]pra[karaṇaśravaṇādau pravṛttiḥ] [S. 2a] syād iti tadabhidhānasyārthavattā[6]varṇyate | na caitad[7]yuktam | yataḥ prekṣāvatāṃ pravṛttiḥ prayojanārthināṃ tadupāye[8]tadbhāvaniścayāt[9]| yathā kṛṣīva[lādīnāṃ sasyā]dy upāye bījādāva'bījādivivekenā'vadhṛtabījādibhāvānām | anyathā hy aniścitopāyānām upeyārthanāṃ [T. 206b.] pravṛttau prekṣāvattaiva hīyeta | upeye tu [bhāvini pramā]ṇavyāpārāsambhavād aniścaye 'pi vivecitopāyāḥ pratibandhavaikalyayor asambhave `yogyam etad vivakṣitaṃ kāryaṃ niṣpādayitum' iti saṃ[bhāvanayā pravṛttau] prekṣāvat tāto na hīyeran |
  niścayaś ca pramāṇād eva | na ca prayojanavākyasya prāmāṇyam asti, śabdānāṃ bahirarthe pratibandhābhāvāt | vivakṣāyāṃ [tasya prāmāṇye 'pi yathā]vastupravṛttiniyamābhāvāt na tataḥ prakaraṇasya prayojanavise(śe)ṣaṃ prati upāyatāniścayaḥ samasti | na hi ye yathā [S. 2b.] yam arthaṃ vivakṣanti te tathaiva tam anu[tiṣṭhanti vi]saṃvādanābhiprāyāṇām anyathā'bhidhāyānyathāpravṛttidarśanāl loke sarvatrānāśvāsāt |
  prayojanaviśeṣopanyāsāt prakaraṇasya tadupāyatā[viṣayaḥ saṃśayaḥ ja]nyate tatas[10]tadbhāvanirdhāraṇāya[11]kṛṣīvalāder iva bījād avadhṛtaye pravṛttir yukteti cet; na, prayojanaviśeṣopāyatāsaṃśayasya tadabhidhā[nāt prāg api] bhāvāt | tatsādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāve tasya[12]nyāyaprāptatvāt | anumānādivyutpattyarthānāṃ ca prakaraṇānāṃ darśanāt kim asyānumā[navyutpādanaṃ pra]yojanam anyad vā, na vā kiñcid apīty evaṃ rūpaś ca saṃśayaḥ prāk pravarttamānaḥ kena nivāryeta | api ca kim idaṃ niṣprayojanam, uta prayojana[vat, asmad abhima]tena vā prayojanena tadvad iti jijñāsoḥ pravṛttisambhave vyartha eva prayojanavākyopanyāsaḥ | [S. 3a.]
children.translated_text:
Thus. But this is inappropriate. For [the argument runs:] by demonstrating that 'this is the purpose of this treatise,' one ascertains the treatise's being a means toward that specific purpose; since engagement is impossible without a means, intelligent persons, desiring that [purpose], would engage in listening to the treatise and so forth — thus the meaningfulness of stating [the purpose] is described. But this is not correct. For the engagement of intelligent persons, who desire a purpose, [comes] from their ascertainment that the means exists when its means [is recognized] — just as farmers and the like, having determined the existence of seeds and so forth as the means to crops and so forth, by distinguishing seeds from non-seeds, [engage accordingly]. Otherwise, for those whose means are not ascertained, though they desire the goal, their engagement would lack the very quality of being intelligent. But when the goal is [already] going to occur, since the operation of a means of valid cognition is impossible [regarding what is already established], even without ascertainment, those who have discerned the means, when there is no impossibility of connection or deficiency, [thinking] 'this intended result is fit to be accomplished' — through [such] estimation they would engage, and their intelligence would not be diminished.
Moreover, ascertainment comes only from a means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>). And the statement of purpose has no validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since words have no [intrinsic] connection to external objects. Even if, through the speaker's intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>), it were valid, since there is no restriction that [engagement] accords with reality, from that there is no complete ascertainment of the treatise's being a means toward the specific purpose. For those who intend a certain meaning in a certain way do not necessarily act accordingly — since in the world, because of the observation that those with deceptive intent describe one thing and act otherwise, there would be universal distrust everywhere.
If [one objects:] the presentation of a specific purpose generates doubt regarding the treatise's being a means to that, and then, for the purpose of resolving that [doubt], engagement is appropriate — like a farmer's [engagement] for the sake of determining [the existence] of seeds — [we say:] No, because the doubt regarding being a means to the specific purpose exists even prior to that statement. Because in the absence of a validating or invalidating <s>pramāṇa</s> for that, such [doubt] is naturally obtained. And since treatises aimed at instruction in inference and the like are observed, a doubt of this form — 'Is its purpose the instruction of inference, or something else, or nothing at all?' — which arises prior [to the statement], by what would it be prevented? Moreover, when engagement is possible for one who wishes to know 'Is this purposeless, or purposeful, or purposeful with the purpose I have in mind?' — the presentation of a statement of purpose is entirely superfluous. [S. 3a.]

children.text: tasmād `yat prayojanarahitaṃ vākyam, tadartho vā, na tat prekṣāvatā''rabhyate kartuṃ pratipādayituṃ vā | tadyathā [T. 207a.]
children.translated_text: Therefore, 'that which is a purposeless statement, or its meaning — an intelligent person does not undertake to perform it or to communicate it. For example,

children.text:
{p. 3.1} daśadāḍimādivākyaṃ kākadanta[parīkṣā ca | niṣprayojanaṃ cedaṃ] prakaraṇaṃ tadartho vā' iti vyāpakānupalabdhyā pratyavatiṣṭhamānasya tadasiddhatodbhāvanārtham ādau prayojanavākyopanyāsaḥ |[prakaraṇatadabhidheyayoḥ prayojanacintā |]
  tatra
children.translated_text:
the statement about ten pomegranates, or the examination of a crow's teeth. If this treatise or its meaning were purposeless' — for one who resists through the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>), the presentation of the purpose-statement at the beginning is for the sake of removing [the charge of] that being unestablished.
[Inquiry into the purpose of the treatise and its subject matter.]
Therein,
'For the purpose of instruction in that (<s>tadvyutpādanārtham</s>)' —

children.text: iti vākyena svayam asya prakaraṇasya prayojanam āha | yathāsvam abhidheyapratītir hi vākyasya prayojanam | tac cehāsti padānām avāntaravākyānāṃ ca parasparasaṃsargāt samāsārthapratīteḥ | tathā hi -- anumānamatra prakaraṇe vyutpādyata iti tad abhidheyam | tasyaiva tacchabdena sambandhāt | yady api parokṣārthapratipattau gu[ṇībhūtam anu]mānaṃ tathāpi vaktur abhiprāyānuvidhāyitayā śabdavṛtteḥ tacchabdena parāmṛśyate | anyathā pradhānasaṃsparso(śo)pi kathaṃ syāt? | śabdānāṃ sva[bhāvataḥ] sambhaddhā(ndhā)yogāt |
children.translated_text: by this statement, he himself states the purpose of this treatise. For the cognition of the subject matter as it is — that indeed is the purpose of a statement. And that exists here, from the comprehension of the composite meaning arising from the mutual connection of words and sub-sentences. Namely: inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is what is taught in this treatise — that is the subject matter. Because the word 'that' (<s>tad</s>) is connected with that very [inference]. Although inference is subsidiary in the cognition of imperceptible objects, nevertheless, because verbal usage follows the speaker's intention, it is referred to by the word 'that.' Otherwise, how could there even be contact with the principal [topic]? Since words do not have a natural connection [to things].
'A property of the thesis-subject' (<s>pakṣadharma</s>) —

children.text: ityādinā cānumānasyaiva vyutpādanāt | tasya [S. 3b.] vyutpatti[r aviparītasvarū]papratītir asya prakaraṇasya prayojanam, tasmādhyatvāt | ata eva cānumānavyutpattiviṣayaṃ prakaraṇa[vyāpāraṃ darṣa]yituṃ ṇicā nirdiśati --
children.translated_text: and by [the statement beginning with] this, since it teaches inference itself, the instruction (<s>vyutpatti</s>) of that — i.e., the cognition of its undistorted nature — is the purpose of this treatise, since it is that which is to be accomplished through it. And for this very reason, to show the treatise's operation as pertaining to the instruction of inference, he indicates [the purpose] with the causative suffix (<s>ṇic</s>) —
'for the purpose of instruction in that' (<s>tadvyutpādanārtham</s>).

children.text:
iti | tataś ca prakaraṇaprayojanayoḥ sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇaḥ[13]sambandho
'py ukto bhavati | yady api śabdavṛttenā[numānavyutpattivi]ṣayasya[14]prakaraṇavyāpārasya prādhānyaṃ tathāpi vastuvṛttena vyutpatter eva pradhānatā tasyās tatsādhyatvāt[15]| itarasya[16]ca tadupāyatvenāpradhānatvāt | tasmād anumānavyutpattir [T. 207b.] eva prayojanatayā pratīyate na prakaraṇavyāpāra iti |
children.translated_text: And from this, the relation between the treatise and its purpose — characterized as that which is to be accomplished and that which accomplishes — is also stated. Although by verbal convention the treatise's operation pertaining to the instruction of inference is principal, nevertheless in reality, instruction itself is principal, since it is what is to be accomplished by that [operation]. And since the other [i.e., the treatise's operation] is subordinate by being a means to that. Therefore, the instruction of inference alone is understood as the purpose, not the treatise's operation.
'Because the cognition of imperceptible objects has inference as its basis' (<s>parokṣārthapratipatteḥ anumānāśrayatvāt</s>) —

children.text:
ity anena tu prakaraṇārthasyānumānalakṣaṇasya prayojanam āha | na hi vākyasya svārthapratītilakṣaṇaṃ phalam[17]astīty etā[v ataiva prekṣāvān prava]rttate 'pi tu tadabhidheyārthasya puruṣārthopayogitve sati | tac cehāsti yataḥ parokṣārthasya yā pratipattiḥ -- niścayaḥ -- tasyā anumā[naṃ -- trirūpaliṅgam] [S. 4a.] kāraṇe kāryopacārāt | ananyopāyasādhyatāṃ darśayituṃ
{p. 4.1} paramatanirāsārtham āśrayaḥ -- kāraṇam, anumānam āśrayo yasyeti sāmānyena vigṛhya | [tadanu ca] kasyānumānāśrayatvād iti viśeṣāpekṣāyām -- yady api parokṣārthapratipattiśabdasambhandhe strītvaṃ gamyate tathāpi tat[18]padasaṃskāravelāyāṃ buddhyasaṃnihitatvāt bahiraṅgam iti na strīpratyayanimittaṃ yathābhūtam iyaṃ brāhmaṇī, āvapanam iyam uṣṭriketi |
children.translated_text: by this, he states the purpose of the treatise's subject matter, i.e., the definition of inference. For a statement does not have as its fruit merely the cognition of its own meaning — an intelligent person does not engage [merely] for that much — but rather when the subject matter stated [in it] has utility for human purposes. And that exists here, since the cognition — i.e., the ascertainment — of an imperceptible object has inference — i.e., the triple-characterized logical mark (<s>trirūpaliṅga</s>) — as its basis — i.e., its cause, through the figurative transfer of the effect [term] to the cause. To show that there is no other means [for this], and for the purpose of refuting opposing positions, [it is called] the basis — analyzed generally as 'that whose basis is inference.' [And then] when the specific [referent] is sought — [the question arises:] 'the basis in inference of what?' — although femininity [of the word] is understood from the connection with the word 'cognition of imperceptible objects' (<s>parokṣārthapratipattiśabda</s>), nevertheless, since at the time of word-formation that [feminine gender] was not present to awareness, it is extraneous, and hence is not the occasion for a feminine suffix — just as in '[this is] a Brahmin woman' (<s>iyaṃ brāhmaṇī</s>), 'this is a she-camel' (<s>iyam uṣṭrikā</s>).

body.translated_text:
Nevertheless, there are some who are even duller of intellect than I;
for their sake, this <s>Hetubindu</s> (Drop of Reason) is being analyzed by me as well. || 4 || [Exposition of the purpose of the opening statement.]

body.text:
anena ca sarvā parokṣā[rtha]pratipattiḥ pramāṇabhūtā, anyasmāt tatpratipatty ayogāt, trirūpaliṅgāśrayaivety uktaṃ bhavati [S. 4b.] anumānāśrayatvād eveti avadhāraṇāt | [tataś ca śabdādī]nāṃ sati prāmāṇye 'numānatā, anyathā[19]teṣām api vyutpādyatāprasaṅgo nimittasya[20]samānatvāt |
  tathā hi -- sarvā parokṣārthapratipattiḥ pra[māṇabhūtā], na svatantrā bhavati | tasyāḥ[21]svārthapratibandhābhāvena niyamena tatsaṃvādāyogāt[22]| avisaṃvādalakṣaṇatvāc ca pramāṇasya | anyato 'pi [asambaddhād

children.text: yadi syā]t [T. 208a.] sarvataḥ sarvapratipattiprasaṅgāt dharmyasambandhe 'pi sarvatra pratītiṃ janayet, pratyāsattiviprakarṣābhāvāt |
children.translated_text: if [valid cognition] were [possible from that], there would be the unwanted consequence of cognition of everything from everything; even without connection with the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), it would generate cognition everywhere, since there would be no [distinction of] proximity and remoteness.

children.text: evambhūtaś ca[23]trirūpa[liṅgam evārtho bhava]tīti sarvā parokṣārthapratipattis trirūpaliṅgajatvenānumānāt na bhidyata iti | eṣa cārthaḥ
children.translated_text: And a [mark] of such nature is nothing other than a triple-characterized logical mark (<s>trirūpaliṅga</s>). Therefore, all cognition of imperceptible objects, being born from the triple-characterized mark, is not different from inference. And this meaning —
'A property of the thesis-subject, pervaded by a portion of that — [is] the logical reason (<s>hetu</s>)' —

children.text: , kasya?, parokṣā[rthapratipatte]r iti [S. 5.a] prakṛtena saṃbandhād darśitaḥ, pakṣadharma eva tadaṃśena vyāpta eva ca parokṣārthapratipatter hetur ity avadhāraṇāt |
children.translated_text: of what? — 'of the cognition of imperceptible objects' — is shown through connection with the topic under discussion, since the restrictive sense is: it is only a property of the thesis-subject and only pervaded by a portion of that which is the logical reason for the cognition of imperceptible objects.

body.translated_text:
And by this, it is stated that all cognition of imperceptible objects that constitutes a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), since the cognition of that is impossible from anything other [than a triple-characterized mark], has as its basis only the triple-characterized logical mark (<s>trirūpaliṅga</s>) — because of the restrictive particle 'only' (<s>eva</s>) in 'because of having inference as its basis.' [And from this,] when verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) and the like are valid, they are [forms of] inference; otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence that they too would need to be taught [separately], since the ground [for their validity] is the same.
Namely: all cognition of imperceptible objects that constitutes a <s>pramāṇa</s> is not independent. Because of that [cognition's] lack of intrinsic connection with its object, since there can be no reliable correspondence with it by necessity. And because a <s>pramāṇa</s> is defined by non-deceptiveness. Even from another [source] that is unconnected —

body.text:
avadhāraṇābhāve
[20] parokṣārthapratipattikāraṇatvasya
[21] svatantrapratipatteḥ
[22] svārtha-
[23] pratibaddhaṃ pakṣasaṃbaddhaṃ ca

<s>avadhāraṇābhāve</s>

Establishing that only the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) is real, not the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>).

body.text: arthagrahaṇaṃ tu parokṣārthapratipatter ity a[numā]nasyāpi svalakṣaṇaviṣayaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ darśayitum | arthakriyāsamartho hy arthaḥ, svalakṣaṇaṃ caivamātmakam | ata eva --

children.translated_text: 'Because the establishment of the [system of] valid cognition depends on [the existence of] real entities (<s>vastu</s>)' —

children.text:
-- [iti va]kṣyati | anyathā'numānāt tatra pravṛttir na syād arthakriyārthinaḥ |
{p. 5.1} sāmānyasyāvastutve 'pi jñānamātralakṣaṇatvāt tadarthakriyāyāḥ tasyāś ca tadu[tpādya]tvena siddhatvāt | na hi jātir dāhapākādāv upayujyate, svalakṣaṇasyaiva tatropayogāt[24]| tatsambandhāt tatra pravṛttir iti cet; na, nityasyānupakāra[katvena] kenacit sambhandhābhāvāt | saty api ca sambandhe katham anyapratipattāv anyatra pravṛttiḥ, atiprasaṅgāt | [S. 5b.] samavāyasya sūkṣmatvenānavasitavivekasyāvasāyād bhrāntyā tatra pravṛttir iti cet; [T. 208b.] evaṃ tarhi bhrāntimātram evāstu, kim antargaḍunā sāmānyena? | nirbbījabhrāntyayogād iti cet; tā eva vyaktayas tadekakā[ryakāriṇyo bhrānter bījam] | varṇākṛtisamānākāraṃ hi sāmānyajñānam | na ca sāmānyaṃ tadrūpam, tat kathaṃ tad bhrānter bbījam | sādṛśyanibandhanā hi bhrāntir iṣyate paraiḥ | vyaktya eva cā[samānajā]tīyavyāvṛttāḥ sāmānyākārajñānasvarūpās tatas tā eva bhrāntibījam, atadrūpavyāvṛttes tāsu bhāvāt | vastubhūtasya tu sāmānyasya sambhandh[āsaṃbhave]na
tāsu bhāvāyogāc ca |
  yais[25]tu vyaktyātmakam eva sāmānyaṃ kalpitaṃ taiḥ svalakṣaṇaviṣayam anumānasya prāmāṇyam abhyupagatam eva bhavati | svalakṣaṇātmakaṃ tu sāmānyaṃ katham anumāne[26]pratibhāsate, vaiśeṣikadarśanopagamaprasaṅgāt | .............................................................................................................. ................................................................................................................................[S.6a
children.translated_text: — [thus] he will state. Otherwise, there would be no engagement [toward an object] for one desiring effective action, from inference. {p. 5.1} Even though the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is unreal, since effective action pertaining to it is established as being produced by cognition alone, which has the character of mere awareness. For the universal (<s>jāti</s>) is not useful in burning, cooking, and such — since only the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) is useful therein. [Objection:] Engagement there is due to [the universal's] relation with that [particular] — [Reply:] No, because the permanent (<s>nitya</s>) has no relation with anything, being incapable of assistance. And even if there were a relation, how could there be engagement toward one thing upon the cognition of another? — due to the absurd consequence of over-extension. [Objection:] Due to the subtlety of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), engagement there is from the determination of one whose discrimination has not been ascertained, i.e., from error — [Reply:] Then let there be mere error alone; what need is there for the universal as an internal intruder (<s>antargaḍu</s>)? [Objection:] Because error without a seed is impossible — [Reply:] Those very particulars (<s>vyakti</s>), being producers of a single [kind of] effect, are the seed of error. For the cognition of the universal has the same form as [that which has] similar color and shape. And the universal is not of that form — so how is it the seed of error? For error is accepted by the opponents as grounded in similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>). And the particulars themselves, distinguished from those of dissimilar class, are of the nature of cognition having the form of the universal — therefore they alone are the seed of error, since exclusion from what is not of that form exists in them. But a real universal, since relation [with particulars] is impossible, and since [it] cannot exist in them — [it cannot be the seed]. Those who have posited the universal as being of the nature of particulars themselves have thereby accepted the validity of inference as pertaining to particulars (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>). But how does the universal that is of the nature of particulars appear in inference? — since the absurd consequence of accepting the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> view [would follow]. ............ [S. 6a

body.translated_text: ............ has been stated. Therein, since the [reasons of] effect (<s>kārya</s>) and essential nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) function as positive proof (<s>vidhi-sādhana</s>), they have no operation in proving a negation. From non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) too, there is no ascertainment of the absence of another reason, since it [non-apprehension] is established in fourfold form: non-apprehension of essential nature, of cause (<s>kāraṇa</s>), and of the pervader (<s>vyāpaka</s>), and contradictory positive proof (<s>viruddha-viddhi</s>). The non-apprehension of essential nature — which has the form of apprehension of something else, being of the nature of equal eligibility as concomitant of a single cognition — is accepted as the ground for the convention of absence. And no other reason has been acknowledged as being absolutely non-existent that has the enumerated form; for if it were [existent], there would be only negation regarding place and such, not absolute non-existence. And the non-apprehensions of cause and pervader obtain when the effect-cause and pervaded-pervader relationships are established. And this manner is not possible when another reason has been accepted as absolutely non-existent. Then how will those [non-apprehensions] demonstrate its absence? And contradiction too, being of [the nature of] an entity whose complete cause is present, is understood from its absence when the other exists — thus contradictory apprehension (<s>viruddhopalabdhi</s>) too is impossible. Or, if [these non-apprehensions] are possible, how can there be absolute negation of [other reasons through] non-apprehension of cause and such? — Anticipating this, he says —
'Pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) are other than those [three]'
— thus.
'From those' (<s>tataḥ</s>) —
from the threefold reason (<s>hetu</s>);
'other' (<s>apare</s>) —
different;
[are] pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>);

body.translated_text: since from that, it [the reason] is exactly threefold. He considers thus: Here, when something is restricted to something [else], that restriction is established through the converse [relation], i.e., by the pervasion of the counter-class of the latter by the opposite of the former. Just as when the restriction of existence (<s>sattva</s>) to momentary things (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) is stated — 'whatever exists is momentary alone' — it is established by the pervasion of the counter-class of the momentary, i.e., the non-momentary, by the opposite of existence, i.e., non-existence. So here too, when reason-hood (<s>hetutva</s>) is restricted to the threefold, through the opposite of reason-hood, i.e., pseudo-reason-hood (<s>hetvābhāsatva</s>), by the pervasion of what falls outside the count of three, it becomes restricted to the three-count alone. Therefore, he demonstrates the pseudo-reason-hood of things other than the threefold reason. Thus, by the essential-nature [reason] and contradictory apprehension, the ascertainment of the absence of reason-hood in things other than effect-essential-nature-non-apprehension [is achieved]. And the contradiction between reason and pseudo-reason, being of the nature of mutual exclusion, is understood at the very time of apprehending the definition of reason. Since from cognition that invariably manifests as restricted to that [reason's] nature alone, the otherness of what is contrary to that is apprehended as pseudo-reason-hood — from the mutual ascertainment of the absence of each other's form in one another. Therein, pseudo-reason-hood perceived in things other than the threefold reason eliminates reason-hood, which is contradictory to it. And those things outside the three reasons are not acknowledged as absolutely non-existent, nor is reason-hood being negated in them; rather, reason-hood that is well-known elsewhere has been merely superimposed or suspected there through confusion — and it is removed by the apprehension of what contradicts it. Therefore, what is [the point of] saying —
'How can there be contradiction for what is absolutely impossible?'

body.translated_text: For it is not [the case] that 'cold-touch does not belong to fire [only] in the subject' — the contradiction of cold-touch with fire exists not only in the subject but everywhere; just as the negation of fire in the subject [is established] by the previously established contradiction with fire elsewhere — so too, from the apprehension of pseudo-reason-hood, there is the elimination of reason-hood in things outside the three reasons. And even of the absolutely non-existent, a characterizing contradiction is perceived — just as the non-momentary is [contradicted] by momentariness, since it [the non-momentary] is impossible anywhere in reality; or just as absence [is contradicted] by existence, since [absence] is characterized by the complete absence of all powers — but enough with excessive attention to the flutterings of poor intellects. This stands established: reason-hood restricted to the threefold, when the pervasion of its opposite also holds, becomes restricted therein — with this intention, to demonstrate the converse pervasion, this has been said —
'Pseudo-reasons are other than those [three]'
— thus.

And the deficiency of invariable concomitance is established through the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>) of those other than the threefold reason, precisely because they differ from the threefold reason. 'like color (<s>rāga</s>).' || [PV I 33-34]
— thus. For the invariable concomitance of taste and such with form and such too is not intrinsic (<s>svataḥ</s>), but rather mediated through non-deviation from one's own cause — therefore, origination from that cause is alone the ground of invariable concomitance. Otherwise, if invariable concomitance were imagined with what is independent of that, or with what is independent of the mode of that, there would be invariable concomitance of everything with everything — due to the absence of distinction. [Objection:] The invariable concomitance of form, taste, and such is caused by inherence in a single substance (<s>ekārtha-samavāya</s>) — [Reply:] But inherence too is described as belonging to things that are container and contained. And that container-contained relationship, since identity [between them] does not assist [in establishing it] — being an absurd consequence — cannot be established; therefore, inherence in a single substance is to be understood as dependent on a single causal complex alone. Or another real relation is impossible — as has been explained in detail by the author of the treatise [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] in the Examination of Relations — therefore, it should be ascertained from that [text] itself. Whether _ _ or not, {p. 9.1} even when the producer-produced relationship exists, or in the case of identity (<s>tādātmya</s>), invariable concomitance is with that alone and not with another — the reply here should be given through the essential natures of things themselves. [Objection:] 'These [natures] that are thus are not [made] by us; we are merely observers' — [Reply:] Then that nature of things is causeless (<s>ākasmika</s>), and therefore would belong to none. For the restriction to [particular] place, time, and substance is not justified without a cause. For that which has some dependence or non-dependence on something somewhere might or might not be brought to [a particular] place. Otherwise, in the absence of distinction, what would prevent existence in other places and such, as [it exists in] the established places and such — due to the absence of distinction? Therefore, when something is observed as invariably concomitant with something, the investigators of reality must identify the cause of its non-deviation from that — and not cling to [the position of] stretching one's legs [in laziness]. And that cause of non-deviation is not justified as being other than what has been stated [i.e., identity and causal origination] — therefore, those deficient in that [relation] do not possess the definition of a reason. And thus he says —

athavā `tridhaiva saḥ' iti sa pakṣadharmas triprakāra eva svabhāvakāryānupalambhākhyas tadaṃśena vyāpto nānyaḥ | [sa] triprakāras
{p. 10.1} tadaṃśena vyāpta eveti sambhandhaḥ | kiṃ kāraṇam? |

children.translated_text: Because of the restriction of invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāvaniyamāt</s>).

children.text: | avinābhāvasya -- vyāpteḥ | trividha eva pakṣadharme niyamāt | trividhasya ca pakṣadharmasyāvinābhāvaniyamāt | tena ca [sva]bhāvakāryānupalambhātmakatrividhapakṣadharmavyatiriktā [T. 212a.] na tadaṃśena vyāptā iti | trividhaś ca kāryasvabhāvānupalabdhirūpaḥ pakṣadharmas tadaṃśena vyāpta eveti na tasyāhetutvam ity uktaṃ bhavati | tatas trividhahetubāhyeṣv avi[nābhāvābhā]vād dhetuvyavahāraṃ kurvantaḥ, trividhe ca hetāv avinābhāvasyāvaśyam bhāvā[bhāvā]d ahetutvam ācakṣāṇā[53]nirastā bhavati | [S. 11a.]
children.translated_text: Of invariable concomitance — that is, of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion). Because of the restriction to only a threefold <s>pakṣadharma</s>; and because of the restriction of invariable concomitance to the threefold <s>pakṣadharma</s>. Therefore, [reasons] other than the threefold <s>pakṣadharma</s> consisting of essential nature, effect, and non-apprehension are not pervaded by that portion. And the threefold <s>pakṣadharma</s>, having the form of effect, essential nature, and non-apprehension, is pervaded by that portion alone — thus it has been stated that it is not a non-reason (<s>ahetu</s>). Therefore, for those who apply the designation 'reason' to [things] outside the threefold reason — where invariable concomitance is absent — and for those who declare non-reason-hood where invariable concomitance necessarily obtains in the threefold reason — [both positions] are refuted.

body.translated_text: Alternatively, 'threefold alone is it' — that <s>pakṣadharma</s> (property of the thesis-locus) is of exactly three kinds, designated as essential nature, effect, and non-apprehension (<s>svabhāvakāryānupalambha</s>); pervaded by that portion (<s>tadaṃśa</s>), and no other. [That] three-fold [reason], pervaded by that portion alone — this is the connection. What is the reason?
the <s>Cārvākas</s> (materialists)
Section: 4. Even without stating the definition of pseudo-reasons, their indication [is achieved

body.text: tatraitat syāt -- hetvābhāsānām api [lakṣaṇam a]bhidhānīyaṃ tatra śiṣyāṇāṃ hetuvyavahāranivṛttaya ity āha

children.translated_text: 'Pseudo-reasons are other than that' —
thus.
'Than that' —
than the definition of a reason, namely 'a <s>pakṣadharma</s> pervaded by that portion' —
'other' —

children.text: a[nye ta]llakṣaṇavikalā hetvābhāsā gamyanta eveti na tallakṣaṇam ucyate | tathā hi --
children.translated_text: others, deficient in that definition, are understood to be pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>); therefore their definition is not [separately] stated. For thus —
'<s>Pakṣadharma</s>' —

children.text: ity ukte yatra pakṣadharmatā nāsti na sa hetuḥ |
children.translated_text: when this is stated, that which lacks the property of being a <s>pakṣadharma</s> is not a reason.
'Pervaded by that portion' —

children.text: iti vacane yatra tadaṃśavyāptiviraho viparyayavyāpter vyāpakasya vā tatrāvaśyam bhāvābhāvāt, te heturūpavikalatayā
children.translated_text: by this statement, wherever there is absence of pervasion by that portion — [either] because of pervasion by the contrary, or because of the necessary presence or absence of the pervader — those, being deficient in the form of a reason,
are pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) —

children.text: asiddhaviruddhānaikāntikā gamyanta eva | tathā hi -- yallakṣaṇo[54]yo 'rthaḥ śiṣyasya vyutpāditaḥ tallakṣaṇavirahite na tadvyavahāraṃ svayam eva pravartayiṣyati a[tadrūpa]parihārenaiva tadrūpapratipattor iti na tatra yatnaḥ phalavān bhavati | [S. 11b.] yat tv anyatra hetvābhāsavyutpādanaṃ tanmandabuddhīnadhikṛtya | idaṃ tu prakaraṇaṃ vipulamatīn uddiśya praṇītam
children.translated_text: the unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), the contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), and the inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) — are understood [automatically]. For thus: when an object has been made known to a student through a certain definition, he will not of his own accord apply the designation to what lacks that definition — since the apprehension of that form comes precisely through the exclusion of what is not of that form — therefore no effort [to define pseudo-reasons] bears fruit. Whatever instruction on pseudo-reasons [is given] elsewhere is intended for those of dull intellect. But this treatise is composed for those of expansive intellect,
'in brief' —

children.text:
iti vacanāt | [T. 212b.] ta eva hi saṃkṣepoktaṃ yathāvad avagantuṃ kṣamāḥ na mandamatayaḥ, teṣāṃ vistarābhidhānam antareṇa yathāvad arthapratipatter abhāvāt | ata evārthākṣiptopanyāsapūrvakam eva hetvābhāsalakṣaṇaṃ tatropavarṇitam iti | tadatra vyākhyāne hetulakṣaṇaṃ 1
{p. 11.1} hetusāmkhyāniyamaḥ 2 tasya ca trividhasya hetutvāvadhāraṇaṃ 3 tadubhayakāraṇaṃ[55]śliṣṭanirdeśā[t 4-5] hetvābhāsalakṣaṇānabhidhānakāraṇaṃ 6 ceti ṣaḍarthāḥ śloke 'tra nirdiṣṭā iti |
  kiñcid -- idam api sādhu dṛśyate --
children.translated_text: as indicated by this word. For only those [of sharp intellect] are capable of properly understanding what is stated in brief, not those of dull intellect, since without detailed exposition they cannot properly apprehend the meaning. For this very reason, the definition of pseudo-reasons has been described there [i.e., elsewhere] only after preliminary indication through what is implied by the meaning. Thus in this explanation, the verse here indicates six meanings: the definition of a reason [1], the restriction on the enumeration of reasons [2], the ascertainment of the reason-hood of the threefold [reason] [3], the cause of both of these, from the combined exposition [4-5], and the reason for not stating the definition of pseudo-reasons [6]. Furthermore — this too appears well:
'Threefold alone' —

children.text: kāryasvabhāvānupalabdhi[bheda]bhinnaḥ sa hetuḥ | tathā, tridhaiva pakṣadharmānvayavyatirekarūpabhedāt
children.translated_text: that reason, differentiated by the divisions of effect, essential nature, and non-apprehension. Thus, threefold alone, because of the difference in the forms of <s>pakṣadharma</s>, positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), and negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) —
'is of exactly three kinds' —

children.text: trirūpa eva | [S. 12a.] tadaṃśavyāptivacanenānvayavyatirekayor abhidhānāt | nābādhitaviṣayatvādirūpāntarayogy api sa hetuḥ | kutaḥ? yataḥ
children.translated_text: is of exactly three forms. Because by the statement 'pervaded by that portion,' both positive and negative concomitance are expressed. And that reason is not also possessed of additional forms such as having an uncontradicted domain (<s>abādhitaviṣayatva</s>) and the like. Why? Because
'pseudo-reasons are other than that'
'than that' —
than the threefold [reason] beginning with essential nature, or than that which possesses the triad of forms beginning with <s>pakṣadharma</s>,
'other' —

children.text: anye saṃyogyādayo 'bādhitaviṣayatvādivyatiriktarūpavanto vā | kasmād? | avinābhāvasya atraiva trividha eva trirūpa eva ca hetau niyamād anyatra svabhāvādivyatirikta(kte) rūpāntarasambhavini vā avinābhāvābhāvād ity arthaḥ | na hi svabhāvādivya[ti]rikte pratibandhanibandhanasyā 'vinābhāvasya saṃbhavaḥ tadvati vā rūpāntarasya | tathā cā(ca) satyevāvinābhāve rūpā[T. 213a.]ntarasya na sambhavas tathā
children.translated_text: others such as conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and the like, or those possessing forms other than having an uncontradicted domain and the like. Why? Because of the restriction of invariable concomitance to only the threefold reason, which is only of three forms — meaning that in anything other than essential nature and the like, or in that which is susceptible of additional forms distinct [from these three], invariable concomitance is absent. For there is no possibility of invariable concomitance — which is grounded in restriction (<s>pratibandha</s>) — in what is other than essential nature and the like, nor of additional form in what possesses it. And since additional form is impossible when invariable concomitance obtains, thus
'six-characterized' —
and so forth, he will state [later].

body.translated_text: Here one might [object]: the definition of pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) should also be stated, so that students may desist from applying the designation 'reason' [to them]. To this he says:

body.text:
yadrūpa-
[55] tasyomayasya hetusaṃkhyāniyamasya hetutvāvadhāraṇasya kāraṇaṃ avinābhāvaniyama ity eta .........
body.translated_text:
of which form
[55] the cause of both — the restriction on the enumeration of reasons and the ascertainment of reason-hood — is the restriction of invariable concomitance .........
Section: 5. Following <s>Dignāga</s>, the word '<s>pakṣa</s>' refers to the <s>dharmin</s> (property-locus) alone
'<s>Pakṣadharma</s>' —

body.text: ity atra hetulakṣaṇe 'pi kriyamāṇe yadi samudāyaḥ pakṣe(kṣo) gṛhyate yo 'numānaviṣayas tadā sarvo hetur asiddhaḥ, siddhau vā 'numānavaiyarthyam ity āha
body.translated_text: even in this definition of a reason being formulated, if <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis) is taken as the aggregate [of property-locus and property], which is the object of inference, then every reason would be unestablished, or if established, inference would be pointless. Therefore he says:
'<s>Pakṣa</s> is the <s>dharmin</s>' —

body.text: iti | kathaṃ punaḥ samudāyavacanaḥ [S. 12b.] pakṣaśabdo dharmimātre vartata iti cet?
body.translated_text: thus. But how does the word '<s>pakṣa</s>,' which denotes the aggregate, refer to the <s>dharmin</s> alone?
By metaphorical transfer (<s>upacāra</s>) of the aggregate to a part.

body.text: pakṣākhyasya hi samudāyasya dvāv avayavau dharmī, dharmaś ca | tad atra dharmimātre samudāyopacārāt pakṣaśabdo vartate | tadekadeśatvaṃ[56]ca samudāyopacāranimittam iti na sādhyadharmiṇo 'nyatra tatprasaṅgaḥ | taduktam --
body.translated_text: For the aggregate called '<s>pakṣa</s>' has two parts: the <s>dharmin</s> (property-locus) and the <s>dharma</s> (property). Therefore here, by metaphorical transfer of the aggregate to the <s>dharmin</s> alone, the word '<s>pakṣa</s>' refers [to it]. And the ground for metaphorical transfer of the aggregate is being a part of it (<s>tadekadeśatva</s>); therefore there is no occasion for [extending this] elsewhere than the <s>dharmin</s> of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum). As stated:
Since the aggregate is the <s>sādhya</s>, even for the <s>dharmin</s> alone, which is the <s>dharma</s> [part],
though not primary, because of being a part [of the aggregate], <s>sādhyatva</s> (probandum-hood) is metaphorically attributed. ||
PS III 9 (cf. HB
transl.

body.text: yasya hi ya ekadeśas tatra tādrūpyopacāraḥ, na hi paṭasyaikadeśe dagdhe kambalo dagdha ity upacāraḥ
body.translated_text: For that which is a part of something — with respect to that part, there is metaphorical transfer of that form; but when a part of a cloth is burnt, there is no metaphorical transfer [saying] 'the blanket is burnt.'
{p.12.1} [Section: 6. <s>Īśvarasena</s>'s objection to <s>Dignāga</s>'s interpretation and its resolution]

children.translated_text: 'In the purpose' —
and so forth.
Without purpose, transgression of the primary word-meaning is not prescribed.
PS III 39cd (cf. HB
transl.

children.text:
)
 ity asati prayojane nopacāro yuktaḥ | tato dharmidharma ity evāstv itiparaḥ|
children.translated_text: ) Thus, without purpose, metaphorical transfer is not appropriate. Therefore, let it just be '<s>dharmin</s> [and] <s>dharma</s>' — this is the opponent's [position].
[But] no —

children.text: prayojanābhāvaḥ | kutaḥ? sarvaś cāsau vivādāśrayo 'nyo dharmī yas tasya pratiṣedho 'rthaḥ prayojanaṃ yasyopacārasya tadbhāvas tasmāt
children.translated_text: there is no absence of purpose. Why? For every <s>dharmin</s> other than the one that is the locus of dispute — the purpose of the metaphorical transfer is its exclusion; because of the existence of that [purpose], therefore:
Because the metaphorical transfer serves to exclude all [other] <s>dharmin</s>-<s>dharma</s> [combinations].

children.text:
iti prayojanābhāvād ity asiddho hetuḥ |
 ka evaṃ sati guṇa iti ced āha [S. 13a.] [T. 213b.] --
children.translated_text: Thus 'because of absence of purpose' is an unestablished reason. What, then, is the advantage in this case? To this he says:
'For thus' —
when the metaphorical transfer obtains,
'visual perceptibility (<s>cākṣuṣatva</s>) and the like' —
by the word 'and the like,' the unestablished [reason] in a different substratum (<s>vyadhikaraṇa</s>), such as 'because of the blackness of a crow' and so on,
'is excluded' —
is rejected as a reason,
'becomes [so].'

children.text:
| dharmidharma iti tu sāmānye[nābhi]dhānāt teṣām api hetutā syād[57]iti |
 asaty upacāre dharmigrahaṇād apy etat[58]sidhyati | tato 'narthaka evopacāra ity āha paraḥ --
children.translated_text: But if one says '<s>dharmin</s> [and] <s>dharma</s>' — because of the general statement, even those would have reason-hood. Without the metaphorical transfer, this could be accomplished even by the mention of <s>dharmin</s> [alone]. Therefore the metaphorical transfer is purposeless — so the opponent says:
'Even by the statement of <s>dharma</s>' —
not only by the statement of <s>dharmin</s>,
'when the resort to <s>dharmin</s> is established' —

children.text: dharmiṇa āśrayaṇam āśrayaḥ parigrahas tasya siddhis tasyāṃ satyām | kiṃ punar ddharmasya dharmyākṣepanimittam iti cet[59]?
children.translated_text: the resort to <s>dharmin</s> means its inclusion, its acceptance; when that is established, i.e., when that obtains. But what is the ground for <s>dharma</s>'s implication of <s>dharmin</s>?
Because of dependence on another (<s>parāśrayatva</s>) —
because <s>dharma</s> is dependent on <s>dharmin</s>,
of <s>dharma</s> —

children.text: avaśyam asau dharmiṇam ākṣipati | tato dharmivacanam atiricyamānaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ sādhyadharmiṇam eva pratipādayati, [na dharmimātram] | syān matam -- dharmigrahaṇād viśiṣṭo 'tra dharmī kaścid abhipreta iti gamyate, sa tu sādhyadharmīti kuta ity āha --
children.translated_text: it necessarily implies the <s>dharmin</s>. Therefore, the statement of <s>dharmin</s>, being additional, indicates precisely the qualified <s>dharmin</s> of the <s>sādhya</s>, not the <s>dharmin</s> merely. One might think: from the mention of <s>dharmin</s>, it is understood that some qualified <s>dharmin</s> is intended here, but how [do we know] that it is the <s>sādhyadharmin</s> (property-locus of the probandum)? To this he says:
By the principle of proximity (<s>pratyāsatti</s>).

children.text:
nyāyāt | pratyāsattiś cātra dharmi[vacanasāmarthyād a]bhipreteti gamyate | vyāptau[60]tu nyāye dharmavacanenāpi dharmimātrākṣepāt[61]dharmigrahaṇavaiyarthyam | [S. 13b.] pratyāsannatā ca sādhyadharmiṇa eva, tatra
{p. 13.1} prathamaṃ he[tūpa]darśanāt | na pratyāsatteḥ sādhyadharmiparigrahaḥ | kutaḥ? |
children.translated_text: And proximity here is understood through the force of the statement of <s>dharmin</s>. But if, by the principle of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>), the statement of <s>dharma</s> also implies the <s>dharmin</s> merely, then the mention of <s>dharmin</s> would be pointless. And the proximity is precisely to the <s>sādhyadharmin</s>, because the reason is first shown there [in the thesis-locus]. [But one cannot say that] the inclusion of the <s>sādhyadharmin</s> is due to proximity. Why?
'Of the example's <s>dharmin</s> too' —

children.text:
na kevalaṃ sādhyadharmiṇaḥ pratyāsatteḥ | kadācid[62]vyāptidarśanapūrvake prayoge dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇy api prathamaṃ hetusadbhāvopadarśanāt |
 yadi na pratyāsatteḥ sādhyadharmisiddhiḥ pāriśeṣyāt tarhi bhaviṣyati | yataḥ
children.translated_text: not only of the <s>sādhyadharmin</s>, there is proximity. Because sometimes, in an application preceded by the observation of pervasion, the existence of the reason is first shown in the <s>dharmin</s> of the example as well. If the establishment of the <s>sādhyadharmin</s> is not by proximity, then it will be by elimination (<s>pāriśeṣya</s>). Because:
'By pervasion with that portion' —
which constitutes the reason,
'in the <s>dharmin</s> of the example' —

children.text: dharmasya satva(ttva)siddheḥ | na hi [T. 214a.] dṛṣṭāntam antareṇa hetoḥ sādhyena vyāptiḥ pradarśayituṃ śakyata iti manyate | tato dharmigrahaṇād vyatiricyamānāt sādhyadharmiṇa eva parigrahaḥ |
children.translated_text: the existence of <s>dharma</s> is established. For one thinks that without an example, the pervasion of the reason by the <s>sādhya</s> cannot be demonstrated. Therefore, from the statement of <s>dharmin</s> being additional, the inclusion is precisely of the <s>sādhyadharmin</s>.
'By that portion' —

children.text: iti ca tacchabdena dharmavacanākṣipto dharmī sambhantsyata iti tatsambhandhanārtham api dharmigrahaṇaṃ nāśaṅkanīyam | yatra prayojanāntaraṃ na sambhavati sa pāriśeṣyaviṣayaḥ, dharmivacanasya tv anyad api prayojanaṃ sambhāvyate | tat kutaḥ pāriśeṣyāt
children.translated_text: and by the word 'that' (<s>tad</s>), the <s>dharmin</s> implied by the statement of <s>dharma</s> will be connected — therefore it should not be suspected that the mention of <s>dharmin</s> is for the purpose of connecting with that [<s>dharmin</s>]. Where no other purpose is possible, that is the domain of elimination; but for the statement of <s>dharmin</s>, another purpose too is conceivable. So how can the inclusion of the <s>sādhyadharmin</s> be from elimination
[merely] from the statement of <s>dharmin</s>?
— thinking thus, the proponent of the established doctrine (<s>siddhāntavādin</s>) says:
'Granted [that]' —
when, by pervasion with that portion, the existence [of the reason] in the example's <s>dharmin</s> is [already] established, then again the statement of <s>dharmin</s>

children.text:
vacanaṃdṛṣṭāntadharmiṇa eva yo dharmaḥsa hetur iti niyamārthamāśaṅkyeta | tataśca cākṣuṣatvādaya eva hetavaḥsyuḥ,
na kṛtakatvādaya iti aniṣṭam eva syāt tasmād upacāraḥkartavyaḥ
children.translated_text: might be suspected to serve the purpose of restriction — [namely,] that only the <s>dharma</s> of the example's <s>dharmin</s> is a reason. And then only visual perceptibility (<s>cākṣuṣatva</s>) and the like would be reasons, not being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) and the like — which would be an undesired [consequence]. Therefore the metaphorical transfer must be applied.

children.text:
iti |
  kiṃ punastarkkaśāstre dṛṣṭaṃ kvacit niyamārthavacanam ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: But has a statement serving the purpose of restriction ever been seen in the science of logic? To this he says:
'It has been seen — in the same class (<s>sajātīya</s>) alone' —
and so forth.
There, that which [63] in the same class [64]

children.text: -- [NMu 7] ity atrā ''cāryīye hetulakṣaṇe `sajātīya e[va] satva(ttva)m' ity avadhāraṇena siddhe 'pi hetor vyatireke | kutra? | sādhyābhāve yadetat
children.translated_text: Here, in the master's definition of the logical reason, [<s>NMu</s> 7], even though the absence (<s>vyatireka</s>) of the reason is established by the restrictive particle in 'existence (<s>sattva</s>) only in what is homogeneous (<s>sajātīya</s>)' — where? — in the absence of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>), this
non-existence when that [homogeneous class] is absent (<s>asaṃstadatyaye</s>)
<s>NMu</s> 7

children.text:
iti asatva(ttva)vacanaṃ tanniyamārthamācāryeṇa vyākhyāta[m a]saty[65]eva nāstitā yathā syāt nānyatra na viruddha iti | tathehāpi dharmivacanaṃ[66]tatraiva bhāvaniyamārtham āśaṅkyeta | kadā? siddhe 'pi dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi [sa]tve(ttve) | kutaḥ?
{p. 14.1} tadaṃśavyāptivacanāt | kva bhāvaniyamārtham?
children.translated_text:
— this statement of non-existence was explained by the master as being for the purpose of restricting the rule: the non-existence should be only when [the provable is] absent, not otherwise, not in what is contradictory. And here likewise, the mention of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) might be suspected to be for the purpose of restricting the locus — when? — even though the existence in the example's property-bearer is [already] established. Why?
Because of the statement of pervadedness by a portion of that (<s>tadaṃśavyāpti</s>). Where [is it] for the purpose of restricting the locus?
In that very [place]

children.text: dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi, [T. 214b.] sati cāśaṅkāsambhave | kutaḥ? | pāriśeṣyāt sādhyadharmiparigrahaḥ | [S. 14b.] nanu apakṣadharmasyāhetutvāt na niyamārthāśaṅkā | tathā hi -- sādhyadharmeṇa vyāpto 'pi dharmo yadi kvacid dharmiṇy upalabhyeta tadā tatraiva svavyāpakapratītiṃ janayet nānyatra [pratyā]sattiviprakarṣābhyāṃ yathākramam | anupalabdhas tu kvacid dharmiṇi kathaṃ gamakaḥ? | tathābhāve[67]vā sarvatra svavyāpakaṃ gamayet pratyāsattiviprakarṣābhāvād e[vety ata] āha --
children.translated_text: in the example's property-bearer — and when there is no possibility of doubt. Why? By the method of elimination, the thesis-subject (<s>sādhyadharmin</s>) is included. But [one may object:] since a property that does not belong to the thesis-subject (<s>apakṣadharma</s>) is not a logical reason (<s>hetu</s>), there should be no suspicion of a restrictive rule. For thus: a property, even though pervaded by the provable property (<s>sādhyadharma</s>), if it is apprehended in some property-bearer, then it would generate the cognition of its own pervader in that very [property-bearer], not elsewhere, due to proximity and remoteness respectively. But how can [a property] that is not apprehended in any property-bearer be an indicator? And since commonness (<s>sādhāraṇatā</s>) is demonstrated through pervadedness by a portion of that. Therefore, if [it is] a property of the thesis-subject, then there is no pervadedness by a portion of that; if [there is] pervadedness by a portion of that, then it is not a property of the thesis-subject — thus the definition is self-contradictory.
But [one replies:] pervadedness by a portion of that (<s>tadaṃśavyāpti</s>) means precisely the existence of the pervading provable property in that logical reason when it is present there [in the thesis-subject's locus] — or the existence of the pervaded logical reason only when its pervading provable property is present — this will be stated as the characteristic of inseparable connection with what is to be proven (<s>svasādhyāvinābhāva</s>). And this does not necessarily entail occurrence in [places] other than what has been made the thesis-subject, so that a contradiction with the definition should be suspected. For thus: the logical reason, occurring in the very [thesis-subject] that has been made the thesis-subject only when the provable property is present, does indeed achieve pervadedness by a portion of that. And it is its inseparable connection with what is to be proven in the thesis-subject's property-bearer that is the basis of its indicative power, not [its occurrence in] another property-bearer. And that inseparable connection with what is to be proven (<s>svasādhyāvinābhāva</s>) is grounded in a <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>), not [merely] in the observation of co-occurrence, whether occasional or frequent, in the homogeneous instances. For a diamond is not scratchable on metal because of being earthy, like wood and so forth — even the inseparable connection of earthiness with metal-scratchability elsewhere is not a fact in this case. And if it were a rule that pervasion must be shown only in [instances] other than the thesis-subject, then how could existence (<s>sattva</s>) establish momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatā</s>)
in all entities? For one who maintains momentariness as pervading all entities has no homogeneous instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>) whatsoever [other than the thesis-subject]. Even the momentariness of flames and the like acknowledged by some is not [established] through perception, because the distinction of moments is too subtle to be discerned. And what principle is this that pervasion must be shown only elsewhere and not even in the thesis-subject's property-bearer? For thus the definition of the logical reason would be admitted as conventional, not as operating by the force of reality. Therefore, from the necessary connection with what is to be proven, the logical reason is established as pervaded by that. And that [necessary connection] is established even in the thesis-subject's property-bearer through the operation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the negative concomitance (<s>viparyaya</s>). Therefore, there is no need whatsoever
for occurrence elsewhere. For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere:

in [the definition beginning with] 'and so forth,' there too, only one possessing the provable property is called the homogeneous instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>). Therefore, this amounts to: 'presence only when the provable property exists.' And from that, the actual status as a homogeneous instance (<s>sapakṣatva</s>) of that property-bearer that possesses that [provable] property is not excluded — since it is impossible to exclude that [status] by the thesis-nature characterized as being established through the desire expressed as 'wished to be proven' (<s>sādhyatveneṣṭa</s>). Therefore, since the statement of pervadedness by a portion of that denotes inseparable connection with what is to be proven, grounded in necessary connection — because otherwise that [statement] would be inapplicable — occurrence elsewhere is not necessarily entailed. So how was this objection raised? True, this should indeed not be objected, if the necessary connection of every logical reason with what is to be proven could be ascertained by a <s>pramāṇa</s> in the very property-bearer that has been made the thesis-subject. Just as, for the essential-nature reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>) characterized by existence (<s>sattva</s>), [there is] identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) with momentariness as the provable, through the operation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> [that establishes] the negative concomitance (<s>viparyaya</s>). But for the effect-reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>), [whose necessary connection is with] the property-bearer that has been made the thesis-subject — [and for] some essential-nature reason — the necessary connection established through perception and non-apprehension (<s>pratyakṣānupalambha</s>)
how could it be grasped regarding an imperceptible provable property? Therefore, the establishment of that [necessary connection] is only elsewhere. Since [the property], when it requires that qualifier, would by not occurring elsewhere [result in] uncommonness — this was objected to as a mere possibility. For then, [a reason] not occurring elsewhere, [would fail] the negative concomitance with the absence of the provable (<s>sādhyaviparītavyatireka</s>) ................ ......................... since the impossibility of being outside both [the homogeneous and heterogeneous classes], by the exclusion from the provable's occurrence in that property-bearer and by universal inclusion, it becomes a reason for doubt (<s>saṃśayahetu</s>) in that [case]. One might think: for the purpose of recalling the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the necessary connection which was previously operative, grasped, and [then] forgotten regarding the existence of [the property] in some locus, occurrence elsewhere needs to be considered. This word 'archer' (<s>dhanurdhara</s>), though a common term, by its capacity and so forth applies to one of preeminent quality. For regarding <s>Pārtha</s>, archery is already established, so there is no suspicion of impossibility. But [the question arises:] does such supreme [archery] exist elsewhere or
not? When the doubt concerns connection with another, when it is said '<s>Pārtha</s> is an archer,' then the exclusion of connection with another is naturally obtained, because of the mutual opposition of the two alternatives — that which is to be established and that which is [merely] suspected — [such that] by the indication of one, the exclusion of connection with another comes by the force of logic. Thus here, when there is doubt regarding the thesis-subject — 'does this property exist or not?' — when it is said '<s>pakṣadharma</s>' (property of the thesis-subject), [it means] it is indeed a property of the thesis-subject, not a non-property. And the property, being dependent [on the thesis-subject], is a qualifier; through that, impossibility is excluded, not connection with another — since by pervadedness by a portion of that (<s>tadaṃśavyāpti</s>), that [connection with another] has been established, [and] there is no doubt in the example.

Section: 8. Pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) as having the nature of both the pervaded and the pervader.

body.text:
tasya pakṣadharmasya sato vyāptiḥ -- yo vyāpnoti yaś ca vyāpyate [tadubhayadharmatayā[87]pratīteḥ | yadā vyāpakadharmatayā vivakṣyate ta]dā vyāpakasya gamyasya[88]| tatreti [T. 217a.] sat saptamy arthapradhānam etat nādhārapradhānam, dharmāṇāṃ dharmādhāratvā saṃbhavāt |
{p. 18.1} tenāyam arthaḥ -- yatra dharmiṇi vyāpyam asti tatra sarvvatra bhāva eva[89]vyāpakasya svagato dharmo vyāptiḥ | tata[ś ca vyāpakabhāvāpekṣayā vyāpyasyaiva vyāptatāpratītiḥ] [S. 19a.] | na tv evam avadhāryate | vyāpakasyaiva tatra bhāva iti | hetvabhāvaprasaṅgād[90]avyāpakasyāpi mūrttatvādes tatra bhāvāt | nāpi `tatraive'[91]ti[92]

prayatnānantarīyakatvāder ahetutāpatteḥ[93]| sādhāraṇaś ca hetuḥ syāt | nityatvasya prameyeṣv eva bhāvāt | yadā tu vyāpyadharmatā (rmatayā) vivakṣā vyāptes tadā vyāpyasya vā gamakasya tatraiva vyāpake gamye sati | yatra dharmiṇi vyāpako 'sti tatraiva bhāvo, na tadabhāve 'pi vyāptir iti | atrāpi vyāpyasyaiva tatra bhāva ity avadhāraṇaṃ hetvabhāvaprasakter[94]eva nāśritam, avyāpyasyāpi[95]tatra bhāvāt | nāpi vyāpyasya tatra bhāva eveti sapakṣaikadeśavṛtter[96]hetutvaprāpteḥ[97]| sādhāraṇasya [ca] hetutvaṃ syāt | prameyatvasya nityeṣv avaśyaṃ bhāvād iti | vyāpyavyāpakadharmatāsaṃvarṇanaṃ

children.translated_text:
because of the unwanted consequence that [things like] being immediately preceded by effort (<s>prayatnānantarīyakatva</s>) and the like would not be reasons. And [the reason] would be a common reason (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>), since permanence exists only in provable things (<s>prameya</s>). But when pervasion is intended as having the nature of the pervaded, then [it pertains to] the pervaded, i.e., the indicator, [existing] only there — in the pervader, the thing to be indicated — when [the pervader] exists. Wherever the pervader exists in a property-bearer, only there is the existence [of the pervaded], not even in the absence of that — this is pervasion. Here too, the restriction 'the pervaded alone exists there' is not adopted, because of the unwanted consequence of the elimination [of valid reasons], since even a non-pervaded [property] such as impermanence exists there. Nor [can one say] 'the pervaded exists only there,' because of the unwanted consequence that a [reason] occurring in only one part of the similar instances (<s>sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti</s>) would qualify as a reason. And a common [reason] would [erroneously] be a [valid] reason, since provability (<s>prameyatva</s>) necessarily exists in permanent things too.
But the description of pervasion as having the nature of the pervaded and pervader is for the purpose of showing that the cognition of pervasion does not have a single form (<s>ekākāra</s>) in both cases, like conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>). For in the former case, the determination is by exclusion of non-connection (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>), and in the latter by exclusion of other-connection (<s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s>) — so how could pervasion have a single form in both? As it has been stated —

children.text: liṅge liṅgībhavaty eva liṅginy evetarat punaḥ|
children.translated_text: In [the presence of] the mark, the marked [thing] necessarily exists; in [the presence of] the marked, the other [i.e., the mark necessarily exists];
if the restriction were reversed, there would be no connection between mark and marked. ||
By this, the defect stated by the Master regarding indication through the force of conjunction —

children.text: etenācāryeṇa saṃyogabalāt gamakatve yo doṣa uktaḥ --
na ca kenacid aṃśena na saṃyogīhutāśanaḥ|
children.translated_text: 'Fire is not in any respect not conjoined [with smoke];
nor is smoke [not conjoined with fire] in every respect' —
'from this it would follow that smoke indicates [fire completely]' ||

iti |
sa iha nāvataratīty ākhyātaṃ bhavati | tathā hi -- saṃyogasya ubhayatrāviśeṣāt eṣa prasaṅgo na tu vyāpteḥ | na hi yādṛśī
{p. 19.1} vyāpakadharme vyāptiḥ tādṛśy eva vyāpyadharma iti | tathā cāha -
children.translated_text: — that [defect] does not apply here, as has been explained. For since conjunction is non-distinct in both [directions], this unwanted consequence [arises], but not from pervasion. For the pervasion in the pervader-property is not of the same kind as that in the pervaded-property. And so he says —
'Although the connection is bi-located — in the co-existent and in the marked —

children.text: ādhārādheyavad vṛttis tasya saṃyogivan na tu
children.translated_text: its operation is like that of container and contained, not like that of conjunction.' ||

|| iti | [S. 20a.]
tena vyāpako vyāpyo na bhavati vyāpyaś ca [na] vyāpaka iti |
children.translated_text: Therefore, the pervader does not become the pervaded, and the pervaded does not become the pervader.
'pervaded by a portion of that — [is] the reason' (<s>tadaṃśena vyāpto hetuḥ</s>) —

children.text: iti vacanāt na saṃyogipakṣokto doṣaḥ | nā 'py ubhayor ggamyagamakatāprasaṅgaḥ, yathoktād hetulakṣaṇād vyāpakasyaiva gamyatvapratīteḥ, vyāpyasyaiva gamakatāsampratyayādīti |
children.translated_text: because of this statement, the defect stated in the conjunction-thesis does not [apply]. Nor is there the unwanted consequence that both would be the thing to be cognized and the indicator [of each other], since from the definition of reason as stated, only the pervader is understood as the thing to be cognized, and only the pervaded is understood as the indicator — and so forth.

body.translated_text:
The pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) of that which is a property of the thesis-subject — that which pervades and that which is pervaded — [is understood] through the cognition of having the nature of both. When [pervasion] is intended as having the nature of the pervader, then [it pertains] to the pervader, i.e., the thing to be cognized. 'Therein' (<s>tatra</s>) — this locative has its principal force as [denoting] the object, not the substratum, since it is possible for properties to be the substratum of [other] properties.
Hence the meaning is this: wherever the pervaded exists in a property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), there in every case the existence of the pervader is its own inherent property — that is pervasion. And therefore, the cognition of pervadedness belongs to the pervaded alone, with respect to the existence of the pervader. But it is not determined thus: 'the pervader alone exists there' — because of the unwanted consequence of the absence of a [valid] reason, since even a non-pervader such as corporeality and the like exists there. Nor [can one say] 'there alone' —

Section: 9. Indication that pervasion has the forms of positive concomitance and negative concomitance.

children.translated_text: 'a property of the thesis-subject,'
'pervaded by a portion of that' —

children.text: ity etad dhetulakṣaṇaṃ tataḥ pakṣadharmatvaṃ tadaṃśavyāptiś ceti dvirūpo hetuḥ syāt, anyatra ca trirūpa uktaḥ tat kathaṃ na vyāghātaḥ? ity āha
children.translated_text: if this is the definition of reason, then the reason would be two-fold: being a property of the thesis-subject and being pervaded by a portion of that. But elsewhere it is stated as three-fold — how then is there no contradiction? To this he says —
'by this' —
by this statement of pervasion by a portion of that —
'positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) or negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) is stated' —

children.text: veditavya iti sambandhaḥ [T. 218a.] | anvayavyatirekarūpatvād vyāpter iti bhāvaḥ | tathā hi -- ya[100]eva yenānvito[101]yan[102]nivṛttau ca nivṛttate sa[103]eva tena[104]vyāpta ucyata iti tadātmakatvād vyāpter vyāptivacanenānvayavyatirekābhidhānam | tato vyāptivacanena rūpadvayābhidhānāt na vyāghāta iti | [S. 20b.]
children.translated_text: 'is to be understood' — this is the connection. The import is: because pervasion has the form of positive and negative concomitance. Namely: that which is accompanied by something, and in the absence of which that [something] also ceases — that alone is said to be pervaded by that. Since pervasion is identical with that [i.e., anvaya and vyatireka], by the statement of pervasion, positive and negative concomitance are stated. Therefore, since two forms are stated by the single statement of pervasion, there is no contradiction.

Section: 10. The ascertainment of pervasion by perception or by inference.

children.text: niścayaśca tayor naikenaiva pramāṇena api tu yathāsvam
children.translated_text: And the ascertainment of those two is not by a single <s>pramāṇa</s> alone, but rather each by its own [appropriate means] —

children.text: | yasya yad ātmīyaṃ pramāṇaṃ niścāyakaṃ tena | yasya ca yat niścāyakaṃ pramāṇaṃ tad uttaratra vakṣyati |
children.translated_text: whichever [concomitance] has whichever <s>pramāṇa</s> as its own ascertainer, [is ascertained] by that. And which <s>pramāṇa</s> ascertains which — that he will state later.
'positive concomitance or negative concomitance' —

children.text: iti tulyakakṣatāsūcanārtho `vā'śabdaḥ | tena sādharmyavaidharmyavatoḥ prayogayor ekenaiva dvitīyagater vidhipratiṣedharūpatayā vyāvṛttibhede 'pi paramārthatas tādātmyāt nobhayopadarśanam iti sūcitaṃ bhavati | vyatireko hi sādhyanivṛttau liṅgasya nivṛttidharmakatvaṃ[105]svabhāvabhūto dharma ity anvayarūpatā vastuto 'sya na virudhyate |
children.translated_text: the word 'or' (<s>vā</s>) is for the purpose of indicating equal standing. By this, it is indicated that of the two formulations — by similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) and by dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>) — by one alone the other is reached; although they differ in form as affirmation and negation, since in ultimate reality they are identical, there is no need to present both. For negative concomitance — the property of the mark's cessation upon the cessation of the <s>sādhya</s> — is an essential property, so in reality its nature as positive concomitance is not contradicted.
'and the property of the thesis-subject' —
what [about it]?
'is ascertained by one's own [appropriate] <s>pramāṇa</s>' —
'by perception' (<s>pratyakṣeṇa</s>) —

although [perception] has the form of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) by its own nature, it is well-established [as ascertaining the mark] because it generates the immediately subsequent universal-concept (<s>sāmānyavikalpa</s>).

children.text: upacārato niścaya ucyate -- pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvino vikalpasyānadhigatārthādhigantṛtvābhāvaṃ darśayituṃ | tena yady api sāmānyarūpaṃ liṅgam avasthāpyate tathāpi svalakṣaṇapratītir eva tadvyavasthānibandhanam iti pratyakṣataḥ pakṣadharmasya sādhyadharmiṇi prasiddhir ucyate | etac cānantaram eva vyaktīkariṣyate |
children.translated_text: The ascertainment is said [to be] by perception figuratively (<s>upacāra</s>) — to show that the conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) following perception does not have the character of cognizing what has not been [previously] cognized. Therefore, even though the mark is established in its universal form (<s>sāmānyarūpa</s>), nevertheless, the cognition of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) alone is the basis for that establishment — thus, the establishment of the property of the thesis-subject in the <s>sādhyadharmin</s> is said to be from perception. And this will be clarified immediately after.
'or from inference, the establishment of the property of the thesis-subject in the <s>sādhyadharmin</s>' —

[this is] the ascertainment.
And because of the distinction between the <s>pramāṇa</s> and its result —
'from inference' —
[i.e.,] 'by inference there is ascertainment' — he says.
'Here, the examples' —
'in due order' —
'in the appropriate place' —
'of smoke' —
of smoke-in-general — the ascertainment is from perception — thus.

body.translated_text: And these two [positive and negative concomitance] are ascertained — since the context concerns the indicating reason.

na tu nivṛttimātraṃ tuccharūpam
