children.translated_text:
But those who explain [it thus]: in the employment through similarity, the declaration of the absence of the reason in the counter-class (<s>vipakṣa</s>) alone — where that [provable] is absent — should be such that [the absence obtains] only there, not elsewhere — because of the unwanted consequence that in what is other than the counter-class, or what is contradictory, there would be absence of the reason, and hence the unwanted consequence of exclusion from what is merely contradictory — [they say] the employment through negative concomitance is for the purpose of declaring this restriction. But that purpose is also improper. Why? Because the counter-class-hood is not of what is merely other or contradictory alone — for: what is merely other as a counter-class is one possessing a different property, or one that is different — not what does not contain the intended property; and what is merely contradictory — [characterized] only by the contradiction of being unable to coexist, not by [the contradiction] characterized as existing in mutual exclusion — is also a counter-class. [For such a counter-class:] regarding an object possessing properties other than impermanence, such as non-self and the like, since being-produced and the like occur [there], there would be the unwanted consequence of the absence of the reason. And when heat is the provable, since the reason characterized as fire would be excluded not only from what is contradictory, namely cold, but also from what is neither hot nor cold, i.e., from what is merely other — fire would not invariably grasp heat — this would be the fault for that [position]. Against that, the master stated: if the counter-class-hood of one [alone] is accepted, then let [it] be of that which is the absence of that [provable] alone,
not of what is contradictory or other, since those [latter] exist elsewhere too — in what does not contain the intended property and in what is contradictory — [and] without the absence of that [provable],

children.text: tayor anyaviruddhatvāyogāt[323] | na tv asmākaṃ[324]trividham api vipakṣam icchatām[325], vivakṣitadharmānāśrayaṃ cā 'nyam iti bhāvaḥ |
children.translated_text: there would be no possibility of their being other or contradictory. But for us who accept the counter-class as threefold — [including] what does not contain the intended property as ‘other’ — this is the purport.

body.translated_text: But [the objection:] it was improperly said that the reason has a twofold employment. Because the reason is threefold — positive-only (<s>anvayin</s>), negative-only (<s>vyatirekin</s>), and positive-and-negative (<s>anvayavyatirekin</s>) — according to the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>; therefore its employment should be said to be threefold — through similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>), through dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>), and through both similarity and dissimilarity — to this he says:

children.text: ti sato naśvarasvabhāvatvena | satva(ttva)lakṣaṇasya hetoḥ kṣaṇikatvasvabhāvatveneti yāvat | pṛcchataś cāyam abhiprāyaḥ -- iha [T. 258b.] dvividhāḥ santaḥ -- kṛtakāś ca ghaṭādayaḥ akṛtakāś cākāśādayaḥ | tatra ye tāvad akṛtakās te
children.translated_text: means: by virtue of having a perishable essential nature as an existent thing. That is to say: by virtue of the reason characterized as <s>sattva</s> (being/existence) having <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> (momentariness) as its essential nature. And the questioner's intent is this: here, existing things are of two kinds — produced (<s>kṛtaka</s>) things such as pots and the like, and unproduced (<s>akṛtaka</s>) things such as space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like. Therein, those that are unproduced —
'What is existent without a cause is permanent'
<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 4.1.1

children.text:
iti nityalakṣaṇayogād anityā eva na bhavanti kuta eva kṣaṇikāḥ? iti na satva(ttva)sya kṣaṇikatvasvabhāvatā | ye 'pi santaḥ kṛtakās teṣām api mudgarādyanvayavyatirekānuvidhāyitayā vināśasya sahetukatvāt taddhetvasannidhāv
vināśāt kṛtakātmano 'pi satva(ttva)sya kṣaṇikatvasvabhāvatā na samasty eveti nānvayavyatirekayoḥ sambhava iti | avaśyaṃ ca vināśo daṇḍādyanvayavyatirekānuvidhāyī, dṛṣṭatvāt | tathā hi -
children.translated_text: — by virtue of conforming to the definition of permanence, they are simply not impermanent; how much less momentary? Thus <s>sattva</s> does not have <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> as its essential nature. And even those existing things that are produced — because their destruction, following the presence and absence of a club and the like, is caused, and because in the absence of that cause there is no destruction — even the <s>sattva</s> of what has a produced nature does not have <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> as its essential nature at all; therefore neither positive nor negative concomitance is possible. And destruction necessarily follows the presence and absence of a club and the like, because this is observed. For thus:
'In the proximity of the conditions of destruction — impact, fire-contact, and the like —
[things] undergo association with destruction; but destruction [does not arise] from pots and the like [spontaneously].' ||
And even elsewhere [in cases like sprouts and the like]

anyatrāpi[328]cānvayavyatirekānuvidhānam eva hetumattāvyavahāranibandhanam abhyupeyatesaugatair api, tad ihāpy[329]astīti kin na tadvyavahāraḥ pravarttyate? iti |
 nanu cānvayaniścayaṃ pratipādayatā bādhakapramāṇavṛttivaśāt tatsvabhāvatā pūrvam eva pratipāditā `anvayaniścayo 'pi svabhāvahetau' ityādi vicanāt | tat kuto 'sya pūrvapakṣasyāvasaraḥ? | satyam, kintupūrvācāryaiḥkṛtakatvasya kṣaṇikatāyāṃ sādhyāyāṃ paraiḥ kṛtakānām ante 'vaśyaṃ hetunibandhanavināśopagamāt taddhetvayogapratipādanenānapekṣā vināśaṃ prati viparyaye bādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ tādātmyaprasādhakam uktaṃ tat prasaṅgamukhena[330]kṛtakalakṣaṇasyaiva sattvasya tadātmatām[331]gamayati nānyasya [T. 259a.] iti darśayitum | arthakriyāvirodhalakṣaṇaṃ[332]tu sarvasya sattvasya iti vastumātreṇa[333]{p. 77.1} prāg uktam api vipañcayituṃ pūrvapakṣopanyāsaḥ | akṛtakalakṣaṇaṃ tu sattvaṃ na sambhavaty eva, niyāmakaṃ hetum antareṇa deśakālasvabhāvaniyamāyogāt | tataḥpūrvācāryair na [S. 81a.] tasyaikāṅgavaikalyād eva
children.translated_text: , this very following of presence and absence [of the cause] is accepted even by the <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) as the ground of the usage of 'having a cause' — so here too [in the case of destruction] it is present; why then is that usage not applied? But has not the essential-nature-ness [of <s>sattva</s> and <s>kṣaṇikatva</s>] been established earlier by the force of a contradicting <s>pramāṇa</s>, in demonstrating the ascertainment of positive concomitance, from the statement 'the ascertainment of positive concomitance too, in the essential-nature reason' and so forth? Then whence the occasion for this <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (objection)? True; but the earlier masters (<s>pūrvācārya</s>) — because the opponents accept that for produced things there is necessarily destruction caused by a factor at the end — by demonstrating the absence of that causal factor, stated a contradicting <s>pramāṇa</s> establishing identity (<s>tādātmya</s>), independent of destruction. That [argument] through the door of an incidental consequence shows that it is only <s>sattva</s> characterized as being-produced (<s>kṛtaka</s>) that has that identity [with momentariness], not any other. But the [<s>pramāṇa</s>] characterized by contradiction with causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāvirodha</s>) applies to all <s>sattva</s> in general — so the presentation of the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> [here] is for the purpose of elucidating in detail what was previously stated only in general terms for the real entity as such. And <s>sattva</s> characterized as unproduced (<s>akṛtaka</s>) is simply impossible, because without a determining cause, restriction of place, time, and nature is impossible. Therefore, because of the deficiency in even one component of that [unproduced-permanent entity], the earlier masters, [recognizing] 'what is existent without a cause is permanent' —
'What is existent without a cause is permanent'
<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 4.1.1

children.translated_text: — [recognizing] the impossibility of permanence [for what exists] — did not make an effort regarding its identity [with momentariness]. But the author of the treatise [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] will demonstrate, in general, the momentary-essential-nature of <s>sattva</s>, and also of what is characterized as produced, and even of what is distant in place, time, and nature — its identity [with momentariness] by the very standing of the real entity through contradiction with causal efficacy — [and] by the consequence of the absence [of the entity] as soon as it arises, since the opponents' [accepted position of] necessarily-future destruction being causeless yields no distinguishing feature [between their view and the Buddhist one].

body.translated_text: If, in the essential-nature reason, the essential-nature-ness (<s>sādhyasvabhāvatā</s>) of the proving property is the ground for both positive and negative concomitance — and by the application possessing concordance and discordance being stated, through the implication of identity (<s>tādātmyākṣepa</s>), the implication of the other is also implicitly stated — then [one might argue that] the essential-nature-ness of those two [<s>sādhya</s> and <s>sādhana</s>], which is the ground, must be established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, not merely apprehended from words alone. body.translated_text: Section: 11. Examining the essential-nature-ness of destruction in entities, in order to refute externally-caused destruction

body.text: tatrapūrvācāryoktaṃ `sarvasya sataḥ kṛtakasyāvaśyamante hetukṛto vināśa iti' yaḥ parair iṣyate taṃ pratyanapekṣatvaṃ kyāpayitum upakramate --

children.translated_text: thus. If then destruction has no [external] cause, whence would there be the destruction of those produced, existing things that necessarily [must undergo destruction]? For no essential nature [arises] accidentally — so he says:
'From [their very] essential nature alone' —

thus.

from impact and the like,
'there is no arising of destruction.'

children.translated_text: For thus: at the time of fire-contact and the like, we observe a triad — that very fuel-wood and the like [which is] the thing to be destroyed, the charcoal and the like [which is] an alternative state, and the absence characterized by the cessation of wood and the like, which is of a void nature. There is nothing else in which the operation of fire-contact and the like could be conceived. And in this extent
of the course of real entities, the capacity of the cause of destruction is nowhere tenable. Because:
'For the cause of destruction does not make the essential nature of an entity' — of fuel-wood and the like, which has arisen in a stable form from its own causes —
'[into] its very essential nature' —
characterized by instability;
'it does not make [it so].'
Why?

of fuel-wood and the like,
'from its own causes'
'alone'

children.translated_text: when this is accepted, because fire and the like have no operation on fuel-wood and the like, the fuel-wood and the like remain in their [prior] condition. And therefore, just as before fire-contact there is apprehension of fuel-wood and the like, and also other causal efficacy to be accomplished by it — so too even at the production of charcoal and the like, the consequence is that apprehension and the like [of the fuel-wood should persist]. 'But since the alternative entity has the nature of <s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s> (posterior absence), at its production the fuel-wood and the like, having been destroyed, being non-existent — how can there be such a consequence of apprehension and the like?' — True; [but] it is considered thus: [you] must state the ground for the determination that the charcoal and the like is the destruction of all of the fuel-wood and other things, and not such a [destruction] of other things like cows and the like. If [you say:] 'when that [alternative entity] is present, the cessation of that [prior entity follows]' — oh, what verbal dexterity! Since you do not accept that cessation is of a void nature, you call that very alternative entity — charcoal and the like — the cessation. Then this meaning is accomplished: the charcoal and the like is the destruction of wood and the like because of the existence of charcoal and the like when charcoal and the like exist! But the existence of charcoal and the like when charcoal and the like exist is not [due to it being] a cause of itself, since self-causation is impossible. And if [you say:] 'from fire and the like, there is the production of charcoal and the like; from the destruction of fuel-wood and the like, [comes] the existence of charcoal and the like; therefore this [charcoal] has the nature of destruction' — what is this 'destruction' (<s>upamarda</s>)? If it is cessation, that is characterized precisely as charcoal and the like — so it does not differ from the previous [position]. Therefore, the wood and the like ceases of its own accord, and from fire and the like there is the birth of charcoal and the like — just that is fine. Otherwise, how would the consequence of the apprehension and the like of wood and the like
not obtain?

children.translated_text: Moreover: if the alternative entity is <s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s>, then for those modifications that arise without a subsequent modification — such as lamp-light, cognition, and the like — which are destroyed, which alternative entity is to be determined as [their] destruction? If [you say] 'they too have destruction as a modification into an imperceptible state (<s>avyaktatā</s>) or into their own essential nature (<s>ātmabhāva</s>)' — no, because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the existence of an imperceptible form-state of lamp-light and the like. For if the imperceptible state is an occurrence in the form of a power (<s>śakti</s>), then since the form of a power is inferred only from seeing the effect, in the absence of that [effect], how could lamp-light and the like be conceived as persisting in the form of a power? Or if the imperceptible state is an occurrence in the form of being deficient in the capacity for apprehension — even here, there is simply no <s>pramāṇa</s> for persisting in that form. And the discerning do not heed a statement lacking <s>pramāṇa</s>. And since the self (<s>ātman</s>) is non-existent, how could cognition and the like have a modification or transformation into that state? Since the counter-measure has been provided elsewhere, it is not elaborated here — enough with this digression. [If] one thinks: 'because of being covered (<s>āvṛta</s>) by the alternative entity — charcoal and the like — apprehension and the like of fuel-wood do not occur' — to this he says:

children.translated_text: and so forth. The intended meaning is this: if destruction (dhvaṃsa) is merely cessation, of a void nature (tuccharūpa), without contact with any alternative entity, then no operation of a causal agent is at all possible with respect to it, since such [operation] is possible only in a thing that comes into being (bhavanadharmin). [If one says:] 'Since that [destruction] too is accepted as coming into being when it had not been before, the status of being an effect is not contradicted' — no, because since the thing-that-comes-into-being acquires the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpatā), it would lose its status as absence (abhāvatva). For what comes into being (bhavati) is considered a positive entity (bhāva), and there is no other ground for the application of the word 'bhāva' beyond this, even for sprouts and the like. [If one says:] 'The ground is capacity for causal efficacy (arthakriyāsāmarthya)' — then how can that which is devoid of all capacity be an object of cognition? For what is without a cause is not an object of cognition, because of the absurd consequence [that anything could be cognized]. Or if it is not an object [of cognition], how can its having a cause be ascertained? Or [how can it have] substantiality (vastutā)? — by which one says 'that very thing of void nature is a real entity.' Or if it does produce cognition, how can it not possess causal capacity? [If one says:] 'How can that which is not the object of the cognition "it exists" be a positive entity?' — [we reply:] then how also can it have the status of being an effect? [If one says:] 'Because it exists when its own cause is present' — then how can it not be the object of the cognition 'it exists'? For thus: if it is cognized as 'it exists when its own cause is present,' then it should be cognized as 'it exists' and so forth, since the learned say 'sat' (existent) because it is (asti). And there is no ultimate difference in meaning among the words 'asti' (it is), 'bhavati' (it comes into being), 'bhāvaḥ' (entity),

children.translated_text: 'san' (existing) — among these words there is no [ultimate] difference in meaning. [If one says:] 'It comes into being precisely as having the nature of absence' — no, because of self-contradiction (vyāhatatvāt). For that which is called absence because it does not come into being — how can it be designated as 'coming into being'? [If one says:] 'Because it does not appear in the cognition of itself with any established form, it is not a positive entity' — then the absurd consequence would follow that the eyes and the like, which are entirely beyond [direct] perception, would also be absences. [If one says:] 'No, because they appear as having the form of being causes of cognition' — [we reply:] no, because this [destruction] too appears as having the form of being something that comes into being (bhavitṛrūpa). And how can that which is distinct from every form have a connection with coming-into-being? For coming-into-being is the emergence with some form. And since the appearance of this [destruction] as an object of cognition and as having the form of a cause thereof is equal [to that of the eyes etc.], and since what is not a cause cannot be an object — but for us, cognitions of absence are entirely objectless, arising in accordance with the maturation of their own latent impressions (vāsanā). And if absence has the nature of coming-into-being, how would the nominal negation (prasajyapratiṣedha) differ from exclusion (paryudāsa)? [If one says:] 'It differs from exclusion by the affirmation of something having the form of non-existence (asadrūpa)' — no, because something having the form of non-existence contradicts coming-into-being. For 'it comes into being' is connected with being, with existence (sattā). Then how can there be an affirmation of something having the form of existence [in what is non-existent]? Then exclusion alone would be the single meaning of the negative particle (nañ), since in all cases affirmation predominates. Or even that [exclusion] would not hold. For if something were excluded from something, then something different from that would be touched upon by the exclusion of that. But that is not the case. When it is said 'cessation of everything occurs,' something else entirely is being affirmed. And likewise by this [negation], only some other real entity would be stated, not a distinction between the two. And without distinction, there is no exclusion. And there would be a statement of what is not under discussion — since when the cessation of an entity is under discussion, some other real entity having the nature of non-existence is being affirmed. And this [destruction] is not non-existent by its own nature, because the status of being an effect of what is non-existent even by its own nature is contradicted. But in terms of other forms, every real entity is non-existent-natured, so there is no distinction of this [destruction] from pots and the like. Or let this absence exist [as produced] from fire and the like — [if] when that [fire etc.] is present, why are the wood and the like not apprehended? For thus: since fire and the like have accomplished their purpose in another activity, fuel-wood and the like, unceased from them, should be apprehended as before. [If one says:] 'Because destruction arises through the suppression (upamardda) of that [fuel-wood]' — how is that suppression [accomplished]? Not by pradhvaṃsābhāva (posterior absence), because that is absent during the time the fuel-wood exists. Not by fire and the like, because their operation is accepted only in the manifestation of destruction. And the arisen posterior absence does not harm fuel-wood and the like, because of the absurd consequence of simultaneity. And if destruction destroys [by means of further destruction], the triad of alternatives remains in the same condition. And hence an infinite regress (anavasthā). [If one says:] 'That very destruction, born from fire and the like, is the cessation of fuel-wood, and therefore it is not apprehended' — how can one thing be the cessation of another? — because of the absurd consequence [that anything could be the cessation of anything]. And if this [destruction] has a cause, why does it not experience differentiation of itself due to the differentiation of that [cause]? Rice-sprouts, barley-sprouts, and the like, experiencing entirely distinct self-differentiation precisely due to the differentiation of their causes, are ascertained by direct perception (adhyakṣa) itself. But destruction, characterized as mere cessation without contact with any alternative entity, is not like that — because, its void nature being uniform despite the differentiation of causes such as impact, fire-contact, and the like, it appears [uniformly] in the cognition of itself. For we do not perceive any other form there beyond the mere emptiness of the entity (bhāvaśūnyatā). And this has been examined in detail in the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi) — let that suffice here for now. Therefore, at the time of contact with fire and the like,

And since there is no pramāṇa weightier than perception, such that through establishing difference in its object it would experience invalidation and thus become a non-pramāṇa — anticipating this, he says: 'Therefore' — precisely because of the [respective] natures of being generative and non-generative, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties, 'of those two states' — of the generative and non-generative states of the seed and the like,
a real distinction,
a difference of essential nature,
is to be ascertained,

children.text:
adhyavasātavyaḥ | yathā hi śālibījaṃ tadaṅkurajananasvabhāvaṃ tadbhāve śālyaṅkurabhavadarśanāt pratyakṣato 'vagamyate, yavabījaṃ cātajjananasvabhāvam tadbhave śālyaṅkurānupalabdhyā[356][T. 265a.] tadviviktayavabījagrāhipratyakṣarūpayā
pratīyate tathā 'trāpy avasthādvaye śālibījasya tadaṅkuraviviktāviviktāvasthāgrāhipratyakṣabalād eva svāṅkurajanakājanakasvabhāvatā kinna niścīyate? | iṣyata evāvasthayor bhedo 'vasthāvatas tv abheda iti cet | na | tasyāvasthārūpavivekinā rūpāntareṇa pratyakṣe pratibhāsanaprasaṅgāt | na hi yadanātmarūpavivekena svajñāne na pratibhāsate tasya pratyakṣatā yuktā | avasthātadvatoḥ svabhāvabhedābhāvāt [S. 88a.] kathaṃ rūpāntareṇa pratibhāsanam? iti cet | nanv avasthābhyo 'navāptarūpabhedasyāvasthānām ivātmanas tadbhede saty abhedo na saṅgacchate | [T. 265b.] tataś cāsyāvasthānām ivātmabhedam anubhavataḥ katham avasthātṛtvam? | avasthābhede 'py abhinnarūpasya tathā vyavasthānāt kathañcidbhedasyāpi bhāvād adoṣa iti cet | yadi yam ātmānaṃ purodhaya `ayam avasthātā, avasthāś cemāḥ' iti bhaṇyate tenāvasthātadvator bhedas tadā bheda eveti `kathañcit' ity andhapadam etat | tato 'sya pratyakṣatāyāṃ anātmarūpavivekinā
rūpāntareṇāvabhāsanaprasaṅgo na nivarttate | atha tenātmanā 'bhedaḥ[357]| avasthāvad bhedaprasaṅgo 'vasthātuḥ, tadvad avasthānām abhedasya vā | tayor api kathañcid bhedābhedāv iti cet | tayos tarhy avasthātadvad ātmanor bhedavatoḥ kathañcid abhedanimittaṃ rūpāntaram iṣṭaṃ syāt | {p. 85.1} tathā ca tasyāpi tābhyāṃ kathañcidbhedaḥ, anyathā tadekasvabhāvād atyantam abhedād avasthātadvatoḥ
children.translated_text: is to be determined. For just as a rice-seed is understood through perception to have the essential nature of producing that sprout, from the observation of the rice-sprout arising in its presence, and a barley-seed is understood to not have that generative nature, through the non-apprehension of a rice-sprout in its presence — [which is understood] through perception that grasps the barley-seed as distinct from that — so too here, in the two states of the rice-seed, why should its essential nature of being generative and non-generative of its own sprout not be ascertained precisely through the force of perception that grasps [its] states as distinct and non-distinct from that sprout? If [you say:] 'The difference of the states is accepted, but the identity of the possessor of states [is maintained]' — no, because there would be the absurd consequence that it would appear in perception with a form that is distinct from the form of its states. For it is not reasonable that something which does not appear in its own cognition as distinguished from its non-self-form should be [called] perception. If [you say:] 'Since there is no essential-nature difference between the states and their possessor, how could there be appearance with a different form?' — But for the possessor of states, which has not obtained a difference of form from the states, just as for the states themselves, when there is difference in those [states], non-difference [of the possessor] is not coherent. And therefore, for this [possessor] which experiences a difference of self just like the states, how can it be the possessor of states? If [you say:] 'Even when the states differ, because something with a non-different form is established in that way, since there is also a certain kind of difference, there is no fault' — if the difference between the state-possessor and the states is maintained by positing a certain self, [saying] 'this is the state-possessor, and these are the states,' then it is simply difference, and [the word] 'in a certain way' is a blind term. Therefore the absurd consequence of its appearing with a different form distinct from its own nature, in the case of its being perceived, is not averted. If, on the other hand, there is non-difference with that self — then the absurd consequence of the state-possessor [having] difference like the states, or of the states [having] non-difference like it. If [you say:] 'Between those two also there is a certain kind of difference and non-difference' — then for those two, the self of the state-possessor and the states, which possess difference, a further form would have to be accepted as the ground of their 'certain kind' of non-difference. And of that too there would be a 'certain kind' of difference from those two — otherwise, because of having the same essential nature as those, from absolute non-difference of the state-possessor and the states,

children.text:
parasparam atyantaṃ bhedābhedau prasajyeyātām[358]| rūpāntarasya kathañcidbhede [S. 88b.] tannibandhanam aparaṃ rūpam, tathā 'syāpi tadanyad ity aparimitarūpataivaikaikasya vastunaḥ samāsajyeta | na cāparimitarūpapratibhāsi pratyakṣam anubhavāmaḥ | ananubhavantaś ca kathaṃ tatkalpanayā ''tmanaivātmānaṃ vipralabhemahi? | tasmād avasthārūpavivekenopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalambhād aparimitarūpatāprasaṅgāc ca kathañcid bhedābhedavato 'vasthātur asattvam eva | tāś cāvasthā janakājanakasvabhāvabhedavatyaḥ
[T. 266a.] pratyakṣata evāvagamyanta iti tadekatvādhyava-sāyi pratyabhijñānaṃ tadbādhām[359]anubhavat kathaṃ pramāṇaṃ syāt?, yato bījādīnāṃ aṅkurādijananasvabhāvānām api tadātmatāyāṃ hetvantarāpekṣaṇāt prāktanasya[360]hetor anaikāntikatā bhavet |
  bhavatu vā 'vasthātā kaścit, tasyāpy etad[361]eva bhedaṃ sādhayati | tathā hi --
children.translated_text: absolute difference and non-difference with respect to each other would absurdly follow. If there is a 'certain kind' of difference of the further form, then another form dependent on that, and similarly another different from this too — thus unlimited multiplicity of forms would attach to each single entity. And we do not experience perception that manifests unlimited forms. And not experiencing it, why should we deceive ourselves by such fabrication? Therefore, because of the non-apprehension of what has obtained the characteristic of being perceived as distinguished from the form of the states, and because of the absurd consequence of unlimited multiplicity of forms, the state-possessor that has 'a certain kind' of difference and non-difference is simply non-existent. And those states, possessing a difference of essential nature as generative and non-generative, are understood through perception alone — so how can recognition that determines their unity, experiencing invalidation from that [perception], be a <s>pramāṇa</s>? Because even for seeds and the like, which have the essential nature of generating sprouts and the like, since with respect to their identity another reason is required, the previous reason would become inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). Or let there be some state-possessor; this very [argument] establishes difference even for it. For thus —
'Of those two' —
of the generative and non-generative states — this is a locative dual. Then the meaning is this: in the generative state and in the non-generative state,

niścayalakṣaṇas tatra vyavahāraḥ kartavyaḥ, viṣayasya [S. 89a.] viruddhadharmādhyāsalakṣaṇasya darśanād iti |
  na ca śakyate vaktum -- avasthā evāṅkurādijananasvabhāvā nāvasthātā iti | tasya sarvasāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇasyāsattvaprasaṅgāt | [T. 264b.] tato yad ekarūpatayā pratyabhijñānaṃ bhaveṣu tat pūrvottarakālayor janakājanakasvabhāvabhedavyavasthāpakapratyakṣanibandhanām anubhavadbādhāṃ katham iva pramāṇaṃ syāt? | tatpratibhāsinaś cābhinnarūpasyālīkatve 'kṣasamudbhavām api vṛttim anubhavato 'sya satsamprayogajatvābhāvāt taimirikādidhiyām iva kutaḥ pratyakṣatā? | na {p. 86.1} cārthakriyānibandhanaṃ rūpama-pāsya bījāder aparaḥ paramārthataḥ svabhāvo 'sti, yasyādhigamāt pratyabhijñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ bhavet, arthakriyāsāmarthyalakṣaṇatvāt paramārthasataḥ | tasmāt sadṛśāparabhāvanibandhana evāyaṃ keśakadalīstambādiṣv ivākārasāmyatāmātrāpahṛtahṛdayānāṃ bhrānta [S. 89b.] eva tattvādhyavasāyo mantavyaḥ | tataḥ sato 'pi pratikṣaṇaṃ bhedasyānupalakṣaṇaṃ
bālānām | yadā tu vidhurapratyayopanipātād visadṛśāparabhāvaprasavaḥ tadā 'sya tattvādhyavasāyī pratyabhijñāpratyayo na bhūtim avalambate | na ca tadekākāraparāmarśapratyayajanakatvād aparaṃ sādṛśyam | bhedā 'viśeṣe 'pi ca svahetubalāyāt aprakṛtivaśāt kecid[362]evaikākāraparāmarśapratyayalakṣaṇām arthajñānādilakṣaṇāṃ vā 'rthakriyāṃ kurvanti nāpara iti vipañcitaṃpramāṇavārtika evaśāstrakṛteti neha prapañcyate |
children.translated_text: the determination-characterized procedure (<s>vyavahāra</s>) should be applied there, because of observing the superimposition of contradictory properties upon the object. And it cannot be said that the states alone have the essential nature of generating sprouts and the like, not the state-possessor — because of the absurd consequence that it, characterized by the absence of all capacity, would be non-existent. Therefore, the recognition that [determines] the entities as having a single form, experiencing invalidation grounded in perception that establishes the difference of generative and non-generative essential natures at the earlier and later times — how could it be a <s>pramāṇa</s>? And since the non-different form that appears in it is false, even though it experiences an occurrence born from the senses, because of the absence of being born from actual contact, like the cognitions of one with eye-disease (<s>taimirika</s>) and the like — whence its perceptual status? And apart from the form that grounds causal efficacy, there is no other essential nature of seeds and the like in ultimate reality, through the knowledge of which recognition could become a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since what is ultimately real is characterized by the capacity for causal efficacy. Therefore, this determination of reality is to be regarded as simply erroneous — grounded only in the succession of similar [but different] entities, just as in the case of hair, plantain-trunk and the like, for those whose minds are captivated merely by the similarity of appearance. Hence, even though difference exists at every moment, it is not noticed by the ignorant. But when, from the occurrence of a discordant condition, there is the production of a dissimilar successor, then the recognition-cognition that determines reality does not take effect. And there is no further similarity beyond the capacity to generate a cognition that apprehends a single form. And even without a specific difference of distinctions, through the force of their own causes and not through the influence of [external] nature, only some [entities] perform the causal function characterized as the cognition apprehending a single form, or the causal function characterized as object-cognition and the like — not others. This has been elaborated in the <s>Pramāṇavārttika</s> itself by the author of the treatise, so it is not expanded upon here.

body.translated_text: But [the opponent says:] from the direct perception of recognition (pratyabhijñā) itself, seeds and the like are observed as having a single essential nature. In that case, where does this distinction characterized by having-the-nature-of-generating and not-having-the-nature-of-generating come from? So that the inconclusiveness would not arise. And recognition is not a non-pramāṇa (invalid cognition),

body.text: section: 17. anumānenāpi pratyabhijñāyā bādhāt na tataḥ sthirabhāvasiddhiḥ |
body.translated_text: Section: 17. Because recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) is invalidated even by inference, permanent existence is not established from it.

body.text: avaśyaṃ ca bījāder janakājanakāvasthayor vastubhedo yathokto 'vagantavya iti darśayitum anumānam abhedasya [T. 265a.] bādhakam āha --

children.translated_text: 'Of entities' —
of seeds and the like, [the nature] that is generative of their own effects,
'the essential nature' —
when those [conditions] are present,
'because of the impossibility of becoming otherwise' —
because of the impossibility of [it] being non-generative at any time,
'of that essential nature' —
of the essential nature that generates sprouts and the like,
'as before' —
just as at the proximity of water and other conditions,
'even earlier' —
even at the time of being stored in a granary and the like, its own effect —
there would be the absurd consequence of generation.

children.text:
| tatha hi -- salilādisannidhāne 'pi bījādiḥ svarūpeṇaiva kāryaṃ karoti, na pararūpeṇa | yaś cāsya tadā [T. 266a.] kāryajanakaḥ svabhāvaḥ, sa cet prāg apy asti, `sa evāyam' iti pratyabhijñāyāṃ puro 'vasthāyino janakasvabhāvasya prācyarūpābhedādhyavasāyāt, tataḥ kim iti prāg api tatkāryaṃ na kuryād iti? | prayogaḥ -- yad yadā yajjananasvabhāvaṃ tat tadā tajjanayaty eva | ajanakasya janakatvasvabhāvavirodhāt | anyasyāpi vā tatsvabhāvatāpatteḥ
| yathā -- tad eva bījādikaṃ salilādisannidhikāle | kuśūlādyavasthāsv api cedaṃ bījādikaṃ svakāryajananasvabhāvam {p. 87.1} eva pratyabhijñayā vyavasthāpyata iti svabhāvahetuprasaṅgaḥ | na ca janayati | tasmān na tajjananasvabhāvam iti | viparyayaprayogaḥ -- yad yadā yajjananasvabhāvaṃ(va) nirvarttyaṃ kāryaṃ na janayati na tat tadā tajjananasvabhāvam, tad yathā -- śālyaṅkurajananasvabhāvanirvartyaṃ kāryam ajanayat kodravabījam | na janayati
children.translated_text: For thus: even in the proximity of water and the like, a seed and the like produces its effect by its own form alone, not by another's form. And if the essential nature that is generative of the effect at that time also exists earlier — since in recognition [expressed as] 'this is the same one,' there is the determination of non-difference of the generative essential nature of the presently-existing [entity] from its prior form — then why would it not produce that effect even earlier? The formal argument: whatever, whenever, has the essential nature of generating something, that generates it at that very time — because non-generativeness contradicts generative essential nature; or because anything else would also absurdly possess that essential nature. For example: that very seed and the like at the time of proximity to water and the like. If this seed and the like, even in the states of being stored in a granary and the like, is established by recognition as having precisely the essential nature of generating its own effect — then there is the absurd consequence of a <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (essential-nature reason). But it does not generate. Therefore it does not have that generative essential nature. The counter-proof: whatever, whenever does not generate an effect to be produced by something having the essential nature of generating that [effect], that does not at that time have that generative essential nature — for example, a <s>kodrava</s>-seed with respect to an effect to be produced by the essential nature of generating a rice-sprout. And the seed and the like does not generate

children.text:
ca salilādikāraṇasannidheḥ[363]prāk tatkāryajananasvabhāvanirvarttyaṃ [S. 90b.] svakāryaṃ bījādikam iti [T. 266b.] vyāpakānupalabdhiḥ | tato 'numānato 'pi bādham anubhavat pratyabhijñānaṃ kathaṃ pramāṇaṃ syāt? |
  nanu cānena[364]bādhyamānasyānumānasyāprāmāṇyāt kathaṃ bādhakatvam? | aniścitapramāṇabhāvena[365]kuto bādhā? | nāpi itaretarāśrayatvam | na hi pratyabhijñānasyāprāmāṇyād etadanumānaṃ pramāṇam, kintu svasādhyapratibandhāt | sa ca viparyaye bādhakapramāṇabalān niścita iti |
children.translated_text: its own effect to be produced by the essential nature of generating that effect, before the proximity of water and other conditions — thus [this is] non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>). Therefore, how can recognition, experiencing invalidation even by inference, be a <s>pramāṇa</s>? But since the inference being invalidated by this [recognition] is itself non-<s>pramāṇa</s>, how can it have invalidating force? With its status as <s>pramāṇa</s> uncertain, whence invalidation? Nor is there circular dependence. For we do not [say] that this inference is a <s>pramāṇa</s> because of recognition being a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>; rather, [it is a <s>pramāṇa</s>] because of the invariable connection with its own <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved). And that [connection] is ascertained through the force of an invalidating <s>pramāṇa</s> in the case of the contrary.

body.translated_text: And in order to show that the real distinction between the generative and non-generative states of seeds and the like must necessarily be understood as stated, he presents an inference that invalidates non-difference:

ca śālyādikā- — T.

[365] uttaram

children.text:
, [T. 267a.] kāryadarśanonnīyamānarūpatvāt tajjananasvabhāvatāyāḥ |
  yadi tarhi sa evāṅkurajananasvabhāvaḥ, pūrvabhāvinām avasthābhedānām atajjananabhāvatvāt kathaṃ teṣu tatkāraṇavyapadeśaḥ? aṅkurārthibhir vā tadupādānam? ity ata āha -- `pūrvabhāvinas tu' kuśūlādyavasthitikālabhāvinas tu
children.translated_text: because the nature of generating that [sprout] has a form inferred from observing the effect. If, then, that alone is the essential nature of generating sprouts, since the prior state-differences are not of that generative nature, how can there be the designation of cause with respect to those? Or why should those desiring sprouts adopt them? Therefore he says: 'But prior' — those existing at the time of being stored in a granary and the like, but
the state-differences that are the causes of the sprout —
of the last state-difference,
are causes,
successively, through the distinctions contributed by other conditions,
because of its arising from them.

children.text: | atas teṣūpacārataḥ kāraṇavyapadeśo 'ṅkurārthibhiś copādānam | yatas tatsvabhāvasya bījāder jananaṃ na hetvantarāpekṣam, yac cājanakam apekṣate na tasya [S. 91b.] tajjananasvabhāvatvam iti |
children.translated_text: | Therefore, in those [cases], the designation of causality is figurative, and the taking up [of causes] is by those desirous of sprouts. Because the production of seeds and the like, which have that essential nature (<s>tatsvabhāva</s>), does not depend on other reasons, and that which is non-productive and yet depended upon — it does not have the essential nature of producing that [effect]. |
Therefore there is no <s>anekānta</s> (inconclusiveness)

children.text:
bījādivat `tatsvabhāvatvāt' ity asya hetoḥ ity upasaṃhāraḥ |
  tad evaṃ yadā tāvat pratyabhijñānaṃ pratyakṣapramāṇatayā sthairyasiddhaye parair ucyate bījādivad anekāntaṃ pratipādayitum, tadā tasyoktena prakāreṇa pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ bādhyamānatvāt tadātmatā nāstīti kutas tata ekatā bhāvānām?, yato 'nekāntaḥ syād iti pratipāditam | yadā tu pratyabhijñāyamānatvāt pūrvāparakālayor ekasvabhāvā bījādaya iti hetutayocyate paraiḥ, tadā 'yam asiddho hetuḥ | na ca sa pakṣe kvacid varttata ity āha --
children.translated_text: like seeds and the like — this is the conclusion of the reason 'because of having that essential nature (<s>tatsvabhāvatvāt</s>).' | Thus, when the opponent adduces the recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) as valid perception (<s>pratyakṣapramāṇa</s>) in order to establish permanence, and [attempts] to demonstrate inconclusiveness (<s>anekānta</s>) like seeds and the like, then it has been demonstrated that since [recognition] is contradicted by perception and inference in the manner stated, identity (<s>tadātmatā</s>) does not exist — so whence would unity of entities [follow], from which inconclusiveness would arise? But when the opponent states as a reason that seeds and the like have one essential nature in earlier and later times because of being recognized [as the same], then this reason is unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>). And [to show] that it does not obtain anywhere in the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>), [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says —
In momentary entities (<s>kṣaṇikeṣu bhāveṣu</s>)
which are accepted by us,
because of the absence of unity (<s>aikyābhāva</s>)
— thus is the syntactic connection.

body.translated_text: If [you say:] 'There is no <s>pramāṇa</s> weightier than perception' — no, because the perceptual status of recognition is unestablished. For we do not say that this [recognition], being perceptual in nature, is invalidated by inference. And what constitutes the superiority of perception? For it is called a <s>pramāṇa</s> because it is absent when the object is impossible, and the same applies to inference as well, since it arises from a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) invariably connected with the object — so there is no special distinction of it [perception]. And if recognition, even while experiencing contradiction with inference, is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, then the cognition that, due to similarity of appearance, recognizes identity between a blue [flower] and another flower and the like — why should it not be a <s>pramāṇa</s>? For the difference that is inferred through observing effects such as blossoms and fruits is not experienced as such through perception. And the detailed refutation of the validity of recognition has been carried out precisely in the proof of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi</s>) — so let that suffice here.
girikāntakā (?)-kanni- (?)

body.text: section: 19. tatsvabhāvatvāt ity atra punar api anekāntadoṣoddhāraḥ |
body.translated_text: Section: 19. Removal of the defect of inconclusiveness (<s>anekāntadoṣa</s>) again regarding '<s>tatsvabhāvatvāt</s>' (because of having that essential nature).

body.text: atha yasyāpi kṣanikā bhāvās tasyāpi bījādīnāṃ [T. 267b.] pratikṣaṇam aikyābhāve 'pi viśeṣānupalakṣaṇād antyakṣaṇavat sarveṣāṃ janakasvabhāvānām api tadbhāvaṃ prati salilādyapekṣatvāt tadavastham anaikāntikatvam ity āśaṅkyāha --

children.translated_text: Because of arising from successive [conditions] (<s>aparāparotpatteḥ</s>)

children.text:
kṣaṇikair api [S. 92a.] nānekāntaḥ, aparebhyo 'parebhyaś ca pratyayebhyaḥ pratikṣaṇam utpatteḥ kṣaṇikānāṃ bhinnaśaktitvād antyakṣaṇavaj janakasvabhāvatāvirahāt kutas tair apy anekāntaḥ syāt? na hi kāraṇabhedopadhīyamānajanmanāṃ viśeṣānupalakṣaṇe 'py abhinnasvabhāvatā yuktā, hetu {p.89.1} bhedānanuvidhāne 'hetukatāprasaṅgāt | tathā ca vakṣyati -- `aparāparapratyayayogena pratikṣaṇaṃ bhinnaśaktayaḥ santanvantaḥ saṃskārā yady api kutaścit sāmyāt samānarūpāḥ pratīyante tathāpi bhinna eva eṣāṃ svabhāvaḥ, tena kiñcid eva kasyacit kāraṇam' iti |
 yad uktaṃ `tatsvabhāvasya jananāt' ity asyānekāntam udbhāvayann āha paraḥ --
children.translated_text:
even by momentary [entities] there is no <s>anekānta</s> (inconclusiveness), because of arising at each moment from successive conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>), since momentary entities have different capacities (<s>bhinnaśakti</s>), and since — like the final moment — they lack the nature of being productive, how could there be inconclusiveness even through them? For it is not reasonable that entities whose births are attended by different causes should have undifferentiated essential nature, even when the difference is not observed, because of the absurd consequence of non-causality if [the effect] does not follow the differentiation of causes. And accordingly [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] will state: 'The <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) which continue with different capacities at each moment through connection with successive conditions, even though they appear to have similar form due to some resemblance, nevertheless their essential nature is indeed different; therefore only something particular is the cause of something particular.' |
 What was stated as '[because of] the production of that which has that essential nature (<s>tatsvabhāvasya jananāt</s>)' — displaying the inconclusiveness in this, the opponent says —
They
— seeds, earth, and the like —
the final [moments] (<s>antyāḥ</s>)
— those existing at the end, each in the production of the sprout —
[are] capable (<s>samarthāḥ</s>)

children.text: khaṇḍaśaḥ kāraṇebhyaḥ kāryotpādābhāvād bhavadbhir iṣyanta iti
children.translated_text: — you accept them [as such], since there is no production of the effect from causes taken piecemeal —
why do they not produce [the effect] individually?

children.text:
? | tataś caiṣām eka eva kaścid aṅkuraṃ janayati, tadanye tu tatsvabhāvā api na janayantīti `tatsvabhāvasya jananāt' ity anekāntaḥ | tadvat kuśūlādyavasthā api bījādayo 'ṅkurādijananasvabhāvā api na janayiṣyantīti tair anekāntaḥ [S. 92b.] tadavastha eveti manyateparaḥ|
  atrāha --
children.translated_text:
And thus, only some one among them produces the sprout, while the others, though having that same essential nature, do not produce — so 'because of the production of that which has that essential nature' there is inconclusiveness. Likewise, seeds and the like in the granary and other states, though having the essential nature of producing sprouts and the like, will not produce — so through them the inconclusiveness remains in the same condition — the opponent thinks. |
  To this [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says —
Thus (<s>iti</s>)

children.text: yad evaṃ tvaṃ manyase | pareṇa sāmānyenābhidhānāt sāmānyenaivottaram āha --
children.translated_text: — that you think so. Since the opponent has stated [the objection] in general terms, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] replies in equally general terms —
They do indeed produce (<s>janayanty eva</s>)
Here there is no (<s>nātra</s>)
in the production of their own effect,
otherwise-becoming (<s>anyathābhāva</s>)
— non-productivity should not be suspected. Why?
Because the essential nature does not deviate (<s>svabhāvasyāvaiparītyāt</s>)

children.text: | yadi hi na janayeyur jananasvabhāvā eva na syuḥ | tatsvabhāvāś ceṣyanta ity avaśyaṃ janayanti, tathā ca kuto 'naikāntaḥ? iti bhāvaḥ |
children.translated_text: | For if they did not produce, they would simply not have the essential nature of producing. And since they are accepted as having that essential nature, they necessarily produce — and so whence inconclusiveness? — this is the purport. |

body.translated_text: Now, even for one who accepts that entities are momentary, since even when there is no unity of seeds and the like at each moment, due to the non-observation of difference, all [moments] — like the final moment — being of a productive nature, [yet] requiring water and the like for [producing] that [effect], the inconclusiveness remains in that same condition — anticipating this [objection], [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says —

body.text: section: 20. ekenaiva samarthyena kāryajanane pareṣām anupayogam āśaṅkya taduddhāraḥ |
body.translated_text: Section: 20. Anticipating that others are useless when the effect is produced by a single capacity, and removal of that [objection

body.text: pratyekam antyānāṃ janakatve kāryasyaikena jananād apareṣām upayogasya nirviṣayatvād ajananam eveti manyamāna āha paraḥ --

children.translated_text: Among those (<s>teṣu</s>)
— among the final [moments] —
co-operative [causes] (<s>sahakāriṣu</s>)
— among those whose nature is to operate simultaneously —
having capable essential nature (<s>samarthasvabhāveṣu</s>)
— among those accepted as being fit for the activity of producing that effect, when they exist —
since the effect is produced by just one, what is the use of the others?

children.text: ? naiva kaścit | tat kim ucyate `janayanty eva' iti? | etat pariharati -- `na vai' naiva
children.translated_text: None at all. Then why is it said 'they do indeed produce'? Resolving this, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says — 'Not indeed' (<s>na vai</s>) — indeed not —
of entities (<s>bhāvānām</s>)
— of seeds and the like — any
<s>prekṣāpūrvakāritā</s> (deliberate purposive agency)
— <s>buddhipūrvakāritā</s> (intelligence-preceded activity),
because of which (<s>yataḥ</s>)

children.text: prekṣāpūrvakāritvāt `ayam asmāsv anyatam eko 'pi samarthaḥ kāryajanane, kim atrāsmābhiḥ karttavyam?' ity ālocya
children.translated_text: — due to having deliberate purposive agency — having reflected 'this one among us, even a single one, is capable of producing the effect, what need for us here?'
the others would withdraw,
adopting indifference, they would not engage in the production of that effect. Since
they (<s>te</s>)
— those entities such as seeds and the like —
are without intentional operation (<s>nirabhiprāyavyāpārāḥ</s>),
having operations devoid of deliberation, when one [part of the] effect is being produced,
all of them indeed operate.

children.text:
| bhavanadharmaṇi ca kārye teṣāṃ prāgbhāva
eva vyāpāraḥ | tadanyasyāyogāt[368]| yadi hi vyāpṛtād anya eva vyāpāraḥ [T. 268b.] tadā tata eva kāryotpādād vyāpāravataḥ kārakatvam eva hīyate |
  tasyāsau vyāpāraḥ tatas tasya kārakatvam iti cet | nanv evaṃ vyāpāropayogasya kāryānupayogini tatropacārāt[369]pāramārthikam asya kārakatvaṃ hīyeta | kaś cāsya[370]vyāpāreṇa sambandhaḥ? | samavāyaś cet | na | tasya prāg eva nirastatvāt | samavāyāc ca vyāpāravattve anyasyāpi[371]tatkāryānupayoginas[372]tadbhāvaprasaṅgaḥ[373], samavāyasyeheti buddhihetor ekatvena sarvatra samānatvāt | abhimatenaiva vyāpṛtena tadvyāpārotpādanāt nātiprasaṅgaḥ iti cet | nanu tena[374]tadutpādanaṃ[375]tatra[376]samavāyād evocyate | sa ca [S. 93b.] sarvatra samānaḥ | yena ca pariśrameṇa vyāpāraṃ janayati tena kāryam eva kin notpādayati? yena vyavadhānam āśrīyate | yathā ca svasannidhimātreṇaivāyaṃ vyāpāraṃ janayati na vyāpārāntareṇa, anavasthāprasaṅgāt, tathā tata
children.translated_text:
| And in an effect that has the character of coming-into-being, their operation is simply their prior existence (<s>prāgbhāva</s>). Because no other [operation] is possible. For if the operation were something other than the operative [cause] itself, then since the effect would arise from that [operation] alone, the very causality of the operative [cause] would be lost. |
  If [one says:] 'that is its operation, and from that, its causality' — but then, since the usefulness of the operation is of no use to the effect, and [causality] there is only figurative, its ultimate causality would be lost. And what is its connection with the operation? If <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) — no, since that has already been refuted. And from inherence, even something else that is of no use to that effect would absurdly have that status, since inherence, being unitary as the basis for the cognition 'here,' is the same everywhere. If [one says:] 'there is no over-extension because that very operative [cause] which is accepted produces that operation' — but that production of that [operation] by it is stated to be precisely from inherence. And that [inherence] is the same everywhere. And with whatever effort it produces the operation, why does it not just produce the effect itself? — for which an intermediary is resorted to. And just as it produces the operation merely by its own proximity, without another operation — lest there be an infinite regress — so too from that very [proximity]

children.text:
eva kāryam[377]apīty uktaprāyam |
  tasmād bhāvini kārye prāgbhāva eva kāraṇasya vyāpāraḥ | sa ca sarveṣāṃ astīti sarva eva kāryotpattau vyāpriyanta iti vyapadiśyante |
children.translated_text:
the effect also [arises] — this has been essentially stated. |
  Therefore, in an effect that is coming into being, the operation of the cause is simply its prior existence. And since that [prior existence] belongs to all of them, all indeed are said to operate in the production of the effect. |
That effect too is born from all of them together.

children.text:
sarveṣāṃ bhāva eva tadbhāvāt | na hi kāryasya kāraṇābhimatabhāva eva bhāvam antareṇāparaṃ janma | tathābhāve[378]hi tatraiva kāraṇavyāpārāt kāryakriyaivaiṣāṃ na sambhavet | tataś ca satsv api kāraṇeṣu katham asya bhāva upalabdhir vā syāt? | tatsambandhino janmanaḥ karaṇāt iti cet | na | asatā {p. 91.1} tena[379]sambandhāyogāt | svata eva sattve vā [T. 269a.] janmārthānupapatteḥ | janmakāle copalabhyasyātmanaḥ[380]prāg[381]api bhāvāt tathopalabdhiprasaṅgaḥ, rūpāntareṇa[382]bhāve na [S. 94a.] tasya bhāvaḥ syāt[383]| rūpabhedalakṣaṇatvād bhāvabhedasya[384]| tasmād upalabdhyātmano[385]janmanaḥ prāganupalambhād asattvam | tato 'sya[386]janmasambandhitā kutaḥ? | tasmāt kāryam evābhūtvā hetubhāve bhavatīti bhāva evāsya[387]tato janmeti sarvebhyas tat jāyate |
  nanv ekasyāpi tajjanane sāmarthyāt apareṣāṃ tatra sannidhilakṣaṇo vyāpāro vyartha eveti na tatrāpareṣāṃ bhāvaḥ saṅgacchata iti ced āha --
children.translated_text:
Because of the existence [of the effect] precisely upon the existence of all [causes]. For the effect has no other birth apart from the existence of what is accepted as its cause. For in such a state [of all causes being present], since the causal operation is precisely there, the production of the effect by them would not be possible [otherwise]. And so, even when causes exist, how could the existence or apprehension of this [effect] be? If [one says:] 'because of the occurrence of a birth related to them' — no, because connection with that [birth] is impossible when it [the effect] is non-existent. Or if it exists by itself, then birth would serve no purpose. And since the self that is apprehended at the time of birth existed even before, the consequence is that it should be apprehended in the same way [before]. If existing in a different form, then its existence [in that form] would not be [the same]. Since difference of existence is characterized precisely by difference of form. Therefore, since the birth — whose nature is apprehension — was not apprehended before, [the effect] was non-existent. So whence its connection with birth? Therefore, the effect, having not existed, comes into being upon the existence of causes — and thus its birth is precisely its existence from them — so it is born from all of them. |
  If one thinks: 'since even one [cause] alone has the capacity to produce it, the operation of the others — characterized by [mere] proximity — is purposeless, and therefore their existence with respect to that [effect] is not coherent' — to this [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says —
of its own cause (<s>svahetoḥ</s>)
— of the aggregate (<s>sāmagrī</s>) characterized by earth, seed, water, and the like —
transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>)

children.text: kāryotpādānuguṇaviśeṣavataḥ pratikṣaṇam upadhīyamānātiśayasya kṣaṇāntarasya prasavaḥ, tataḥ
children.translated_text: — the bringing forth of a subsequent moment that is endowed with a particular quality conducive to the production of the effect, having an incremental increase deposited at each moment; from that [transformation] —
proximity (<s>upanidhi</s>)
— presence at the location of the effect —
[is] the property (<s>dharma</s>)
of those who are
thus-being (<s>tathābhavantaḥ</s>)
— being present at the location of the effect —
they do not deserve reproach (<s>nopālambham arhanti</s>)

children.text: -- `ekasyāpy etatkāryakaraṇe samarthatvāt kim atra bhavantaḥ sannihitāḥ?' iti na paryanuyogam arhanti | na hi tadaparasannidhim[388]antareṇa tatraikasyāpi[389]bhāva upapadyate | kutaḥ?
children.translated_text: — they do not deserve the objection: 'since even one alone is capable of producing this effect, why are you present here?' For without the proximity of those other [causes], even the existence of a single one there is not possible. Why?
Because of having that as their source (<s>tatprakṛte</s>)

children.text:
tatprakṛtitvāt iti bhāvapradhāno [S. 94b.] nirddeśaḥ | kṣitibījasalilādisāmagrīpariṇāmajanyasvabhāvatvād ekaikasya samarthasya tadbhāve[390]kutaḥ kevalasya sambhavaḥ[391]?, sāmagrīśabdavācyaiḥ kāraṇabhedaiḥ samartha-
svasvalakṣaṇāntarārambhāt | tataś[392]ca pratikṣaṇam upadhīyamānātiśayasyotpādāt kevalānāṃ [T. 269b.] ca tajjananasvabhāvavaikalyāt tadaparapratyayayogajanyasvabhāvatvāt samarthajanakasya hetoḥ | etac ca yathāvasaraṃ tatra tatra vyaktīkariṣyati | tasmād yatsāmagrījanyasvabhāvo yo bhāvaḥ sa tatraikābhāve 'pi kāraṇavaikalyān na sambhavatīty ekasāmagrījanmanāṃ sahabhāvo niyataḥ | sarveṣāṃ teṣāṃ bhāva eva kāryasya bhāvāt sarva eva janayantīti `tatsvabhāvasya jananāt' ity atra nānekāntaḥ iti |
  {p. 92.1} yenābhiprāyeṇa `te 'ntyāḥ samarthāḥ kin na janayanti' ity uktaṃ taṃ prakaṭayann āha --
children.translated_text:
— '<s>tatprakṛtitvāt</s>' (because of having that as their essential nature) — this is a statement with the sense of the abstract noun predominant. Since each capable [cause] has an essential nature born from the transformation of the aggregate (<s>sāmagrī</s>) of earth, seed, water, and the like, how could it exist alone in the absence of those [other factors]?, since from the different components denoted by the word '<s>sāmagrī</s>' (aggregate), each produces its own respective particular subsequent moment. And therefore, since what arises has an incremental increase deposited at each moment, and since the individual [causes] in isolation lack the essential nature of producing that [effect] — because the capable productive cause has an essential nature born from connection with those other conditions — and this [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] will make clear in the relevant places. Therefore, whatever entity has an essential nature born from a [particular] aggregate — that [entity] is not possible even when one [component] of the aggregate is absent, due to the deficiency of causes. Thus the co-existence of those born from one aggregate is determined. Since the effect exists precisely upon the existence of all of them, all of them indeed produce — and so in '[because of] the production of that which has that essential nature (<s>tatsvabhāvasya jananāt</s>),' there is no <s>anekānta</s> (inconclusiveness). |
  Revealing the intent with which it was said 'they being final [and] capable, why do they not produce?', [<s>Arcaṭa</s>] says —
'Capable' (<s>samarthāḥ</s>)

children.text: ityādi | siddhāntavādy api `janayanty eva' iti yadabhiprāyavatoktaṃ tam ādarśayati --
children.translated_text: and so forth. The proponent (<s>siddhāntavādī</s>) also shows the intent with which he said 'they do indeed produce' —
'No, in that very [case]' (<s>na, tatraiva</s>)
and so forth. He explains this very [point] —
'Of that very [thing]' (<s>tasyaiva</s>)

children.text: ityādi | [S. 95a.] ayam abhiprāyaḥ -- `idam atra samartham, idam asamartham' iti pratyakṣānupalambhasādhanābhyām anvayavyatirekābhyāṃ vyavahriyate, anyanimittābhāvāt | tau cānvayavyatirekāv ekatraiva kārye dṛśyete nāparāparatreti tasyaivaikasya janane samarthā gamyanta iti nāparāparajananam | te tu yadavasthā janayanto dṛśyante -- kiṃ tajjananasvabhāvās tadaiva? āhosvit prāg api? ity atra vivādaḥ | tatra prāg api tatsvabhāvatve paścād iva prāg api jananaprasaṅga iti pratikṣaṇaṃ bheda ucyata iti |
children.translated_text: and so forth. The purport is this: 'This is capable here, this is incapable' — [such determination] is made through <s>anvaya</s> (positive concomitance) and <s>vyatireka</s> (negative concomitance), which are the means of perception and non-apprehension, because there is no other ground. And those <s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s> are seen with respect to one and the same effect only, not with respect to different ones — so they are understood to be capable of producing that one [effect] alone, and there is no production of different [effects]. But in whatever state they are seen to produce — are they of the nature of producing that [effect] only at that time? Or even before? — here is the dispute. And in that [dispute], if they have that essential nature even before, then the absurd consequence is that they would produce even before, just as [they do] later — therefore difference at each moment is asserted. |

body.translated_text: Thinking that when the final [moments] individually have productive capacity, since the effect is produced by just one, the usefulness of the others has no object, and so they simply do not produce — the opponent says —

body.text:
`nivarteran' ity etad vyākhyāti
[368] kriyārūpasya
[369] vyāpāravati kāraṇe
[370] vyāpṛtasya
[371] ghaṭādeḥ
[372] aṅkura-

body.translated_text: Section: 21. The raising of inconclusiveness (<s>anekānta</s>) by the <s>Kṣapaṇakas</s> (Jainas) and <s>Jaiminīyas</s> (Mīmāṃsakas) who accept difference of effects from difference of causes.

children.translated_text: distinct —
mutually excluded —
is the essential nature
of those, i.e., from the eye and other [sense faculties],
which are co-operative causes,
which act simultaneously,
of a single
entity characterized as cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>) —
when there is the arising of an effect,

children.text: satyām, bahūni bhinnasvabhāvāni kāraṇāni kāryaṃ tv ekam abhinnasvabhāvam iti
children.translated_text: granted that, [although] many causes have distinct essential natures, the effect is but one, having a non-distinct essential nature — thus,
from the difference of causes there would be no difference of effects.

children.text:
| tataś cakṣurādayo na bhinnenātmanaikasya kāryasya janakā eṣṭavyāḥ | kintv abhinnam eṣām ekakāryajanakaṃ sāmānyabhūtaṃ rūpam upeyaṃ yenābhinnaṃ kāryaṃ janayanti | tac ca samagrāvasthāyām eva tatkāryaṃ janayati na vyagrāvasthāyām | na caikaikābhāve tasyābhāvaḥ, sāmānyātmanaḥ [S. 95b.] kadācid abhāvavirodhāt | na ca tadā 'syā 'janakasvabhāvatā, janakājanakarūpavataḥ samagretarāvasthāyor bhedaprasaṅgāt | tathā ca sāmānyātmanā hāniḥ | tato yad asya samagreṣu cakṣurādiṣu
janakaṃ rūpaṃ tad ekaikābhāve 'pi vidyate na ca janayatīti `tatsvabhāvasya jananāt' ity anekānta iti |
children.translated_text: | Therefore the eye and the like should not be regarded as producers of a single effect through distinct natures. Rather, a common form (<s>sāmānyabhūtaṃ rūpam</s>) of these, which is a single-effect-producer, non-distinct, should be accepted — by which they produce a non-distinct effect. And that [common form] produces its effect only in the state of completeness (<s>samagrāvasthā</s>), not in the state of incompleteness (<s>vyagrāvasthā</s>). And the absence of one [member] does not entail the absence of that [common form], because of the impossibility that the universal nature (<s>sāmānyātman</s>) could ever be absent. And at that time it is not of a non-productive nature, because of the absurd consequence of a difference [in its nature] between the states of completeness and incompleteness, since it would possess both productive and non-productive natures. And thus there is loss of the universal nature. Therefore, that productive form which [exists] in the complete [assemblage of] eye and the like — that exists even in the absence of one [member], and yet does not produce — thus 'because of that which has that nature producing' — this is the <s>anekānta</s> (indeterminate position).

body.translated_text: Furthermore, the <s>Ākṣapaṇaka</s>-<s>Jaiminīyas</s>, raising the doctrine of <s>anekānta</s> (non-absolutism), [T. 270a.] say:
Section: 22. Refutation raised by the <s>Siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent of the established doctrine)

children.translated_text: No, each according to its own nature —

children.text: ityādi | evaṃ manyate -- kiṃ punar idaṃ kāraṇam abhimataṃ bhavataḥ? | yadi pratyekaṃ cakṣurādikam; {p. 93.1} tad ayuktam | sāmagrījanyasvabhāvatvāt kāryasya, tasyā eva kāraṇatvāt | nanu tadavasthāyāṃ pratyekam eva sāmagrīśabdavācyānāṃ jananasvabhāvatvābhyupagamāt pratyekam eva cakṣurādikaṃ kāraṇam | [T. 270b.] yady evaṃ ko 'yaṃ niyamo yadanekasmād bhavatā 'nekena bhavitavyam viparyaye bādhakapramāṇābhāvāt, ekenaiva tat kāryaṃ karotīti kuto 'vasitam? | tadbhāve bhāvāt iti cet | anekatrāpi samānam etat | tad uktam --
children.translated_text: and so forth. He thinks thus: What indeed is the cause intended by you? If it is each individual [factor] — the eye and the like — {p. 93.1} that is untenable, because the effect has the nature of being produced by the assemblage (<s>sāmagrī</s>), and that [assemblage] alone is the cause. 'But since in that state [of completeness], each individual member designated by the term <s>sāmagrī</s> is accepted as having productive nature, each individual eye and the like is the cause.' [T. 270b.] If so, what is this restriction that from many there must be many [effects]? In the absence of a refuting <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) to the contrary, how is it ascertained that a single [cause] alone produces that effect? If [you say] 'because of the presence [of the effect] when that [cause] is present' — the same applies to multiple [causes] as well. As has been stated:
'They are capable of producing only that one [effect], not another' — thus there is no successive production of one after another.

children.text:
iti | na cānekasmād bhavad anekaṃ prāpnoti | yato nāsmākaṃ bhavatām iva kāraṇam eva [S. 96a.] kāryātmatām upaiti, yato 'nekapariṇater anekarūpatvāt kāryasyānekatā syāt | kintu apūrvam eva keṣucit satsu bhavati | tac cānekabhāva eva bhāvāt tatkāryam ucyate tasya kuto
'nekatāprasaṅgaḥ? | yat tv abhinnaṃ rūpaṃ janakam ucyate tasyaikasthitāv api bhāvāt tatkāryajananasvabhāvāc ca tataḥ kāryaprasavaprasaṅgaḥ, tadanyasannidhau tasya viśeṣābhāvāt tadāpi vā na janayet | tasmād yeṣu bhāvābhāvavatsu kāryaṃ bhāvābhāvavad dṛśṭaṃ ta eva viśeṣā janakā iti kuto 'nekāntaḥ? |
  atha sāmagrīṃ kāraṇam āśrityocyate `na kāraṇabhedāt kāryabhedaḥ syād iti',
children.translated_text: Thus. And it does not follow that from many [causes] the effect must be many. For, unlike your [view], for us the cause does not itself assume the nature of the effect, such that from the manifold transformation of many [causes], the effect would be manifold due to having manifold forms. Rather, something entirely new arises when certain [conditions] are present. And since it exists precisely when the many [causes] exist, it is called 'their effect' — so whence the absurd consequence of its being many? | As for what is said — that the non-distinct form is the producer — since that [form] exists even when one [member] remains, and since it has the nature of producing that effect, there would be the absurd consequence of effect-production [even then], because there is no distinguishing feature of it in the proximity of others, or else it would not produce even then. Therefore, those particular [factors] in whose presence and absence the effect is seen to be present and absent — they alone are the producers. So whence the <s>anekānta</s>? | Now, if one says, relying on the assemblage (<s>sāmagrī</s>) as the cause, 'from the difference of causes there would be no difference of effects,'
that is not so,
each according to its own nature —

children.text: yasyāḥ sāmagryāḥ ya ātmīyaḥ svabhāvas tadbhedena
children.translated_text: by the difference of that assemblage's own essential nature,
because of the application of its particular [features] —

children.text:
tasya -- vijñānalakṣaṇasya kāryasya, viśeṣāḥ -- sāmagrībhedād bhinnāḥ svabhāvāḥ, teṣūpayogataḥ [T. 271a.] tadupayogaiḥ bhinnasāmagrīvyāpāraiḥ kāryāḥ ye svabhāvaviśeṣāḥ -- kāryāṇāṃ viśiṣṭāḥ svabhāvāḥ [S. 96b.] teṣām asaṅkarāt paras paravyāvṛttarūpatvāt | sāmagrībhedād bhinnarūpataiva kāryāṇām iti kathan na kāraṇabhedād kāryabhedaḥ syāt? | tathā hi -- ekā sāmagrī manaskāratat[393]sādguṇyādilakṣaṇā[394], tato vikalpavijñānamātraṃ[395]jāyate; aparā manaskārendriyamātralakṣaṇā, tato bhrāntendriyavijñānasambhavaḥ[396]; tadanyā viṣayendriyamanaskārātmikā, tato 'py abhrāntavijñānasambhūtir iti
bhinnasāmagrījanmanāṃ {p. 94.1} kāryasvabhāvaviśeṣāṇām asāṅkaryād asty eva sāmagrīlakṣaṇakāraṇabhedāt kāryāṇāṃ bheda iti |
  nanu yadā viṣayendriyamanaskārebhyo vijñānasambhavaḥ tadā teṣām upayogaviṣayasyaikatvāt katham asāṅkaryam? | tathāvidhasya sāṅkaryasyeṣṭatvāt adoṣaḥ | taduktam --
children.translated_text: of that — the effect characterized as cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>) — the particular features — the distinct essential natures arising from the difference of assemblages — through the application of those, [T. 271a.] i.e., through the distinct operations of different assemblages — the particular essential natures that are effects — the distinguished essential natures of effects — because of the non-intermixture (<s>asaṅkara</s>) of those, i.e., because of their being mutually exclusive in form. Since the effects have distinct forms precisely because of the difference of assemblages, how could there not be a difference of effects from a difference of causes? | For thus: one assemblage is characterized by mental attention (<s>manaskāra</s>), the excellence of that, and the like; from it arises merely conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpavijñāna</s>). Another is characterized by mental attention and sense faculty alone; from it there is the arising of erroneous sense-cognition. Yet another has the nature of object, sense faculty, and mental attention; from it too there is the arising of non-erroneous cognition. Thus, because of the non-intermixture of the particular essential natures of effects born from different assemblages, there is indeed a difference of effects from a difference of causes characterized as assemblages. | But when cognition arises from the object, sense faculty, and mental attention, since the domain of their application is one, how is there non-intermixture? | Because such intermixture is accepted, there is no fault. As has been stated:
'Because of the capacity being in that very one [locus]' —

children.text:
ityādi |
  kathaṃ tarhi teṣāṃ tajjanakatvam?, yadi tadbhedāt [S. 97a.] na bhidyate kāryam | kiṃ nu vai samagrāṇām anyānyakāryajananena janakatvam yatas tadbhāve tan na syāt | janakatvaṃ hy eṣāṃ tadbhāva eva kasyacid bhāvāt | tatraikasyānekasya vā bhāve teṣām ekānekajanakatvam ucyate |
children.translated_text: and so forth. | How then is their status as producers [established], if the effect is not differentiated by their differentiation? Is their producer-status through the production of each other's effects, such that in the absence of that [factor], that [effect] would not exist? For their producer-status consists precisely in the existence of something when they exist. Therein, when one or many exist, they are called the producer of one or many [effects].

'Is ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>) produced from causes not distinct from those of cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>)?' ||

children.text:
iti |
 naiṣa doṣaḥ | teṣāṃ yathāsvaṃ svabhāvabhedena nimittopādānatayā tadupayogāt | manaskāro hi vijñānasyopādānakāraṇam | cakṣuṣas tu svavijñānajananayogyasya janmani sahakārikāraṇam | evam itaratrāpi yathāyogam vācyam | tato 'nyādṛśī sāmagrī cakṣuḥkṣaṇasya janikā, anyādṛśī ca vijñānader iti tadvailakṣaṇyād eva [S. 97b.] kāryāṇāṃ vailakṣaṇyam |
  syād etat -- sarveṣāṃ anvayavyatirekāv anuvidhīyete tadā cakṣurādikṣaṇair iti kuto 'yaṃ bhedaḥ -- ihopādānabhāve bheda(-bhāveneda)m upayujyate, anyatra tu sahakāribhāveneti? | bodharūpatāder[398]{p. 95.1} anukārānanukārābhyāṃ tadbhāve[399]vyabhicārāvyabhicārataś ca | tathā hi -- vijñānaṃ manaskārasya bodharūpatām anukaroti, na cakṣurāder jarā(ḍā)dibhāvam | evam anyad api pratyeyam | niyamena ca vijñānamātrabhāve samanantarapratyayasya vyāpāro na cakṣurādeḥ | cakṣuḥkṣaṇāntarodaye[400]ca pūrvabhāvinaś cakṣuṣo[401]na svavijñānayogyatāhetoḥ [T. 272a.] samanantarapratyayasya | evaṃrūpasyāpi vācyam | tasmād avasthābhede 'pi yad ekākāraparāmarṣa(śa)pratyayanibandhanatayā svasantatipatitakāryaprasūtinimittaṃ tad upādāna-kāraṇaṃ | yat santānāntare prāgavasthāpekṣaviśeṣodayanibandhanaṃ tat sahakārikāraṇam | sa ceyaṃ bhāvānāṃ svahetuparamparāyātā prakṛtir
yayā kiñcit kāryaṃ svasantānavyavasthānibandhanaṃ janayanty aparaṃ ca santānāntaravyapadeśanibandhanam iti tasyā eva sāmagryā avāntaraviśeṣakṛtatvāc cakṣūrūpavijñānakṣaṇānāṃ parasparato [S. 98a.] vailakṣaṇyaṃ na virudhyate |
children.translated_text: Thus. | This is not a fault. Because those [factors], each according to its own essential nature, serve as material (<s>nimittopādāna</s>) causes through their application in that [specific] capacity. For mental attention (<s>manaskāra</s>) is the material cause (<s>upādānakāraṇa</s>) of cognition. But the eye is the cooperative cause (<s>sahakārikāraṇa</s>) in the production of a cognition suitable to itself. Similarly in other cases, it should be stated as appropriate. Therefore, the assemblage that produces the eye-moment is of one kind, and the assemblage that produces cognition and the like is of another kind — and due to that very dissimilarity [of assemblages], there is dissimilarity of effects. | One might object: since the co-presence and co-absence of all [factors] — the eye and other moments — are observed together, whence this distinction — that here [mental attention] functions as material cause, and elsewhere as cooperative cause? | Because of the following and not following of the nature of awareness (<s>bodharūpatā</s>), and because of the invariable and variable co-occurrence when that [nature] is present. For thus: cognition follows the awareness-nature of mental attention, not the inert nature of the eye and the like. Similarly, the rest should be understood. And invariably, when there is merely cognition, there is the operation of the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>), not of the eye and the like. And when a subsequent eye-moment arises, the prior eye [operates], not [through] the immediately preceding condition which is the cause of fitness for its own cognition. The same should be stated for form and the like. Therefore, even without a difference in [temporal] state, that which — by virtue of being the basis for the apprehension of a single aspect — is the ground for producing effects within its own continuum (<s>santati</s>), that is the material cause (<s>upādānakāraṇa</s>). That which is the basis for the arising of a distinguishing feature relative to a prior state in another continuum, that is the cooperative cause (<s>sahakārikāraṇa</s>). And this is the innate disposition (<s>prakṛti</s>) of entities, inherited through the succession of their own causes, by which they produce one effect as the basis for the continuity of their own continuum, and another as the basis for designation in another continuum — and because of the sub-distinctions within that very assemblage, the dissimilarity among the eye-moment, form-moment, and cognition-moment from one another is not contradicted.

body.translated_text: But if from a single assemblage many [effects] arise, let there be difference from those produced by another assemblage — but how [is there difference] among themselves? | For entities are accepted as having such-and-such a form because of being produced from causes having such-and-such a form. [T. 271b.] There, when cognition arises from the eye, form, and mental attention, since the eye and the form-moment also exist [in that assemblage], and since they are produced from causes not distinct from those of cognition — the consequence would be that those [eye and form] have the nature of cognition, or that cognition has their nature. And [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:
