body.text: yadi punar gomayetarādijanmanaḥ śālūkāder agnidhūmādijanmano vā dhūmādeḥ pratyabhijñāvaśād vilakṣaṇasāmagrīnibandhanatve 'pi samānasvabhāvataiva syāt ko doṣaḥ syāt? ity ata āha --

children.translated_text: 'For otherwise' —

children.text: ityādi | yadi [S. 155b.] hi yā svajāti[lakṣaṇapratyayāntarasahitā sāmagrī yā ca] svajātinirapekṣā gomayādirūpā śālūkādeḥ, dhūmasya vā yā 'gnīndhanādilakṣaṇā [T. 321b.] yā ca śakramūrddhādisvabhāvā dhūmādyātmikā avi(-kā tasyāḥ vi)lakṣaṇāyā api sāmagryā avilakṣaṇam tādṛśam eva kāryaṃ dhūmaśālūkādikam utpadyeta tadā na `
children.translated_text: and so forth. For if the aggregate characterized by being accompanied by another condition of one's own kind, and the aggregate characterized by cow-dung and the like that is independent of one's own kind — [for the lotus-root and the like]; or the aggregate characterized by fire, fuel, and the like, and the aggregate having the nature of the top of <s>Śakra</s>'s [head] and the like, having the nature of smoke and the like — if even from the different aggregate a non-different effect, i.e., one of that very same kind — smoke, lotus-root, and the like — were to arise, then
'of the cause' —
having the form of the aggregate,
'from difference and non-difference' —
from dissimilarity and non-dissimilarity, of the effect,
'difference and non-difference' —
dissimilarity and non-dissimilarity, having the nature of being of the same kind and of a different kind, would not obtain — and thus
'of the universe' —
of the entire collection of things,
'difference and non-difference would be without cause' —

children.text:
sajātīyavijātīyatve syātām | tasmād yatra vilakṣaṇā
sāmagrī tatra kutaścit sāmyāt sarūpatve 'pi vijātīyataiva kāryasyeti |
  nanu dhūmendhanādisāmagrībhede 'pi dhūmasya na jātibhedamāmanti vidvāṃsaḥ, atadrūpaparāvṛtter ubhayatra samāntatvāt, naiṣa doṣaḥ, kṣaṇabhedāśrayasūkṣmāvāntarajātibhede 'pi sthūlasantānāśrayavijātīyavyāvṛtteḥ samānatvāt | śābaleyādyavāntarajātibhedepy agovyāvṛttinibandhanagojātivad gavāṃ [S. 156a.] sarvadhūmānām ekasantānavyavasthāvyu(py u)pādānakāraṇakṣaṇabhede[612]'py ekākārapratyayanibandhanatayā samānatvāt | ādyasyendhanaprabhavasya katham? iti cet | na | indhanajātyanuvidhānāt[613]sarvadhūmānām | tathā hi -- agurukarpūracandanādijātibhedam anukurvanty eva [T. 322a.] taddhūmāḥ, kās aśvāsādiharadravyanirmitavarttibhedaṃ ca taddhūmāḥ, tadrasavīryavipākānuvidhānāt[614]| na cākārānyatayā[615]vijātīyatvam, yato nākārā 'bhedabhedanibandhane sajātīyavijātīyatve | na hi {p. 163.1} śālyaṅkurādayaḥ tadvījādyākāram anukurvate | na ca tajjātīyatāmaśālyādi-
vyāvṛttinibandhanāṃ nānubhavanti | tasmād indhanam eva tasyopādānakāraṇam agnyādisahakāripratyayāhitaviśeṣaṃ tathāvidhaṃ dhūmakāryamaṅgārādi bhinnākṛti janyatīty alam atiprasaṅgena |
  nanu ca yadi nāma sāmagrībhede 'pi kāryasya bhedo na jātaḥ tadā kāraṇabhede saty api tasyābhāvāt tasyāhetukatā 'stu, abhedasya tu kim āyātam? yenobhayor ahetukatvam ucyata ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: being of the same kind and of a different kind would be without cause. Therefore, where the aggregate is different, there, even if there is sameness of form due to some similarity, it is the effect that is of a different kind alone. But the learned do not accept a difference of kind in smoke even when there is difference in the aggregate of fuel and the like, because the exclusion from what is not of that form is the same in both cases — this is not a fault, because even when there is a subtle sub-kind difference based on momentary differences, the exclusion from what is of a different kind, based on the gross continuum, is the same. Just as the cow-kind, grounded in the exclusion from non-cow, obtains even when there is sub-kind difference such as <s>śābaleya</s> (spotted) and the like — so for all smokes, even when there is difference in the moment of the material cause within a single continuum-designation, there is sameness because of being the ground of a cognition of a single form. 'But how [is this the case] for the first [smoke], which originates from fuel?' — No, because all smokes conform to the kind of fuel. For thus: the smokes of aloe, camphor, sandalwood, and the like indeed follow the difference of kind [of their fuels], and the smokes [of lamps] follow the difference of wicks made from substances that ward off asthma and the like, because they conform to the taste, potency, and post-digestive effect [of those fuels]. And otherness of form does not [constitute] being of a different kind, because form is not the ground of same-kindness and different-kindness as [established by] non-difference and difference [respectively]. For rice-sprouts and the like do not replicate the form of their seeds and the like. And yet they do not fail to experience same-kindness, grounded in the exclusion from non-rice and the like. Therefore, fuel alone is its material cause — and possessing the specific feature contributed by the cooperative condition of fire and the like, it produces that kind of smoke-effect, charcoal, and the like, with different appearances — so enough with the over-extension. But if, even when there is difference of aggregate, no difference of effect has arisen, then since that [difference] is absent even when the cause differs, let the causelessness of that [difference] obtain — but what has come of non-difference? Such that the causelessness of both [difference and non-difference] is asserted — to this he says —
'For thus' —

children.translated_text: and so forth. For when, even though there is difference of aggregate, no difference of effect has arisen — and thus the causelessness of that [difference obtains] — for it is in no way tenable that what is absent when the cause is present should be caused — then that
non-difference of the effect too,
since the two aggregates are

bhinnatvād asaty abhede[618]jāta iti kutas tasyāpi hetumattā? | yathā hi hetau saty abhavato na hetumattā tathā hetāv asaty api bhavato hetumattā kutaḥ syāt? | hetubhedasyaivā 'bhedanibandhanatvāt na iti cet; na tarhy ayaṃ bhedaḥ kvacit padam ābadhnīyāt, śālīkodravāder api [T. 322b.] hetubhedasyābhedahetutvān nimittam antareṇa kalpanāyāṃ viśeṣābhāvāt | pratibhāsābhedasya ca kutaścid bhrāntinimittāt paramārthato bhede 'py upalakṣaṇāt | syād etat -- yo hy atādṛśād api tādṛśodbhavam
icchati tasya bhedābhedayor ahetukatvam iṣṭam eva bhāvā eva kevalaṃ hetumanta ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: different, has arisen when non-difference [of cause] is absent — so whence is its being caused? For just as what is absent when the cause is present is not caused, so too how could what is present even when the cause is absent be caused? If [you say:] 'Because difference of cause alone is the ground of non-difference [of effect]' — then this difference should never gain a foothold anywhere, because even for rice and <s>kodrava</s> and the like, difference of cause would be the cause of non-difference, and there would be no distinction in imagining [non-difference] without a ground. And because the non-difference of appearance is only a sign of difference in ultimate reality, due to some cause of error. One might think: 'For one who accepts the arising of something of that kind even from what is not of that kind, the causelessness of both difference and non-difference is indeed accepted — only entities themselves are caused' — to this he says —
'And what is distinct from those' —

children.text:
ityādi | na hi bhedābhedavyatiriktaḥ kaścid bhāvānāṃ svabhāvo 'sti yas tayor ahetukatve 'pi hetumān syāt | tasya tābhyām anyatve `asyemau bhedābhedau' iti[619][S. 157a.] sambandhābhāvaprasaṅgāt, tadanyasambandhakalpanāyām anavasthādoṣāt, ananyatve 'pi bhedābhedayor bhāvasvabhāvasya ca svātmanyevāvasthānāt anupakārāc ca kutaḥ sambandhitā? | upakārakalpanāyāṃ ca yadi bhāvasvabhāvaḥ svahetubhya[620]eva na kutaścid bhinno 'bhinno vā samutpanna itīṣyate, tadā tadbhāve[621]'pi svabhāvānyathātvābhāvāt kuto bhinnābhinnatā bhāvasvabhāvasya syāt? | athā {p. 164.1} vyatiriktabhedābhedavaśād bhedābhedau svabhāvaḥ pratipadyeta, tāv api yadi bhinnau tadā bhāvasvabhāvas tadavastha eveti na tasya kutaścit svarūpato bhedo 'bhedo vā syāt | punas tadvaśād bhedābhedakalpanāyāṃ bhāvasvabhāvasya tadavasthaṃ tādavasthyam
anavasthā [T. 323a.] ca bhedābhedayoḥ | athābhinnau tadā bhāvasvabhāva eva bhedābhedābhyāṃ kriyata iti syāt, tasya rūpāntareṇa karaṇāsambhā(bha)vāt; tasya ca hetvantarāt paścād bhavatas tato 'nyatvāpatteḥ | na ca bhāvasvabhāvaḥ kriyate, tasya svahetor eva nirvṛtteḥ | svahetubhya eva bhāvasvabhāvasya kutaścid bhinnābhinnātmana utpattikalpanāyāṃ vā bhedābhedayor vyatirekavatoḥ vayarthyam; [S. 157b.] bhedābhedabuddher api tata eva siddheḥ | tasmādvaiśeṣikādikalpitayor bhedābhedayor viśeṣasāmānyātmanor[622]ayogāt bhāvasvabhāva eva bhedābhedaśabdavācyaḥ tayor[623]ahetukatve bhāvasvabhāvasyaivāhetukatvam āpatitam | tato bhāvānām ahetukatvān nityaṃ sattvam asattvaṃ vā syāt | ahetukatve hi bhāvānāṃ yadi kadācit sattvaṃ sarvadaiva syāt | atha kadācid asattvaṃ tad api sarvadā syāt | kādācitkatvaṃ tu sattvasyāyuktam | kiṃ kāraṇam? | apekṣyasyāhetukatve sati kasyacid[624]abhāvāt | yasmā
children.translated_text: and so forth. For there is no essential nature of entities distinct from difference and non-difference that would be caused even when those two are causeless. If it were other than those two, then the absurd consequence would be the absence of the relation 'these are the difference and non-difference of this [entity]'; and in imagining another relation with those, there would be the fault of infinite regress; and even if not other, since the essential nature of the entity and difference and non-difference abide in their own selves alone, and because of not providing any assistance — whence is their relatedness? And in imagining assistance: if the essential nature of the entity is accepted as having arisen from its own causes alone, without being in any way different or non-different from anything — then, even when that [entity] exists, because of the absence of otherness of essential nature, whence would there be the differentness or non-differentness of the essential nature of the entity? Or if the essential nature were to undergo difference and non-difference by virtue of difference and non-difference that are separate, then if those two [difference and non-difference] are different [from each other], then the essential nature of the entity remains in its own state — and so there would be no difference or non-difference of it from anything at all. And in imagining difference and non-difference by virtue of those [two], the essential nature of the entity would remain in that same state, and there would be an infinite regress of difference and non-difference. But if those two [difference and non-difference] are non-different, then it would follow that the essential nature of the entity is constituted by difference and non-difference themselves — because it is impossible for it to be made by another form; and because what comes into being later from another cause would be absurdly other than it. And the essential nature of the entity is not made [anew], since it is completed from its own cause alone. Or, in imagining that the essential nature of the entity arises from its own causes alone as having the nature of being different and non-different from something, the difference and non-difference as separate [entities] would be purposeless — since the cognition of difference and non-difference too is established from that [own nature] alone. Therefore, because the difference and non-difference imagined by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> and others — having the nature of particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>) and universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) — are untenable, it is the essential nature of the entity itself that is denoted by the words 'difference' and 'non-difference.' When those two are causeless, the causelessness of the essential nature of the entity itself is entailed. Therefore, from the causelessness of entities, there would be either permanent existence or permanent non-existence. For if entities are without cause, if they exist at some time, they should exist always. And if they are non-existent at some time, that too should be always. But occasional existence is not tenable. What is the reason? Because when what is depended upon is without cause, there is the absence of anything [to depend upon]. Because
'for it is by dependence' —

hetor bhāve bhavanto 'bhāve ca na bhavantaḥ

kadācid bhavā yujyante, nānyatheti | tasmān na vilakṣaṇāt kāraṇāt avilakṣaṇasya kāryasyotpattir abhyupagantavyā, yathoktena nyāyenāhetukatvādiprasaṅgāt |

Therefore, arising from a cause of a different kind should not be accepted for an effect of a non-different kind, because of the absurd consequence of causelessness and the like, by the reasoning stated. Furthermore, he states another fault in the arising of a non-different effect from a different aggregate —
'And the determination' —
'the fixed [relation]' —

pots, cloths, and the like,
'of the means of production' —
of clay, threads, and the like, the worldly

children.text: ghaṭārthī mṛtpiṇḍam eva tatra niyuṅkte na tantūn, paṭārthī ca tantūn eva na mṛtpiṇḍam ityādikaḥ sa na [S. 158a.] syāt | kasmāt? ity āha --
children.translated_text: One desiring a pot employs the clay-lump alone for that, not threads; and one desiring cloth [employs] threads alone, not the clay-lump — and so forth. That [restriction] would not obtain. Why? — [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says —
'Of causes' (<s>kāraṇānām</s>)
— of aggregates, whose
'capacities' (<s>śaktayaḥ</s>)
— characterized as increments in their own [essential nature] — of those,
'in the restriction' (<s>pratiniyame</s>)

'for' (<s>hi</s>)
— because

'Of that very' (<s>tasyaiva</s>)
— of clay and the like —
'there' (<s>tatra</s>)
— in the case of a pot and the like —
'the capacity' (<s>śakteḥ</s>)

'Of another' (<s>anyasya</s>)

tantvādes tatrāśakteḥ | kasmāt tasyaiva tatra śaktir nānyasya
ity ata āha

'Of those two' (<s>tayoḥ</s>)
— of clay and the like, and of threads and the like —
'by [having] the essential nature of producing that' (<s>tajjananasvabhāvatvena</s>)

children.text: anyatvabhāvāt | na hi mṛttantvādirūpatāto 'nyad eva tajjananetarasvabhāvatvaṃ nāma | yadā tu sāmagrīṇāṃ parasparavilakṣaṇānām api śaktipratiniyamo neṣyate vilakṣaṇād api avilakṣaṇakāryopagamāt [T. 324a.] tadā
children.translated_text: — because of otherness. For the nature of producing that and the nature of not producing that is nothing other than the forms of clay, threads, and the like. But when the restriction of capacity among aggregates — even those that are mutually dissimilar — is not accepted, because the production of a non-dissimilar effect even from a dissimilar [aggregate] is accepted, then
'even from [something] dissimilar from what has the essential nature of producing that' (<s>tajjananasvabhāvavilakṣaṇād api</s>)

children.text: dhūmādijananasvabhāvaṃ yat kāraṇam agnīndhanādisāmagrīlakṣaṇaṃ tadvilakṣaṇād api śakramūrddhādeḥ kṣaṇāśrayeṇa vā dhūmādes tasyāgnīndhanādisāmagrījanyasya dhūmasya tatlakṣaṇasya cotpattāv iṣyamāṇāyāṃ

'there is no restriction of the capacity to produce that' (<s>na tajjananaśakteḥ pratiniyamaḥ</s>)
— there is no restriction of the capacity to produce the intended effect characterized as smoke and the like. |
'Therefore' (<s>iti</s>)
— for that reason —

— any effect —

yathādṛṣṭam eva yathādṛṣṭāt[625]|
sarvaṃ [S. 158b.] sarvato jāyeteti yāvat | tasmāc chaktipratiniyamaḥ kāraṇānām abhyupagantavyaḥ | tato vilakṣaṇasāmagrījanmanaḥ kāryasya kutaścit sāmyāt sarūpasyopalakṣaṇe 'py anyādṛśataiveti sarvas tādṛśas tathāvidhajanmeti siddham |
  syānmatam -- vilakṣaṇāyā api sāmagryās tallakṣaṇakāryajananaśaktiḥ samāneti tallakṣaṇaṃ kāryaṃ bhaviṣyati kasyāścid eva ca tathābhāvān na yathoditadoṣāvasara ity ata āha
children.translated_text:
only as observed from what is observed. |
Everything would arise from everything — this is the import. Therefore, the restriction of capacities among causes must be accepted. Hence, even when an effect born from a dissimilar aggregate is observed as having a similar form due to some resemblance, its nature is actually different — and so everything of such a kind has such a birth — this is established. |
  One might think: 'even of a dissimilar aggregate, the capacity to produce an effect of that character is equal — so the effect of that character will [still] arise; and since only for some [aggregates] there is such a state, there is no occasion for the stated fault.' To this [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:
'But if the capacity for producing that is equal' (<s>tajjananaśaktisāmye tu</s>)

children.text: ityādi | uktam eva tāvad atra pūrvapakṣe `na ca dhūmasya tadatajjanyasvabhāvaḥ' ityādikaṃ dūṣaṇam | abhyupagamyāpīdam āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. The refutation stated in the prima facie view — 'nor does smoke have the essential nature of being produced by that and not produced by that' — and so forth — has already been stated. But even granting [the opponent's position], [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says —
'Whatever [capacity] of the fire-cooperative-cause' (<s>yādṛśī hy agnisahakāriṇaḥ</s>)
— of fuel whose transformation is being deposited by that [fire] —
— of fuel —
— being the cause of the difference of smoke through its own difference —
'the capacity' (<s>śaktiḥ</s>)

children.text:
ātmātiśayas tādṛśyeva śakramūrddhno[627]{p. 166.1} dhūmasya vā yadi tatsāmagrījanyadhūmāvilakṣaṇakāryajananaśaktir ātmātiśayalakṣaṇā tadā tacchaktisāmye tadevāgnīndhanādikam evārthān nāmāntareṇoktaṃ syāt, tadvilakṣaṇasya tadvilakṣaṇātmātiśayāsambhavāt | sa eva hy agnir ya indhanavikāramādadhāno dhūmaṃ janayati, tac cendhanaṃ yadagninā ''dhīyamānavikāraṃ dhūmaṃ
svajātim anukārayati | yadi [S. 159a.] ca śakramūrddhāder api evaṃ bhavatā 'bhyupagamyate tadā kevalaṃ nāmni vivādaḥ syāt, arthābhedam abhyupagamya tathābhidhānāt yata evam
children.translated_text: — the increment of its own [essential nature] — if [there is] just such [a capacity] of the peak of <s>Śakra</s>'s [throne] or of smoke, i.e., if the capacity to produce an effect non-dissimilar from the smoke produced by that [fire-fuel] aggregate, characterized as an increment of its own [essential nature] — then, given the equality of that capacity, that would simply be the very fire and fuel and the like, stated under another name, since something dissimilar to that cannot possibly have an increment of that [same] nature. For fire is precisely that which, depositing the transformation of fuel, produces smoke; and fuel is precisely that whose transformation, being deposited by fire, replicates its own kind as smoke. If [the opponent] accepts that this is so even of the peak of <s>Śakra</s>'s [throne] and the like, then the dispute would be merely about the name, since a difference in meaning is not accepted even while stating it so. Since thus,
'therefore' (<s>iti</s>)
— for that reason —
'the effect' (<s>kāryam</s>)
— smoke and the like —
'observed' (<s>dṛṣṭam</s>)
— once ascertained through perception and non-apprehension, with a self that is excluded from what does not have that form —
'the cause' (<s>kāraṇam</s>)
— fuel and the like, with reference to the continuum or to the moment —
'does not deviate' (<s>na vyabhicarati</s>)

tadvilakṣaṇād anyato na bhavatīti kāryahetāv anvayavyatirekaniścayaḥ sidhyatīti |[628]

4. Examination of non-apprehension as a reason (<s>anupalabdhihetunirūpaṇam</s>)
Section: 1. Presentation of the essential nature of non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>), preceded by the display of disagreement.

body.translated_text: If, however, of the lotus-root and the like born from cow-dung and the like, or of smoke and the like born from fire and fuel and the like — even though grounded in a different aggregate, by the force of recognition they would have the very same essential nature — what fault would there be? To this he says —

-- `upalambhapratyayāntarāṇāṃ[630]samanantarādhipatipratyayasaṃjñitānāṃ sākalyam, ālambanapratyayasya svabhāvaviśeṣaś ca | yaḥ svabhāvaḥ satsv anyeṣūpalambhapratyayeṣu san pratyakṣa eva bhavatī'ty evaṃrūpāśāstrakṛtā'nyatra {p. 168.1} vyākhyātānaiyāyikavipratipattinirāsārtham | te hy anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptiśabdena mahattvānekadravyavattvarūpāṇi dravyāṇām āhuḥ |
children.translated_text:
generating the cognition 'it does not exist' in the negative aspect, [the cognition] obtains the name 'means of cognizing absence,' just as the sense-faculty obtains the name 'perception' (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) by virtue of generating the apprehension of its own object. Likewise, others say that non-apprehension — whether characterized as the existence of another entity, or as the cognition of that — is the means of establishing only non-existence itself, not the conventional usage of non-existence, since upon the establishment of non-existence from the inferential mark of non-apprehension, the conventional usage itself proceeds spontaneously. The <s>Naiyāyikas</s>, however, say that the cognition 'it does not exist' — being perceptual, arising immediately after a cognition that grasps bare location and the like — is not a separate means of valid cognition but is simply the determination of non-existence, which is of a void nature. If that very [cognition] is called 'non-apprehension' with the word denoting the negatable — the pot and the like — there is no conflict at all. | Thus, since the intellects of the opponents have diverged regarding non-apprehension, in order to refute them, first displaying the essential nature of non-apprehension, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says: 'of what fulfills the conditions for apprehension (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>)' and so forth. 'Fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension' —
'is the completeness of the other conditions of apprehension called <s>samanantara</s> (immediately preceding) and <s>adhipati</s> (dominant) conditions, as well as the specific essential nature [serving as] the objective condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>). That essential nature which, when the other conditions of apprehension are present, becomes directly perceptible' — of such a form, was explained elsewhere by the author of the treatise, for the purpose of refuting the disagreement of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>. For they say that the word 'fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension' refers to the properties of substances such as magnitude (<s>mahattva</s>), being constituted of multiple substances (<s>anekadravyavatva</s>), and form (<s>rūpa</s>). |

children.translated_text: | And thus, they say that non-apprehension of what fulfills the conditions for apprehension is possible even when the real entity exists — so [non-apprehension] is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntikī</s>) in establishing the conventional usage of non-existence. For the visual ray too, even though it is visible, is not apprehended through magnitude, being constituted of multiple substances, or form. And yet, merely because of that, non-apprehension cannot serve to establish the conventional usage of non-existence with respect to it. As the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> says: 'The non-apprehension through direct perception of what is apprehended through inference is not a reason for [establishing] non-existence.'
<s>Durveka</s>: the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> is <s>Pakṣilasvāmī</s>, the author of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s>

upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpter aviparītarūpopadarśanenaśāstrakāro 'bhyadhāt | yadāhy upalambhapratyayāntarasākalyaṃ svabhāvaviśeṣaś ca yathokta upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptir ucyate na mahattvādikaṃ tadā kuto vyabhicārāvakāśaḥ?, sati vastuni tasyāasambhavāt | mahattvādikaṃtv asambhavād eva nopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptiśabdena vācyam | na hi rūpādivyatiriktaṃ dravyaṃ tatpratibhāsavivekinā ''kārāntareṇa svajñāne pratibhāsate | na cāpratibhāsamānam anātmarūpavivekinā
rūpeṇa pratyakṣatām anubhavaty atiprasaṅgāt | tat kuto 'syā 'sato mahattvādisambhavaḥ? | na ca svarūpeṇāmahataḥ tatsambandhe 'py asya mahattāsambhavaḥ | apararūpeṇa[633]vā grahaṇe kathaṃtadgrāhijñānam[634]abhrāntam? | tato na mahattvaṃ dravyasyopalambhakaṃrūpaṃ vā | tasyāpi svarūpeṇa grahaṇe dravyātmano 'tyantaparokṣatvāt | dravyarūpasya ca [S. 161a.] tadvivekenānupalakṣaṇān na tathāgrāhakatvam | na ca mahattvaṃ rūpaṃ vā dravyodayakāle 'bhyupagamyate, yato dravyaṃ guṇasya samavāyikāraṇam iṣyate | tac ca pratilabdhātmakam eva tathātām anubhavatīti prathame kṣaṇe dravyaṃ nirguṇam eva | na cāsya
children.translated_text: — the author of the treatise undertook by demonstrating the correct form of 'fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension.' For when the completeness of the other conditions of apprehension and the specific essential nature as stated are called 'fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension' — not magnitude and the like — then whence the occasion for deviation?, since that is impossible when the real entity exists. Magnitude and the like, however, since they are simply impossible [as the correct definition], should not be expressed by the term 'fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension.' For a substance distinct from form and the like does not appear in one's own cognition with an aspect that discriminates [it] from the appearance of those [form etc.]. And what does not appear — [it] does not undergo direct perceptibility through a form that discriminates what is not its own nature, because of over-extension. So whence the possibility of magnitude and the like for it — something that is non-existent? Nor, even in connection with what is not great by its own nature, is there a possibility of its being great. Or if grasped through another form, how could the cognition that grasps it be non-erroneous? Therefore, neither magnitude nor form is what makes a substance apprehensible. For even in the case of [form], if grasped by its own nature, the substance-nature would be utterly imperceptible. And since the substance-form is not observed as distinct from that [form] — [there is] no such apprehending capacity. Nor are magnitude and form accepted at the time of the arising of substance, since substance is accepted as the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) of quality. And that [substance] experiences that status [as inherent cause] only when it has obtained its own nature — so in the first moment, the substance is without qualities alone. And of it,
'of it' : 'of its own'

dvitīye kṣaṇe prāktanarūpatyāgo 'sti rūpāntaraṃ vā ''virbhavati yataḥ{p. 169.1} prāgapratipannādhārabhāvaṃ mahattvādiguṇapratibandhād ādhāratāṃ yāyāt | na cājanaka ādhāraḥ | janakatve ca [T. 326b.] kṣaṇikatā, arthakriyāvirodhād akṣaṇikasya | tataḥ
kutaḥ samavāyikāraṇasya sambhavaḥ?, yataḥsvotkalitaṃkāryaṃ janayat tathā vyapadiśyate | na caitat kṣaṇikatve sambhavati akṣaṇikatve vā prāg 'nādhārasya paścādādhārābhāvaḥ| samavāyikāraṇāsambhavād evānekadravyavattvam apy asambhavi yasmād anekaṃ dravyam ārambhakaṃ samavāyikāraṇātmanā yasya vidyate tad evaṃvyapadiśyate | dravyābhāvāc ca nānekadravyavattvaṃ | sattve 'pi mahattvāder neyam upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptir asmākam abhimatā |
children.translated_text:
at the second moment, there is either the abandonment of the previous form, or an alternative form manifests — by which, {p. 169.1} having not previously been apprehended as having the nature of a substratum, [the entity], because of the restriction by a quality such as magnitude, would attain the status of being a substratum. And a non-producer is not a substratum. And if it were a producer, then momentariness [would follow], because of the contradiction of causal efficacy for the non-momentary. Then
how is the existence of an inherence-cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) possible? — since that which, having raised up its own effect, produces it, is so designated. And this is not possible in [either] momentariness or non-momentariness — [in the latter] because what was previously not a substratum would not become a substratum later. Since the inherence-cause is impossible, the property of being constituted by multiple substances (<s>anekadravyavatva</s>) is also impossible, because that which has multiple substances as its originative inherence-cause is so designated. And since substances do not exist, there is no property of being constituted by multiple substances. Even if existence [is granted to them] — for magnitude and the like — this [kind of] fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti</s>) is not what we accept.

| yātu pratiṣedhyasyaivopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhiḥ sā 'bhāvavyavahārahetur eveti vāśabdena darśayati | yā tv
anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhiḥ pratyakṣānumānanivṛttilakṣaṇā sā saṃśayahetuḥ pramāṇanivṛttāv apy arthābhāvāsiddheḥ, nimittābhāvāt tu sadvyavahārapratiṣedhahetur ity avagantavyam |
children.translated_text: | But the non-apprehension of that which fulfills the conditions for apprehension of the very thing to be negated — that is a ground only for the convention of absence — this [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] shows by the word 'or' (<s>vā</s>). But the non-apprehension of that which fulfills the conditions for non-apprehension — characterized by the cessation of direct perception and inference — that is a ground for doubt, because the absence of the object is not established even when the <s>pramāṇa</s> ceases, [only] because of the absence of the ground [for affirmation]. However, it is a ground for negating the convention of existence — thus it should be understood.

body.translated_text: Thus, regarding the effect-reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>), since whatever is observed once as arising from something through perception and non-apprehension, then all of that kind arises from that very kind alone and not from what is of a different type — thus, from the observation of even a single instance of an effect arising from something, the establishment of positive and negative concomitance through pervasion has been demonstrated. But regarding non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) as stated — there is no disagreement about the positive and negative concomitance grounded in the demonstration of the absence of alternative causes. The opponents disagree, however, about [its] essential nature alone. For thus: some — <s>Īśvarasena</s> and others — accepting non-apprehension as a mere absence of apprehension, regard it as a separate means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇāntara</s>) that conveys the absolute negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>) [that is] the non-existence [of the object]. Others — the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> — say that either a cognition not transforming in the form of the object of negation,

upalabhamānasya yajjñānaṃ tad upalabdhir ucyate | upalabhamānaś ca buddhīndriyadehakalāpa eva ca pūrvakṣaṇasaṅgṛhīta[636]upalabdhijanaka ucyate | tathā hi -- upalabdher janaka āśrayo vā karttā parair ucyate | na {p. 170.1} cendriyāder anyasya janakatvaṃ [S. 162a.] sambhavati yato 'nvayavyatirekanibandhanaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvavyavahāraḥ, tau cānvayavyatirekau nendriyāder anyasya sambhavataḥ satsv indriyādiṣu niyamenopalabdher bhāvāt | yadi
hīndriyādiṣu satsv api kadācid upalabdhir nopajāyate tadā satsv apy anyeṣu sakaleṣu hetuṣu kāryānutpattiḥ kāraṇāntaravaikalyaṃ sūcayatīti tadvyatiriktakāraṇāntaraṃ parikalpyeta | na caitad asti, tat katham ātmanas tadutpattau nimittabhāvo[637]'bhyupagamyeta? atiprasaṅgāt | yad āha -
children.translated_text:
the cognition that belongs to one who apprehends — that is called apprehension. And 'one who apprehends' is said to be the aggregate of the mental faculty, sense organ, and body, included in the preceding moment — the producer of apprehension. For thus: the producer or the locus of apprehension is called the agent by others. And {p. 170.1} the capacity of producing [apprehension] is not possible for anything other than the sense faculties and the like, because the convention of cause-effect relation is grounded in positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>), and those two — positive and negative concomitance — are not possible for anything other than the sense faculties and the like, since apprehension necessarily occurs when the sense faculties and the like are present. For
if apprehension were sometimes not to arise even when the sense faculties and the like are present, then — just as when all other causes are present but the effect does not arise, it indicates a deficiency of some other causal factor — some other causal factor distinct from those [sense faculties] would be postulated. But this [other factor] does not exist. So how could the status of the self (<s>ātman</s>) as a basis for its production be accepted? — Because of the absurd consequence. As [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:

children.text: yasmin sati bhavaty eva yat tato 'nyasya kalpane |
children.translated_text: 'When something exists and [the effect] necessarily exists, to postulate yet another [cause] —
as its cause — would lead to the non-fixedness of causes everywhere.' ||
PV I 26

  evam upalabdhim ādarśyānupalabdhim ādarśayann āha -- tasmād upalabdhijñānād anyā vastvantaraviṣayā upalabdhiḥ jñānātmikā anupalabdhiḥ | kathaṃ punar upalabdhir evānupalabhdir ucyate? ity āha -- vivakṣitetyādi | yathā bhakṣyābhakṣyaprakaraṇe vivakṣitād bhakṣyād anyatvād `abhakṣyo grāmyakukkuṭaḥ' -- bhakṣyo 'pi san tadanyasya -- ucyate | yathā ca sparśanīyāsparśanīyādhikāre vivakṣitāt sparśanīyād anyatvād `asparśanīyaś cāṇḍālādiḥ' -- tadanyasya sparśanīyo 'pi san -- ucyate | {p. 171.1} tadvad upalabdhir evānupalabdhir mmantavyā | nañaḥ pratiṣedhaviṣayatvāt kathaṃ bhāvaviṣayatā? iti cet, āha --
children.translated_text:
— this is the established doctrine of others. [If one says:] 'The locus is so because of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>)' — but that too is accepted only between what supports and what is supported. And for apprehension, which has the nature of not-falling, a support [serves] no purpose. And if locus-status [is established] through inherence, then the absurd consequence that anything else too would have that status [would follow], since that [inherence] is the same in all selves, because it is accepted as one. And because of the contradiction of causal efficacy through succession and simultaneity, the existence of this self is not [established] — so how can it have the status of producer? Or of being a locus? Enough with pulverizing what has already been crushed.
  Thus, having shown apprehension, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>], showing non-apprehension, says: therefore, non-apprehension is an apprehension — having the nature of cognition — that is different from the cognition of apprehension and has a different object. But how can apprehension itself be called non-apprehension? — he says: 'the intended' and so forth. Just as in the context of what is edible and inedible, the village rooster is called 'inedible' — though edible — because of being other than the intended edible [thing] — 'the village rooster is inedible.' And just as in the context of what is touchable and untouchable, the <s>caṇḍāla</s> and the like is called 'untouchable' — though touchable — because of being other than the intended touchable [thing] — 'the <s>caṇḍāla</s> is untouchable.' {p. 171.1} Likewise, apprehension itself should be understood as non-apprehension. [If one says:] 'Since the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) has negation as its domain, how can it have a positive entity as its domain?' — he says:
'By the function of exclusion (<s>paryudāsavṛtti</s>)' —

children.text:
| paryudāsena pratiṣedhyasyārthasya varjanena yā viśiṣṭe 'rthe vṛttis tayā, nañaḥ āgṛhītapratiṣedhasya[640]bhāvaviṣayatā | yatra vidheḥ [S. 163a.] prādhānyaṃ pratiṣedho 'rthagṛhītaḥ vidhibhāk svapadena nocyate ekavākyatā ca tatra paryudāsavṛttitā
| vidheś ca prādhānyaṃ `vivakṣitopalabdher anyopalabdhir bhavati' ity evaṃ vākyenānyopalabdher vidhānāt [T. 328a.] anyopalabdhisāmarthyād eva vivakṣitopalabdheḥ pratiṣedhaḥ pratīyate | vivakṣitopalabdher anivarttane tadapekṣayā 'nyasyā vidhānāyogāt svapadena nañā vidhibhāṅ nocyate | kiṃ tarhi? | anyaśabdena paryudāsāśrayeṇā 'nyaśabdasyaiva vākye prayogāt anyā upalabdhir anupalabdhir iti | nañaś ca subantena sāmarthyaṃ na tiṅantena ity ekavākyatvaṃ `na upalabdhir anupalabdhiḥ' iti | prasajyapratiṣedhaḥ punar etadviparīto mantavyaḥ | tatra hi pratiṣedhasya prādhānyaṃ vidhir arthād gamyate vākyabhedaḥ svapadena nañā pratiṣedhabhāk sambadhyate |
  tad evaṃ jñātṛdharmalakṣaṇām anupalabdhiṃ vyākhyāya jñeyadharmalakṣaṇāṃ pratipādayann āha --
children.translated_text:
thus. By exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>) — by the elimination of the meaning to be negated — the function that obtains with respect to a qualified meaning — by that [function], the negative particle, whose negation is implicitly grasped, has a positive entity as its domain. Where affirmation predominates, [and] the negation is grasped by implication, partaking of affirmation, not expressed by its own word, and there is syntactic unity — there is the function of exclusion.
And the predominance of affirmation [obtains] because, by the statement 'there is an apprehension other than the intended apprehension,' the other apprehension is being affirmed; and through the very capacity of the other apprehension, the negation of the intended apprehension is understood. Without the exclusion of the intended apprehension, the affirmation of the other with reference to it would be untenable; [the negation] is not expressed by its own word, the negative particle, as partaking of affirmation. What then? By the word 'other' — which is the basis of the exclusion — since the word 'other' alone is used in the sentence: 'the other apprehension is non-apprehension.' And the negative particle has syntactic connection with a nominal form, not with a verbal form — thus the syntactic unity [is]: 'not-apprehension is non-apprehension.' The verbal negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>), on the other hand, should be understood as the opposite of this. For there, negation predominates, the affirmation is understood from the meaning, there is sentence-division, [and] the negative particle, partaking of negation, is connected by its own word.
  Thus, having explained non-apprehension characterized as a property of the knower (<s>jñātṛdharma</s>), [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>], establishing [non-apprehension] characterized as a property of the knowable (<s>jñeyadharma</s>), says:
'Having the property of being apprehended' —

children.text: tyādi | yadā karmasthakriyāpekṣayopalabhyamānasya vastuno dharma upalabdhir vivakṣyate tadā viṣayasvabhāva upalabdhir mantavyā | kīdṛśo [S. 163b.] viṣayasvabhāvaḥ? ity āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. When apprehension is intended as a property of an object (<s>vastu</s>) being apprehended, from the standpoint of the activity with respect to the object (<s>karmastha</s>), then apprehension should be understood as the nature of the object-domain (<s>viṣayasvabhāva</s>). What kind of object-domain nature? — he says:
'In its own domain' —

children.text: tyādi | pratiṣedhyasya ghaṭāder yadātmaviṣayaṃ vijñānaṃ tajjanane yā yogyatā tallakṣaṇo viṣayasvabhāva upalabdhiśabdenocyate | yadi viṣayasvabhāva upalabdhiḥ kathaṃ yogyatālakṣaṇaḥ? | tathā hi yogyatā dharmaḥ, dharmadharmiṇoś ca bheda eva ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. The fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) for generating the cognition whose domain is the self of the thing to be negated — a pot and the like — that which has such a character is called 'apprehension' in the sense of the nature of the object-domain. If apprehension is the nature of the object-domain, how is it characterized by fitness? For thus: fitness is a property, and there is indeed a distinction between property and property-bearer — therefore he says:
'Of the fitness' —

children.text:
ityādi | yogyatā hi paramārthato [T. 328b.] bhāvarūpaiva na vastusvarūpād bhidyate, anyathā bhāvo yogya eva na syāt | yogyatā 'syeti ca sambandho bhāvato na syāt | sambandhakalpanāyām anavasthety uktaprāyam |
  tad evam upalabdher viṣayadharmatāṃ pratipādyānupalabdher api pratipādayann āha
children.translated_text:
and so forth. For fitness, in ultimate reality, is of the very nature of a positive entity and does not differ from the intrinsic nature of the real thing. Otherwise, the entity would not be fit at all. And the relation 'fitness belongs to this [entity]' would not be real. And in postulating a relation, [there would be] an infinite regress — this has been mostly stated.
  Thus, having established the object-property-nature of apprehension, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>], establishing that of non-apprehension as well, says:
'Therefore, another' —
and so forth.
'Therefore' —

children.text: pratiṣedhyād ghaṭādeḥ {p. 172.1} svaviṣayajñānajananayogyād[641]yo 'nya upalambhajananayogya eva na tadviparītaḥ svabhāvo ghaṭaviviktapradeśarūpaḥ sa eva cātrānupalabdhiśabdenocyate | prāktanam eva nyāyam atrādiśann[642]āha
children.translated_text: another essential nature — different from the thing to be negated, a pot and the like, which is fit for generating cognition of its own domain — [an essential nature] that is fit only for generating apprehension and not its opposite — having the form of a location distinct from the pot — that alone is here called 'non-apprehension.' Indicating the same principle as before, he says:
'As before' —
thus.

children.text: | vivakṣitopalabdher anyatvād abhakṣyāsparśanīyavat paryudāsavṛttyeti | kathaṃ punar ayaṃ nañ anyārthavṛttiḥ sāmānyaśabdaḥ san ghaṭaviviktapradeśasya [S. 164a.] tajjñānasyaiva
children.translated_text: | Because of being other than the intended apprehension, like the inedible and the untouchable, by the function of exclusion (<s>paryudāsavṛtti</s>). But how does this negative particle, being a general word that functions in the sense of 'other,' establish the non-apprehension-ness of precisely the location distinct from the pot, or of precisely

children.text: vā ghaṭaviviktasyānupalabdhitvaṃ[643]paryudāsavṛttyā prakalpayati, na punar aviśeṣeṇa sarveṣām evānyaśabdavācyānām? ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: the cognition distinct from the pot, by the function of exclusion, and not of all other things that are expressible by the word 'other' without distinction? — Therefore he says:
'Where' (<s>yatra</s>) —
and so forth.
'Where' —
in a place, time, or condition characterized by non-obstruction and the like,
'which' (<s>yasmin</s>) —
a form of a location and the like —
'being apprehended, necessarily' —
with certainty —
'of which other' —
entity — a form of a pot and the like — 'there is apprehension' —
'that' —
entity — a form of a pot and the like —
'is connected with that' —

children.text: tena pradeśarūpādinā saṃsṛṣṭaḥ | katham ekasminn upalabhyamāne parasyāpi niyamopalabdhiḥ? iti cet, yogyatāyā aviśeṣāt | [T. 329a.] pradeśaghaṭayor hi svaviṣayavijñānajanane yogyatā tulyā | yadā hi pradeśarūpaṃ vyavadhānaviprakarṣādirahitaṃ vijñāne svākāraṃ samarppayati tadā ghaṭarūpam api tatra[644]tathāvidhaṃ svākāraṃ samarppayaty eva | yadi nāma yogyatā tasya tena tulyā svasvabhāvavyavasthites tu kathaṃ tatsaṃsṛṣṭatā? ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: connected with that form of a location and the like. How is it that when one is apprehended, there is necessarily the apprehension of the other too? — if asked: because of the non-distinction of fitness. For the fitness of the location and the pot for generating cognition of their own domains is equal. For when the form of a location, free from obstruction and remoteness and the like, delivers its own image to cognition, then the form of a pot too, being of such a character, necessarily delivers its own image to that [cognition]. [If one says:] 'Even if the fitness of that [pot] is equal to that [location], because of the fixedness of their own respective essential natures, how can there be connection with that?' — therefore he says:
'Because of the contact in a single cognition' —

children.text: ti | ekatra hi jñāne dvāv api tau svākāradvāreṇa saṃsṛṣṭau na sākṣāt, tadvijñānaṃ padārthadvayākāram ājāyamānaṃ tayor ātmani saṃsarggaṃ darśayati | kim iti punas tat jñānaṃ padārthadvayākāram avaśyaṃ [S. 164b.] bhavati yatas tayor jñānadvārakaḥ saṃsarggaḥ? ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: thus. For in a single cognition, both of those are connected through the door of their own images, not directly. That cognition, arising with the image of both objects, shows their connection in its own self. But why must that cognition necessarily have the image of both objects, such that their connection would be through the door of cognition? — Therefore he says:
'When both of those exist' —

children.text:
ityādi
| yāv etau tulyayogyatārūpau tau yadi santau bhavatas tadā naivaikākāraniyatā pratipattir bhavati | kasmāt? asambhavāt | na hy eṣa sambhavo 'sti -- yat tulyayogyatārūpayor eka eva pratibhāseta nāpara iti | tathā hi -- aviśiṣṭatvād yogyatāyāḥ kas tatra svākāraṃ na samarppayet? | anubhavasiddhiṃ ca yugapad anekapratibhāsanam | na cānubhavaviruddham ācakṣaṇā viduṣām avadheyavacaso bhavanti | laghuvṛttitvād yaugapadyābhimāna iti cet; na, {p. 173.1} bādhakapratyayaviraheṇa bhrāntikalpanānupapatteḥ [T. 329b.] sarvatra tathābhāvaprasaṅgāt | karaṇadharma evāyaṃ yad ekasminn eva karmaṇi kriyāṃ niṣpādayati nānekatra, karaṇaṃ cendriyaṃ tato nānekapratipattihetur iti cet, kathaṃ pradīpādir anekatra bahūnāṃ pratipattijanakaḥ? | kartṛbhedād adoṣa iti cet; karttrekatvāt tarhi kriyaikatra karmāṇīti kathaṃ `karaṇadharmaḥ' ityādi vaco na plavate? | na ca pratikṣaṇaviśarāruṣu bhāveṣu paramārthataḥ kartṛkaraṇādibhāvo [S. 165a.] yuktaḥ
kriyā vā kācit | na ca sarrvakārakānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyini kārye kasyacid atiśayo 'sti yenāyaṃ karttā kā(ka)raṇaṃ cedam ityādi parikalpyeta | tasmād aviśiṣṭayogyatayoḥ kuta ekarūpaniyatāyāḥ pratipatteḥ sambhavaḥ? iti siddha ekajñānasaṃsarggaḥ | tulyayogyatārūpatvasya caitad[645]eva liṅgam | na hy asati tulyayogyatārūpatve yugapad ekendriyajanitajñānapratibhāsitā rūparasavat sambhavatīti |
  tatra yeṣāṃsaugatānām idaṃ darśanaṃ `ekāyatanasaṅgṛhīte 'nekatrāpy ekam evendriyajñānam ājāyate' iti teṣāṃ mukhya evaikajñānasaṃsarggaḥ | ye tu `tatrāpi pratyarthaṃ bhinnāny evaikendriyanimittāny ekakālāni tadviṣayāṇāṃ yugapat sannihitānāṃ svajñāneṣu sāmarthyāviśeṣāt, ata[646]evaikatayā loke 'dhyavasīyamānāni jñānāny upajāyante` iti varṇayanti [T. 330a.] teṣām ekendriyajatvenaikāyatanaviṣayatvena caikakāleṣv
children.translated_text:
and so forth. If those two, which have the form of equal capability, exist, then the cognition restricted to a single form does not occur. Why? Because it is impossible. For there is no possibility that of two [objects] with equal capability, only one would appear and not the other. Thus: since their capability is undistinguished, who among them would not contribute its own form [to cognition]? And the simultaneous appearance of many [objects in cognition] is established through experience. And those who assert what contradicts experience do not have words worthy of attention from the learned. If [one argues:] 'the notion of simultaneity is due to the swiftness of [cognitive] operation' — no, because in the absence of an invalidating cognition, the supposition of error is untenable, and the absurd consequence of the same [error] everywhere [would follow]. If [one argues:] 'it is the very nature of the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) that it accomplishes action with respect to only one object and not many, and the instrument is the sense-faculty, therefore it is not the cause of cognition of many [objects]' — then how does a lamp and the like produce cognition of many [objects] in many [persons]? If [one argues:] 'there is no fault because of the difference of agents' — then, since the agent is one, the action [applies] to the objects in one [locus] — so how does the statement 'it is the nature of the instrument' and the like not float away [i.e., fail]? And in entities that are disintegrating at each moment, the agent-instrument relation and the like is not ultimately tenable, nor is there any action whatsoever. And in an effect that conforms to the positive and negative correlation of all the <s>kāraka</s>s, there is no pre-eminence of any one [factor] by which 'this is the agent and this is the instrument' and the like could be supposed. Therefore, for those two with undistinguished capability, whence the possibility of cognition restricted to a single form? Thus, the association in a single cognition is established. And this very [association in a single cognition] is the mark of having the form of equal capability. For without having the form of equal capability, simultaneous appearance in cognition generated by a single sense-faculty is not possible, as with color and taste.
There, for those <s>Saugata</s>s (Buddhists) whose view is: 'even with respect to many [objects] comprehended under a single sense-base (<s>āyatana</s>), only a single sense-faculty cognition arises' — for them, the association in a single cognition is primary. But for those who explain: 'even there, with respect to each object, the cognitions generated by a single sense-faculty, being simultaneous, [are in fact] distinct, because there is no distinction in capacity among their [respective] cognitions with respect to [objects] that are simultaneously proximate in their own [perceptual fields]; and therefore cognitions arise that are determined as one in the world' —

children.text:
ekatvavyapadeśo loke[647]tathādhyavasāyād aupacārikaḥ |
  yadi nāmaikajñānasaṃsarggāt tatsaṃsṛṣṭasyāpi [S. 165b.] sāmānyena sarvam anyam ayaṃ nañ kin na pratipādayati? iti ata āha --
children.translated_text:
for them, the designation of unity, due to being generated by a single sense-faculty and having a single sense-base as [their] object at the same time, is figurative (<s>aupacārika</s>), based on such determination in the world.
Even if, from the association in a single cognition, the negative [particle] excludes everything else from that which is so associated — even in general — why does it not indicate [that]? To this he says:
'Therefore' —

children.text: ityādi | yasmād aviśiṣṭatvād yogyatāyā yathoktena prakāreṇaikatra jñāne dvayor api saṃsarggaḥ tasmād aviśiṣṭaṃ yogyatārūpaṃ yayoḥ tata evaikajñānasaṃsarggiṇau tau tasmāt tayor evaṃrūpayoḥ
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since, because of the undistinguished nature of capability, there is the association of both in a single cognition in the manner stated, therefore those two that are associated in a single cognition precisely because of their undistinguished form of capability — therefore, of those two of such a form,
'the otherness is only with reference to each other' —
'not with reference to all other objects' —
'otherness here' —
'in the section on non-apprehension' —
'is intended' —

children.text: | loke tu yady aviśeṣapadārthāntarāpekṣam anyatvaṃ nañā kvacid ucyate vyāptinyāyasamāśrayāt, tathāpi tad iha na gṛhyate, {p. 174.1}
children.translated_text: but in the world, if otherness with reference to other undistinguished objects is sometimes expressed by the negative [particle] based on the principle of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion), even so that is not accepted here,
'because of relying on proximity (<s>pratyāsatti</s>)' —

children.text:
ekajñānasaṃsarggalakṣaṇā prattyāsattir āśrīyate nā 'nyā pramāṇacintādhikārāt anyathā 'nupalabdhir anaikāntikyeva syāt | tasmāt tattvacintakais tathāvidham anyatvam āśrayaṇīyam yad anupalabdher avyabhicāranibandhanam | tac ca yathoktam evety abhiprāyaḥ |
  tad evam ekajñānasaṃsarggāpekṣayā 'nyatvaṃ pratipādyānupalabdhiṃ darśayann āha --
children.translated_text:
the proximity characterized by association in a single cognition is relied upon, and no other, since this is the domain of <s>pramāṇa</s>-investigation. Otherwise, non-apprehension would simply be inconclusive. Therefore, those who contemplate reality should rely on such otherness as is the basis for the non-deviation of non-apprehension. And that is precisely as stated — this is the purport.
Having thus explained otherness relative to association in a single cognition, showing the non-apprehension, he says:
'That [place] alone' —

children.text: ityādi | sa eva yadā kevalaḥ pradeśo yathoktaghaṭāpekṣayā tasmād anya ucyate [S. 166a.] tadā ghaṭaviviktapradeśajñānaṃ [T. 330b.] vā 'nupalabdhiḥ, na tu yatheśvaraseno manyate upalabdhyabhāvamātram anupalabdhir iti, vakṣyamāṇadoṣāt; ghaṭaviviktapradeśasvabhāvo vā; na tu tadviviktajñānam eva yathāhakumārilaḥ
children.translated_text: and so forth. When that very place alone is said to be other, with reference to the pot as described — then the cognition of a place devoid of a pot, or [the cognition itself] is non-apprehension; but not as <s>Īśvarasena</s> thinks — that the mere absence of apprehension is non-apprehension — because of the fault to be stated later. Or [non-apprehension is] the essential nature of a place devoid of that [pot]; but not that the cognition devoid of that alone [constitutes non-apprehension], as <s>Kumārila</s> says:
'Or a cognition directed at another object' —
ŚlV <s>abhāvapariccheda</s> 11d.

children.text:
iti | yathā hy anyavastuviṣayaṃ jñānam anubhūyamānaṃ pratiyogismaraṇāpekṣaṃ tadabhāvavyavahāranibandhanaṃ tathā tadviviktaḥ pradeśo 'pi | tathā hi -- kasyacit pratipattuḥ `yataḥ kevalapradeśākāram eva jñānaṃ mayā saṃvedyate na tu ghaṭākāram api tasmād atra ghaṭo nāsti` iti evaṃ nāstitājñānam utpadyate; kasyacit tu `yataḥ kevalaḥ pradeśo 'yaṃ dṛśyate na tu ghaṭasahitaḥ tasmān nāsty atra ghaṭaḥ` ity
evam | tasmād ubhayor nāstitājñānajanmani tulyaṃ sāmarthyam iti dvayor api anupalabdhivyavasthā yukteti | tatra yadā tajjñānaṃ tadā jñātṛdharmalakṣaṇā 'nupalabdhiḥ kartṛsthakriyā 'pekṣayā yadā tatsvabhāvas tadā jñeyadharmalakṣaṇā karmasthakriyāpekṣayeti |
  evam anupalabdhiṃ [S. 166b.] paryudāsavṛttyā vyavasthāpya sādhyam asyā darśayann āha --
children.translated_text:
Thus. For just as cognition directed at another object, being experienced, dependent on the recollection of the counter-correlate, is the basis for the conventional usage of absence — so too is a place devoid of that [object]. Thus: for some cognizer, the absence-cognition arises thus: 'since only a cognition of the form of the bare place is experienced by me and not also one of the form of a pot, therefore there is no pot here.' For another, [it arises] thus: 'since this bare place is seen and not [the place] accompanied by a pot, therefore there is no pot here.' Therefore, both have equal capacity for producing absence-cognition, and so the determination of non-apprehension is appropriate for both. There, when [one considers] that cognition, it is non-apprehension characterized as a property of the knower (<s>jñātṛdharma</s>), with respect to the action situated in the agent. When [one considers] that essential nature [of the place], it is non-apprehension characterized as a property of the knowable (<s>jñeyadharma</s>), with respect to the action situated in the object.
Having thus established non-apprehension through the function of term-exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>), showing what it proves, he says:
'That [non-apprehension] [proves] absence' —

children.text:
ityādi | sarvānyopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptavivikte 'pi [T. 331a.] pradeśādau dṛśyamāne yatra ghaṭādau pratiyoginy arthitvādibhiḥ smṛtir asya bhavati tasyābhāvaṃ sādhayati, abhāvavyavahāraṃ vā | kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhī abhāvam abhāvavyavahāraṃ ca sādhayataḥ | svabhāvānupalabdhis tu abhāvavyavahāram eva | abhāvavyavahāraś ca jñānabhidhānapravṛttilakṣaṇaḥ | tatra `nāsty atra ghaṭaḥ` ity evam ākāraṃ jñānam, evaṃvidhavastvabhidhāyakaṃ cābhidhānaṃ niḥśaṅkasya ca tatra pradeśe gamanāgamanalakṣaṇā pravṛttir iti |
  {p. 175.1} atreśvarasenakumārilayor vacanāvakāśam āśaṅkya siddhāntavyavasthām eva kurvatā tanmate niraste 'pyāhatya tanmatanirāsārtham āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. When a place and the like, devoid of everything else that meets the conditions of apprehensibility, is perceived — with respect to the counter-correlate such as a pot and the like, for one in whom recollection arises due to desire and the like — [non-apprehension] proves its absence, or the conventional usage of absence. Non-apprehension of the cause and of the pervader proves both absence and the conventional usage of absence. Non-apprehension of essential nature, however, [proves] only the conventional usage of absence. And the conventional usage of absence is characterized by cognition, verbal expression, and purposive activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>). There: the cognition of the form 'there is no pot here'; and verbal expression that designates such a state of affairs; and the purposive activity characterized by coming and going at that place for one who is without doubt.
'How is other-being [i.e., absence]' —

children.text:
ityādi |īśvaraseno hi manyate -- kārya-svabhāvahetubhyāṃ bhāvarūpābhyāṃ anupalabdheḥ pṛthakkaraṇād avaśyam abhāvarūpatvam asyāḥ, anyathā pṛthakkaraṇam anarthakam eva syāt | tvayā [S. 167a.] cānyasya pratiṣedhyaviviktasya pradeśādes tajjñānasya vā bhāvarūpānupalabdhir ākhyāyate tannūnam anyabhāvas tadabhāvo yenaivam abhidhīyate | na caitad yujyate, bhāvābhāvayor virodhād ekātmatānupapatter iti |
  kumārilo 'py evaṃ manyate -- yeyaṃ jñātṛ-jñeyadharmalakṣaṇā dvidhā 'nupalabdhir abhāvarūpā tvayocyate tasyā bhavatu nāstitājñānaṃ prati sādhanabhāvaḥ | kintu sa evānyasya pratiṣedhyaviviktasya vastunaḥ [T. 331b.] pratiṣedhyajñānād anyasya vā tajjñānasya yo bhāvo bhāvāṃśaḥ sa katham abhāvaḥ? pratiṣedhyasya tajjñānasya vā katham abhāvāṃśaḥ? | naiva yujyate, dharmarūpatayā bhāvābhāvāṃśayor bhedāt | saty api dharmirūpeṇābhede tayoś codbhavābhibhavābhyāṃ grahaṇāgrahaṇavyavastheti | yad āha --
children.translated_text:
and so forth. <s>Īśvarasena</s> indeed thinks: since non-apprehension is treated separately from the causal ground and the essential-nature ground, which are of the form of positive entities, its form must necessarily be that of absence; otherwise, the separate treatment would be pointless. And you declare non-apprehension to be a positive-entity-form — [namely] another [object] devoid of connection with the counter-positive, such as the place and the like, or the cognition of that [place devoid of the pot]. Then surely the other-being [i.e., the being of the other object] is the absence of that [counter-positive] — by which it is so described. But this is not tenable, because of the contradiction between positive entity and absence, and the impossibility of their having a single identity.
<s>Kumārila</s> too thinks thus: this twofold non-apprehension — characterized as a property of the knower and a property of the knowable — which you call 'of the form of absence,' let it have the nature of a means of proof with respect to absence-cognition. But that very being of the other — the positive entity devoid of connection with the counter-positive, or the being of another cognition different from the cognition of the counter-positive — that positive aspect: how is it absence? And how is it the absence-aspect of the counter-positive or its cognition? It is simply not tenable, because of the difference between the positive aspect and the absence-aspect, since they are of the nature of properties. Even though there is non-difference in their property-bearer form, the determination of apprehension and non-apprehension [is made] through their emergence and suppression. As he said:

children.text: dharmayor bheda iṣṭo hi dharmyabhede 'pi naḥsthite |
children.translated_text: 'For we accept difference of properties even when the property-bearer remains non-different;
and apprehension stands, because [they] have the nature of emergence and suppression.' ||
ŚlV <s>abhāva</s> 20.

Thus.
Showing that the response to this has already been given, he says:
'It has been stated' —
'the response' —
'here' —
'to this objection, [is] as follows:' —
'through the function of term-exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>), from the standpoint of reference' —

children.text:
| `pratiṣedhyaṃ tajjñānaṃ vā apekṣya tadvivikto 'rthas tajjñānaṃ [S. 167b.] vā 'bhāvo 'nupalabdhiś cocyate` itiīśvarasenasya prativacanam | na hi prasajyapratiṣedha evaiko nañarthaḥ kin tu paryudāso 'pi | tato 'nyabhāvasyābhāvarūpatā na virudhyate, prasajyapratiṣedharūpatā 'py anyabhāvasya yathā tathottaratra vakṣyate | svabhāvahetos tv anupalabdheḥ pṛthakkaraṇaṃ pratipattrabhiprāyavaśāt | pratipattā hi svabhāvahetau vastupratipattyadhyavasāyī | anupalabdhau tv abhāvapratipatty adhyavasāyī | paramārthatas tu pratiṣedhyābhāvavyavahārayogyatā {p. 176.1} vastubhūtaiva pradeśasya sādhyata iti na svabhāvahetoḥ svabhāvānupalabdhir bhidyata[649]iti |
  yat tu `anapekṣitārthāntarasaṃsarggaṃ pratiṣedhamātram anupalabdhiḥ` itīśvaraseno manyate tannirākurvann āha --
children.translated_text:
'with reference to the counter-positive, the object devoid of that, or the cognition of that, is called absence and non-apprehension' — this is the reply to <s>Īśvarasena</s>. For the exclusive sense of the negative [particle] is not only the propositional negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>); it is also term-exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>). Therefore, the absence-form-nature of other-being is not contradicted, and the propositional-negation-form-nature of other-being too — just as that, so it will be stated further below. But the separate treatment of non-apprehension from the essential-nature ground is due to the intent of the cognizer. For the cognizer, with respect to the essential-nature ground, has the determination of cognizing a positive entity. But with respect to non-apprehension, [the cognizer] has the determination of cognizing absence. But in ultimate reality, what is proved is the fitness for the conventional usage of the absence of the counter-positive, which is itself a positive entity of the place — so non-apprehension of essential nature does not differ from the essential-nature ground.
But as for <s>Īśvarasena</s>'s view that 'non-apprehension is mere negation without association with any other object' — refuting this, he says:
'Not mere negation' —
and so forth. Why? He says:
'Because its being a means of proof is not established' —

children.text:
ityādi | [T. 332a.] na hy abhāvasya sarvasāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇasya sādhanatvaṃ siddhihetutvaṃ sidhyati, sarvasāmarthyaviraharūpasya tadayogāt[650]| hetutve vā kathaṃ na sāmarthyayogitā? bhāvarūpatā vā?, sāmarthyalakṣaṇatvād vastunaḥ | abhāvasya [S. 168a.] cānapekṣitasahakāriṇo anādheyātiśayatayā nāstīti jñānajanane nityaṃ tajjananaprasaṅgaḥ | tataś ca sādhakatvāyogād abhāvavyavahāra eva na sidhyet | athavā tasya prasajyapratiṣedhātmana upalabdhyabhāvasya sādhanam eva kiñcin na sidhyatīti | sa hy abhāvatvād apareṇopalabdhyabhāvena sādhyaḥ syāt, so 'py apareṇety anavasthānam | na cendriyavad ajñātasya pratiṣedhajñānahetutā, sadā sannihitatvenānapekṣitasahakāriṇo nityaṃ tadudayaprasaṅgāt
| idaṃ cārthadvayaṃ `katham abhāvaḥ kasyacit, pratipattiḥ pratipattihetur vā? | tasyāpi kathaṃ pratipattiḥ` ity
children.translated_text:
and so forth. For the being-a-means-of-proof — i.e., being a cause of establishment — of absence, which is characterized by the absence of all capacity, is not established, since what has the form of the absence of all capacity is not suited to that [role as a means of proof]. Or, if it does have the nature of a cause, how would it not possess capacity? Or [how would it not have] the form of a positive entity? — since a real entity is characterized by capacity. And since absence, which does not depend on auxiliary causes and to which no distinguishing feature can be added, always exists — the absurd consequence of always producing the cognition 'it does not exist' [would follow]. And consequently, due to the impossibility of being a means of proof, even the conventional usage of absence would not be established. Alternatively: of that [absence] — which has the nature of propositional negation, i.e., the absence of apprehension — no means of proof at all is established. For it, being of the nature of absence, would have to be proved by another absence of apprehension, and that by another — and so there is an infinite regress. And the causation of negation-cognition by something unknown, like a sense-faculty [which operates without being known], is not [tenable], because of the absurd consequence of its always arising, since [absence] is always proximate and does not depend on auxiliary causes.
And this double meaning — 'how is absence the cognition of something, or its cause of cognition? And how is there cognition of that too?' —

children.text:
atrāntare svayam eva vipañcayiṣyati[651]|
  kumārilasyāpy uttaram āha --
children.translated_text:
[<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] himself will elucidate in the sequel.
He states the response to <s>Kumārila</s> as well:
'Of that [entity]' —

children.text: anyasya pratiyoginā vastvantareṇāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpasya | na hy asau vastvantaraiḥ saṃsṛṣṭasvabhāva ekarūpaḥ | tathātve hy abhāvāṃśo 'pi na kvacit sidhyet | tasyaivaṃvidhasya
children.translated_text: of the other [entity] whose form is not associated with the counter-correlate, another real entity. For that [entity] does not have a single form associated with other real entities. For if it did, then even the absence-aspect would not be established anywhere. Of that entity of such a nature,
'the establishment of positive being itself' —
'the establishment of the positive aspect itself' —
'of the other' —

children.text: pratiyogino vastvantarasyābhāvasiddhir abhāvāṃśasya tvadabhimatasya siddhir astu bhāvāṃśasyaivābhāvāṃśarūpatopapatter iti manyate | tathā hi -- abhāvāṃśo 'pi pararūpāsaṃsṛṣṭatayaivābhāva iti vyapadiśyate, anyathā [S. 168b.] tadayogāt | sā ca bhāvāṃśasyāpi samāneti sa evābhāvo 'stu tannimittasya samānatvāt kim anyenābhāvāṃśopagatena? | ata [T. 332b.] evāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpasyeti viśeṣaṇam | yata {p. 177.1} evam
children.translated_text: let the establishment of the absence of the other real entity that is the counter-correlate — the establishment of the absence-aspect as you intend it — be [nothing other than] the very absence-aspect-nature of the positive aspect. He thinks thus: the absence-aspect too is designated as absence precisely because of its non-association with the form of the other — otherwise that [designation] would not be appropriate. And that [non-association with the form of the other] is the same for the positive aspect too — so let that itself be the absence, since the ground for it is the same; what [need] for another [factor] endowed with an absence-aspect? And for this very reason, the qualifier 'whose form is not associated [with the counter-correlate]' [is used]. Since this is so,
thus —
therefore,
even other-being

children.text:
anyasya vastuno bhāvo 'pi tvadabhimato bhāvāṃśo 'pi na kevalam abhāvāṃśas tvanmatyā 'bhāva iti vyapadiśyate 'smābhiḥ | tato bhāvāṃśasyābhāvarūpatā saṅgataiveti
na kiñcid virudhyata iti |
  yad uktaṃ `jñātṛ-jñeyadharmalakṣaṇayā svabhāvānupalabdhyā abhāvavyavahāra eva sādhyate nābhāvaḥ`[652]iti tat paro vighaṭayituṃ, yac coktaṃ `na pratiṣedhamātram anupalabdhiḥ, tasya sādhanāsiddheḥ`[653]iti dvitīye vyākhyāne[654]pratiṣedhamātrasyānupalabdhi[r i]ty
children.translated_text: the existence of another entity — indeed even the positive aspect (<s>bhāvāṃśa</s>) as accepted by you — not merely the negative aspect — is designated by us as 'absence' according to your understanding. Therefore, the positive aspect having the nature of absence is quite consistent, and nothing is contradicted. | As for what was said — 'by <s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s> (essential-nature non-apprehension), characterized as a property of the knower and the knowable, only the practice of absence is established, not absence [itself]' — [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] wishes to dismantle the opponent's position. And as for what was said — 'non-apprehension is not mere negation, because of the unestablished-ness of its means of proof' — in the second interpretation, in order to show the means of proof of non-apprehension being mere negation,
he says:
'Characterized by the existence of another' —

children.text:
ityādi | evaṃ manyate -- loko hi kevalapradeśadarśanāt ghaṭābhāvam eva prathamaṃ pratipadyate kevalapradeśajñānasaṃvedanadvāreṇa ghaṭajñānābhāvapratipattyā vā tato ghaṭābhāvasya vyavahāram | tena lokapratītyanusāreṇa pratiṣedhyād anyasya pradeśasya pratiṣedhyajñānād vā tajjñānasya yo bhāvas tallakṣaṇo 'bhāvaḥ svayaṃ pramāṇenendriyapratyakṣeṇa svasaṃvedanapratyakṣeṇa ca siddho 'laṃ [S. 169a.] ghaṭābhāvaṃ sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa ca yathākramaṃ sādhayitum, sa ca ghaṭābhāvavyavahāram ity evaṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ
yuktam | na caivam api vyavasthāpane [asma]tpakṣasya kācit kṣatiḥ | tathā hi -- pāramparyeṇāpi yad anupalabdheḥ tvadabhyupagatāyāḥ siddhaṃ tat tat eva siddhaṃ bhavatīti [T. 333a.] pratiṣedhamātrasyānupalabdhitve tatsādhanapratipādane 'pi | ayam abhiprāyaḥ -- yathā bhavato jñātṛ-jñeyadharmalakṣaṇā bhāvarūpā dvividhā 'nupalabdhis tathā mamāpi jñātṛ-jñeyadharmalakṣaṇopalabdhyabhāvo 'py anupalabdhisaṃjñito dvividho bhaviṣyati | tatra jñeyadharmalakṣaṇenānyabhāvena pratyakṣasiddhena pratiṣedhyābhāvo jñeyadharmalakṣaṇopalabdhyabhāvarūpa 'nupalabdhisaṃjñitaḥ setsyati | jñātṛdharmalakṣaṇena cānyabhāvena kevalapradeśajñānātmanā svasaṃvedanasiddhena jñātṛdharmaḥ pratiṣedhyajñānābhāvarūpo 'nupalabdhisamākhyātaḥ setsyati | tataś ca kuto 'navasthā yena sādhanāsiddhiḥ syād iti | tatra[656]
children.translated_text: and so forth. He thinks thus: the world, from merely seeing a bare spot, first apprehends precisely the absence of the pot — either through the gateway of perceiving the cognition of the bare spot, or through the apprehension of the absence of pot-cognition — and thence [derives] the practice regarding the absence of the pot. Therefore, following worldly understanding — the existence of another, namely the spot, distinct from the thing to be negated, or of the cognition of that [spot] distinct from the cognition of the thing to be negated — that absence characterized by that [existence], being itself established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) — sense-perception and self-awareness-perception respectively — is sufficient to establish the absence of the pot, directly and indirectly, in due order, and also the practice of pot-absence. And even with this formulation, there is no harm to our position. For thus: even what is established through your accepted non-apprehension indirectly — that very same thing is established [by our formulation] — even when non-apprehension is [understood as] mere negation, and even when its means of proof is demonstrated. This is the intent: just as for you non-apprehension, characterized by a property of the knower and the knowable, is twofold and of the nature of a positive entity — so too for me, the absence of apprehension, characterized by a property of the knower and the knowable, designated as 'non-apprehension,' will also be twofold. Therein, by the existence of another characterized as a property of the knowable, established through perception, the absence of the thing to be negated — which is non-apprehension in the form of the absence of apprehension characterized as a property of the knowable — will be established. And by the existence of another characterized as a property of the knower, having the nature of the cognition of the bare spot, established through self-awareness — the property of the knower, in the form of the absence of cognition of the thing to be negated, designated as non-apprehension, will be established. Therefore, whence the infinite regress by which the means of proof would be unestablished?
'Characterized by the existence of another' —

children.text:
iti pratiṣedhyāt tajjñānāc ca yo 'nyo bhāvaḥ pratiṣedhyaviviktaḥ pradeśaḥ
tajjñānaṃ ca tadātmako 'bhāvaḥ vivakṣitād bhāvāt pratiṣedhyād bhāvāt tajjñānāc cānyatvād {p. 178.1} anupalabdhitvena bhavato 'bhimataḥ svayaṃ svarūpeṇa pramāṇenendriyapratyakṣeṇa svasaṃvedanapratyakṣeṇa ca siddhaḥ saṃs tasya [S. 169b.] pratiṣedhyasyābhāvavyavahāraṃ jñānābhidhānapravṛttilakṣaṇaṃ sādhayet
children.translated_text: thus, the existence of another — a spot distinct from the thing to be negated, or the cognition [of the spot] distinct from the cognition of the thing to be negated — that absence characterized by that [existence], being other than the intended entity (the thing to be negated) and [other than] the cognition of the thing to be negated, and hence accepted by you as non-apprehension — being itself established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, namely sense-perception and self-awareness-perception respectively — would establish the practice of absence of the thing to be negated, characterized as the activity of cognition and speech,
'or [the absence is] established by the establishment of that [other]' —

children.text: vā tasyānyabhāvalakṣaṇasyābhāvasya yathoktasya siddhyā siddho vā tadabhāvas tasya pratiṣedhyasya tajjñānasya[657]vā 'bhāva iti evam apīṣyamāṇe
children.translated_text: or the absence of that — i.e., the absence of the thing to be negated, or the absence of the cognition thereof — is established by the establishment of that absence characterized by the existence of another, as described. Even if it is accepted thus,
'there is no difference' —

children.text:
tvadabhimatānupalabdhito 'smadabhimatānupalabdheḥ [T. 333b.] tato 'smad darśanaṃ kim iti pratikṣipyate? | nanv asty evaivam iṣyamāṇe viśeṣo 'nyabhāvalakṣaṇānupalabdhir itarayā[658]vyavahitā tadabhāvavyavahāraṃ sādhayed itarā tu sākṣād ity āha -- sa viśeṣo nāsti yena viśeṣeṇānupalabdhyā 'bhāvarūpayā vastusaṃsparśarahitayā 'smadabhimatayā 'bhāvavyavahārasiddheḥ virodhaḥ
syāt | anyasya tu viśeṣasya sato 'py abādhakatvād asatsamatvam eva | yad apy uktaṃ -- `tasya sādhanābhāvad abhāvavyavahārāsiddhiprasaṅgaḥ`[659]iti, tad apy asat, yataḥ sa eva tvadabhimato 'nyabhāvaḥ pratiṣedhyaviviktabhūtalātmakas tadviṣayā copalabdhir anupalabdhitveneṣṭā bhavatas tadabhāvasyānupalabdhitvenāsmanmatasya pratiṣedhyābhāvasya tadupalabdhyabhāvasya ca
children.translated_text: of our accepted non-apprehension from your accepted non-apprehension — so why is our view rejected? | 'But there is indeed a difference when it is accepted thus: non-apprehension characterized by the existence of another would establish the practice of absence mediately, whereas the other [your view of non-apprehension] would do so directly.' He says: that difference does not exist — a difference by which, with non-apprehension being of the nature of absence, devoid of contact with real entities, and accepted by us — there would be a contradiction with the establishment of the practice of absence.
'why' —
for what reason —
'is [it] not accepted as a means of proof' —
as an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) —

children.text: | tathā hi sati lokapratītir anusṛtā bhavati |
children.translated_text: | For when it is so, worldly understanding is followed.
'Moreover' —
for what reason moreover —
'of absence' —
of both kinds —
'the establishment itself is the establishment of the absence of that' —

children.text:
na tatsādhyā kācid anyā [S. 170a] vidyata ity asmanmataniṣedhārthaṃ lokātikrāntam iṣyata iti pūrvapakṣaḥ |
  atrāha --
children.translated_text: there is no other [establishment] that is to be proved by that — for what purpose is something going beyond worldly [understanding] desired, for the purpose of negating our view? — this is the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie position). | To this [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:
'Because of the non-separate establishment, from the existence of another' —

children.text: tadabhāvasya pṛthaksiddher abhāvāt kuto liṅgaliṅgitā | tathā
children.translated_text: because of the absence of separate establishment of the absence of that [negated thing] from the existence of another — whence the relation of inferential mark and that which bears the mark? And likewise,
'and because of the absence of a relation' —

children.text: anyabhāvatadabhāvayor na liṅgaliṅgiteti | prathamaṃ tāvat kāraṇaṃ [T. 334a.] vivṛṇvann āha
children.translated_text: between the existence of another and the absence of that, there is no relation of inferential mark and that which bears the mark. First, explaining the [first] reason, he says:
'The existence of another — having the nature of a spot devoid of that [negated thing] — is not for the time being a means of proof' —

children.text: liṅgaṃ pratiṣedhyābhāvasya, `tadupalabdhir api tadabhāvasya na sādhanam` iti paścād vakṣyate | tadartham eva tāvacchabdaḥ | kasmād anyabhāvo na sādhanam? ity āha --
children.translated_text: i.e., not an inferential mark for the absence of the thing to be negated. 'The apprehension of that too is not a means of proof for the absence of that' — this will be stated afterward. The word 'for the time being' (<s>tāvat</s>) serves that purpose. Why is the existence of another not a means of proof? He says:
'When that is established' —
when a certain entity is cognized —
'of which' —
of another {p. 179.1} entity —
'there is no establishment' —

children.text: r na pratītiḥ tad vastu tasya vastuno liṅgaṃ bhavatīty ayaṃ liṅgaliṅginor nyāyaḥ | tatrodāharaṇam --
children.translated_text: no cognition — that entity is the inferential mark of that [other] entity — this is the principle of the mark and the mark-bearer. An example therein:
'like smoke and fire.' —

children.text: | yathā -- yadā dhūmapratītau nāgniḥ pratīyate tadā tayor lliṅgaliṅgibhāvo bhavati, na tu dhūmapratītikāla eva pratīyamāne 'gnau | yadi nāmaivaṃ tataḥ kim? ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: | For thus: when upon the cognition of smoke, fire is not [yet] cognized — then there is the relation of inferential mark and mark-bearer between those two, but not when fire is cognized at the very time of the cognition of smoke. If so, then what? To this he says:
'The existence of another entity' —
its essential nature —
'by the very establishment of that' —
by the very cognition of that —
'the absence of that' —
the absence of the thing to be negated —
'is established' —

children.text:
pratīyate anyabhāvasyaiva tadabhāvātmakatvāt tatsiddher eva tatsiddhilakṣaṇatvāt |
  naiyāyikās tu manyante -- pratiṣedhyābhāvo hi prasajyapratiṣedhātmakas tuccharūpas tasya kathaṃ tadanyabhāvarūpatā?, bhāvābhāvayor virodhāt | tataḥ kathaṃ tadanyabhāvasiddhyaiva tadabhāvasiddhiḥ syāt? ity ata āha --
children.translated_text: is cognized — because the existence of another is itself of the nature of the absence of that, and because the establishment of the latter has as its defining characteristic the establishment of the former. | But the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> think: the absence of the thing to be negated is of the nature of <s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s> (non-implicative negation), of a void form — how can it have the nature of the existence of another? — because of the contradiction between positive entity and absence. So how could the establishment of the absence of that be [achieved] by the very establishment of the existence of another? To this he says:
'Of that' —

children.text: tadanyabhāvasya pradeśalakṣaṇasya tasmād anyena pratiṣedhyena ghaṭādinā
children.translated_text: of that existence of another, characterized as the spot — from that, by the other, i.e., by the thing to be negated, such as a pot —
'having a form unmixed [with it]' —

children.text: rahitātmanaḥ kevalasya pratiṣedhyena śūnyātmanaḥ | anena kevalapradeśasyāpi prasajyapratiṣedhātmakatām āha | kathaṃ bhāvasya tuccharūpatā svabhāvaḥ, virodhāt?, iti cet; na, pararūpeṇa tasyāpi tuccharūpatvāt | [T. 334b.] yathā hy anapekṣitabhāvāntarasaṃsargaḥ prasajyapratiṣedhaḥ śūnyavikalpapratibhāsī pratiṣedhyena tuccharūpaḥ tadrūpavirahāt, tathā tadanyabhāvo 'pi pratiṣedhyāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpaḥ | tataḥ katham asya pratiṣedhyena tuccharūpatā [S. 171a.] virudhyeta? | svarūpeṇa
children.translated_text: having an unaccompanied nature, being mere, having a nature empty of the thing to be negated.
