children.translated_text: — by this very reasoning, since contradiction would cease through the cessation of cognition — [Dharmakīrti] says: even so, the reason is purposeless. Why? |
'From the mere non-apprehension of contradiction' (<s>bādhānupalambhād eva</s>)

children.text:
hetupayogarahitāt sādhyasiddheḥ | kiṃ kāraṇam? | anupalambhe bādhāyā asambhavāt | tathā hi -- yatra bādhāyā anupalambhas tatra paramārthata eva sā na vidyata iti manyase | yatra cāsau paramārthato nāsti, tatra sādhyadharmasyābhāvo 'pi paramārthenaiva [T. 360b.] nāsti, anyathā paramārthena bādhāyā abhāvāyogāt. tataś ca sādhyadharmasyābhāvābhāve sati bhāva iti bhavanmatya sādhyapratīter vyarthatā hetor iti.
  atha mā bhūd yuktivirodha iti nopalambhanivṛttau bādhānivṛttir iṣyate, tatrāha -- upalambhasya nivṛttāv api satyāṃ bādhāyā anivṛttāv iṣyamāṇāyāṃ tadavasthaṃ hetor asāmarthyam yadavasthaṃ bādhopalambha iti hetor aprayoga iti kasyābādhitaviṣayatvaṃ [S. 200b.] rūpāntaraṃ syāt? |
  etad evopasaṃharann āha --
children.translated_text:
— [there is] the establishment of the probandum, without the service of the reason. What is the reason? Because of the impossibility of contradiction when there is non-apprehension. For thus: where there is non-apprehension of contradiction, you think that it truly does not exist there. And where it does not truly exist, the absence of the property to be proved (<s>sādhyadharma</s>) also truly does not exist — otherwise the true absence of contradiction would be impossible. And therefore, when the absence of absence obtains, the existence [of the probandum follows] — so according to your view, the understanding of the probandum [is achieved], and the reason is purposeless. |
  Or, lest there be a conflict with reasoning, if the cessation of contradiction upon the cessation of apprehension is not accepted — to that [Dharmakīrti] says: even when the cessation of apprehension obtains, if the non-cessation of contradiction is accepted, the incapacity of the reason remains in the same condition as when contradiction is apprehended — so the reason should not be employed — for whom then would the uncontradicted-subject-matter be an alternative form [of the definition]? |
  Concluding this very [argument], [Dharmakīrti] says —
'Therefore, [from] one's own probandum' (<s>tasmāt svasādhya</s>)

children.text: ityādi. yata evaṃ vyāptya hetoḥ sarvatra sādhyenāvinābhāvābhyupagame bahirvyāptaviṣayamāṇāyāṃ vaiyarthyaṃ hetuprayogasyāpadyate tasmāt
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since thus, when the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) of the reason with the probandum everywhere is accepted, purposelessness of the employment of the reason results when the external pervasion [alone] is being considered — therefore:
'by the presence and absence of one's own probandum, even otherwise' (<s>svasādhyabhāvābhāvābhyām anyathā 'pi</s>)

children.text: svasādhyabhāve 'py abhavan na 'bhāve 'pi ca bhavan hetur dharmiṇi kiñcit sādhyaṃ
children.translated_text: — a reason that is absent even in the absence of its own probandum, and present even in [its] presence, does not establish any probandum in the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) —
'does not establish' (<s>na bhāvayati</s>)
— does not prove —
'does not make known' (<s>na vibhāvayati</s>)
— does not negate the contrary of that —
'thus' (<s>iti</s>)
— of [a reason] not performing affirmation and negation,
'the employment' (<s>upakṣepaḥ</s>)
— the application —
'is not capable' (<s>na samarthaḥ</s>)

children.text: ity avaśyaṃ hetuprayogam icchatā svasādhyāvinābhāvaḥ sarvatra hetor abhyupagantavyaḥ | sa ca pratibandhanibandhanaḥ | eṣa ca darśanādarśanamātrāyatto yathoktaṃ prak | tasmiṃś cābhyupagate bādhāvinābhāvayor virodhaḥ [T. 361a.] siddha ity upasaṃharann āha --
children.translated_text: | Thus, one who desires the employment of a reason must accept the invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>) of the reason with its own probandum everywhere. And that [concomitance] is grounded in necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>). And that [necessary connection] depends merely on observation and non-observation, as was stated before. And when that is accepted, the contradiction between absence of contradiction and invariable concomitance is established — [Dharmakīrti] concludes saying —
'Therefore not' (<s>tan na</s>)

children.text:
ityādi | yata evaṃ tena kāraṇenābādhā rūpāntaraṃ na bhavati |
  yadi nāma bādhāvinābhāvayoḥ sahāvasthānābhāvād avinābhāve {p. 212.1} saty abādhā gamyate rūpāntaraṃ tu kim iti na bhavati? iti, ata āha --
children.translated_text:
and so forth. Since thus, for that reason, the absence of contradiction is not an alternative form [of the definition]. |
  If indeed, because of the impossibility of the co-existence of contradiction and invariable concomitance, the absence of contradiction is understood when invariable concomitance obtains — then why is it not an alternative form [of the definition]? — to this [Dharmakīrti] says —
'That, namely' (<s>tan nāma</s>)

children.text: ityādi | tad dhi tasmād viśeṣaṇāntaraṃ bhaved vastusthitayā | [S. 201a.] lakṣaṇakāraiś ca rūpāntaratvenopādānam arhati yasya viśeṣaṇasya bhave 'pi yasyāparasyābhāvaḥ syāt | yataḥ svabhāve vyabhicāre ca viśeṣaṇaviśeśyabhāvo na sambhava eva kevale | udāharaṇam āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. For that would be a different qualifier from that [invariable concomitance] based on the actual state of things. And it deserves to be taken up by the definers as an alternative form — [only] a qualifier in whose presence there could be the absence of the other [qualifier]. Since in [the case of] essential nature and deviation, the property-bearer-property relation is simply not possible for what is alone. [Dharmakīrti] states an example —
'For example' (<s>tad yathā</s>)

children.text: ityādi | saty api hi śrāvaṇatvādeḥ sapakṣe bhāvo nāsti | saty api ca cākśuṣatvādeḥ sapakṣe bhāve sādhyadharmiṇi śabde sambandho nāsti | tato 'nyoḥ sambavavyabhicārayor bhāvād viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvo lakṣaṇāntaratvena copādānam[737]| ihā 'py evaṃ bhaviṣyatīti ced āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. For even when 'being auditory' and the like have presence in the homologue (<s>sapakṣa</s>), [the feature of being auditory] is absent [in some homologues]. And even when 'being visual' and the like have presence in the homologue, there is no connection with sound, the subject (<s>sādhyadharmin</s>). Therefore, because of the existence of the two — possibility and deviation — the property-bearer-property relation, and the taking up [of the property] as a separate definition, [are tenable]. If [one says:] 'it will be so here too' — [Dharmakīrti] says —
'And this' (<s>na caitad</s>)

children.text:
anantaroditam abādhāyā avinābhāve sati sambhavati | saty avinābhāve niyamenābādhāyāḥ sambhavād vyabhicārābhāvāt kuto viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvo
lakṣaṇāntaratvena copādānam[738]arhati? iti na hetoḥ sādhyāvinābhāvino viruddhasya ca sādhyaviparyayāvinābhāvino viṣaye bādhā sambhavati | uktena prakāreṇa viparyaye samyagghetur evāviṣaye tu prayogād dhetvābhāsa ucyate | yata evam
children.translated_text: — what was just stated — the absence of contradiction — is not possible when invariable concomitance obtains. Since when invariable concomitance obtains, the absence of contradiction necessarily obtains — because of the absence of deviation — whence the property-bearer-property relation, and [why] does it deserve to be taken up as a separate definition? | Thus, contradiction is not possible in the domain of a reason that has invariable concomitance with its probandum, nor in that of a contradictory [reason] that has invariable concomitance with the contrary of the probandum. In the contrary case, it is precisely a correct reason, as stated. But when employed outside its domain, it is called a pseudo-reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>). Since this is so,
'therefore' (<s>iti</s>)

children.text: tasmān na tadabhāvo bādhāvirahaḥ [T. 361b.] pṛthagavinābhāvād anvayavyatirekātmano 'nayor hetuviruddhayor lakṣaṇāntaratvena vācyaḥ, [S. 201b.] vyabhicārābhāvena rūpāntaratvāyogāt | yataś cāvinābhāve sati bādhā na sambhavati virodhāt, tasmād dhetor yathoktalakṣaṇasya prayoge sati gamyārthāyā api pratijñāyā doṣāṇāṃ pratyakṣaviruddhādīnāṃ sambhavo nāsti, hetulakṣaṇenaiva teṣāṃ nirastatvāt | tat kathaṃ bādhāviraho heto rūpāntaram ucyate? asambhavināṃ ca teṣāṃ upavarṇanaṃ niṣphalam
children.translated_text: — for that reason, the absence of that [contradiction], i.e., the absence of contradiction, should not be stated as a separate definition apart from the invariable concomitance having the nature of positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>) of the two — the reason and the contradictory [reason] — because the impossibility of being an alternative form [follows] from the absence of deviation. And since contradiction is not possible when invariable concomitance obtains, because of their mutual opposition, therefore when a reason having the stated definition is employed, even the faults of the proposition (<s>pratijñā</s>) — though [the proposition's] meaning is to be understood — such as being contradicted by perception and the like, are not possible, since they are excluded by the very definition of the reason. So how is the absence of contradiction called an alternative form of the reason? And the description of those [faults], which are impossible, is fruitless —

children.text:
ity ākūtam[739]|
  kevalāyāḥ prayoge 'sti sambhava iti cet, āha --
children.translated_text:
— this is the intent. |
  If [one says:] 'there is possibility [of faults] in the employment of a bare [proposition]' — [Dharmakīrti] says —
'Nor' (<s>nāpi</s>)

children.text: ityādi | hetuprayoge hy asati kevalā pratijñaiva na prayujyate, hetuviṣayatvena tadabhyupagamāt | tataś caśāstrakārair na pratijñādoṣāḥ pratyakṣaviruddhādayo vācyā iti |diṅnāgapādais tu
children.translated_text: and so forth. For when the reason is not employed, the bare proposition alone is simply not employed [in argument], since it is accepted as having the domain of the reason. And therefore, the faults of the proposition — being contradicted by perception and the like — should not be stated by the authors of treatises. | But by <s>Dignāga</s>, however,

children.text:
sādhyāsādhyaviparyayeṇa[740]vipratipattidarśanād aprayogārhasyāpi pakṣasya lakṣaṇavidhāne nyāyaprāptam evāpakṣatva na ni(-tvaṃ ni)rākṛtapadena pramāṇaviruddhasyākhyānam, na tv atiprasaktaṃ pakṣalakṣaṇam vyavacchinnam, sandigdhasyaiva sādhyatvāt, pramāṇabādhite sādhakapramāṇāvṛtter iti |
  tad evam abādhitaviṣayatvaṃ nirākṛtya rūpāntaraṃ nirākurvann āha --
children.translated_text:
since the display of disagreement through the contrary of what is to be proved and what is not to be proved [shows that] even a thesis not worthy of employment [has a definition], in the formulation of the definition of the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>), the naturally obtained non-thesis-hood [needs no separate mention]. The statement of 'what is contradicted by a valid means of cognition' through the word 'excluded' (<s>nirākṛta</s>) is not cutting off an over-extended thesis-definition but [rather stating what is] naturally obtained — since only what is doubtful is to be proved, and in what is contradicted by a valid means of cognition, the operation of a proving valid means is barred. |
  Thus, having rejected the uncontradicted-subject-matter as an alternative form, [Dharmakīrti], rejecting [another] alternative form, says —
'By this' (<s>etena</s>)
— by the demonstration that contradiction is impossible when invariable concomitance obtains —
'the desire to state a single number too' (<s>ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā 'pi</s>)
— stated as the counter-correlate of the faults of being contradictory and non-deviating —
'is answered' (<s>pratyuktā</s>)

— is rejected. |
  The opponent asks —
'How?' (<s>katham</s>)
— in what manner — just as the co-existence of contradiction and invariable concomitance is impossible,

children.text:
sahānavasthānaṃ tathā pratihetvavinābhāvayor api?, yenaikasaṃkhyāvivakṣā tadvad eva pratyākhyāyeta iti |
  siddhāntavādī sāmyaṃ darśayann[741]āha --
children.translated_text:
so too [the co-existence] of a counter-reason and invariable concomitance? — by which the desire to state a single number would be similarly rejected. |
  The Siddhantavadin, showing the similarity, says —
'One' (<s>eka</s>)

children.text: ityādi | eko hi hetur lakṣaṇayuktaḥ | svasādhyāvyabhicārī kathaṃ bhavati? | yadi svasādhyabhāva eva bhavet, anyathā tallakṣaṇam avinābhāvo nāma hīyeta | atraiva dharmiṇi sa tallakṣaṇa eko bhavati tatraiva dharmiṇi tasmād anyo 'pi pratihetur viruddhastena hetulakṣaṇayuktaḥ kathaṃ bhavati? | ekasya
children.translated_text: and so forth. For one reason possessing the [correct] definition — how can it be non-deviating from its own probandum? Only if it exists precisely in the presence of its own probandum; otherwise, the definition called 'invariable concomitance' would be lost. In this very property-bearer, that one [reason] having the [correct] definition exists; and in that very property-bearer, another [reason] that is contradictory — how can it too possess the definition of a reason? [Because] of the one

children.text:
hetor yat sādhyaṃ[742]tadbādhakasya tadviruddhasyāparasya dharmasya bhāva eva nābhāve bhāvād avinābhāvād iti bādhayā samānaṃ bādhāsambhavena samānaḥ pratihetur iti [S. 202b.] nirasta iti |
  atraiva dūṣaṇāntaram abhidhātuṃ vikalpayann āha --
children.translated_text:
reason's probandum — the contradicting [reason], which establishes a property contrary to that [probandum], has its invariable concomitance only in the presence [of its own probandum], not in its absence. So, just like contradiction, the counter-reason is impossible — it is rejected by the impossibility of contradiction. |
  Considering another objection to state, [Dharmakīrti] says —
'Moreover' (<s>api ca</s>)

children.text: ityādi | `vastutaḥ` paramārthato yasya pratihetur na sambhavati -- kim asau samyagjñānasya viparyayasya vopanyastasādhyaviparītajñānasya vā hetur iṣṭo [T. 362b.] yato vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvaṃ tallakṣaṇam ucyate, āhosvid yasya pratihetus tatsādhyaviparītasādhako na pradarśitaḥ paramārthataḥ sann apīti | paro doṣam apaśyann āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. 'In reality' — in ultimate terms — for whom a counter-reason is not possible — is the reason intended as a cause of correct knowledge, or of erroneous [knowledge], or of the knowledge contrary to the stated probandum, such that the desired single-number-hood is stated as its definition? Or rather, [is it] one for whom a counter-reason — a prover of the contrary of its probandum — has not been demonstrated, even though it [may] exist in ultimate reality? The opponent, seeing no fault, says —
'What of that?' (<s>kiñ cataḥ</s>)

children.text:
ityādi | yadi nāma pūrvo vikalpa uttaro vā tataḥ ko doṣaḥ? iti[743]|
  {p. 214.1} siddhāntavādy āha -- yady asambhavan pratihetur yasya sa samyagjñānādihetur iṣyate, tadā 'lakṣaṇam etad vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvam | kasmāt? aśakyo niścayo yasya vastuto 'sambhavat pratihetutvasya sa tathoktaḥ | paramatāpekṣayā caitad ucyate | paro hi darśanādarśanābhyām asaty api pratibandhe 'vinābhāvam icchati | paro hi darśanādarśanābhyām asaty api pratibandhe 'vinābhāvam icchati | tatas tasya pratihetor evaṃvidhasya sambhavo 'sti | sa cānupalabhyamāno 'pi kadācit syād iti vastutas tadabhāvo niścīyate | pratibandhanibandhanāvinābhāvavādināṃ tv asmākaṃ [S. 203a.] pratihetvasambhavaḥ suniścita eva | na hi tādātmyatadutpattilakṣaṇe pratibandhe pramāṇataḥ siddhe tannimittāvinābhāvitayā ekena hetuna svasādhye sādhite punas tatraiva dharmiṇi tallakṣaṇasya [T. 363a.] tadviruddhārthasādhakasya pratihetoḥ sambhavaḥ śaṅkhyate, bhāvānāṃ viruddhasvabhāvadvayāyogād, viruddhadharmasādhakasambhave ca tasyaiva
svasādhyāvinābhāvinaḥ prathamasya tatra pramāṇato bhāvasiddhyayogād iti |
  syān matam -- yadi nāma prastutaḥ pratihetvasambhavo 'smābhir niścetum aśakyas tathāpy asambhavat pratihetutvaṃ vivakṣittaikasaṃkhyatvapratipāditaṃ hetulakṣaṇaṃ kasmān na bhavati? ity āha --
children.translated_text:
and so forth. Even if the prior conceptual cognition or the subsequent [is the counter-reason], what is the fault? — thus.
The proponent (<s>siddhāntavādin</s>) says: if one whose counter-reason is impossible — i.e., whose counter-reason does not really exist — is accepted as a cause of correct cognition and the like, then the intended oneness of number is a non-defining characteristic. Why? Because it is said of one whose counter-reason-hood is actually impossible, [yet] whose certainty [about that impossibility] is unattainable. And this is stated relative to the opponent's position. For the opponent, based merely on observation and non-observation, accepts invariable concomitance even in the absence of a necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>). Therefore, [for the opponent,] such a counter-reason is possible. And even though not apprehended [at a given time], it might exist at some other time — so the non-existence of that is not actually ascertained. But for us, who maintain that invariable concomitance is grounded in necessary connection, the impossibility of a counter-reason is well-ascertained indeed. For when a necessary connection characterized by identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and origination from that (<s>tadutpatti</s>) is established through <s>pramāṇa</s>, and when, through [its] being invariably concomitant due to that ground, a single logical reason establishes its own thesis — the possibility of a counter-reason having that [same] defining characteristic and proving a contradictory meaning in that very property-bearer is not suspected, because entities cannot have two contradictory essential natures, and because if the possibility of a counter-reason proving a contradictory property [were accepted], then the very first [reason], which is invariably concomitant with its own thesis, could not have its existence established by <s>pramāṇa</s> there.
One might think: even if the impossibility of a counter-reason at issue cannot be ascertained by us, why should the defining characteristic of a logical reason — taught by the intended oneness of number as being one whose counter-reason is [actually] impossible — not [be accepted]? To this he says:
'For of one whose self is not ascertained' —

children.text: ityādi | pratipādako yo dharmo hetos tasyāniścitasvabhāvasya yasmāt tallakṣaṇatvaṃ pratipādakadharmatā na bhavati | yathā saṃdigdhasya pakṣadharmatvasyeti pūrvakasya sādhanam | nāpi sandigdhaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ yasya sa hetur bhavatīti na kaściddhetur bhaved iti hetvabhāvo [S. 203b.] vā ity asya samarthanam | tataś ca
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since the defining-characteristic-hood — the property of being a demonstrative attribute — of the logical reason whose essential nature is not ascertained does not obtain. Just as with doubtful property-of-the-subject-hood (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>) — this supports the former [alternative, that there is no logical reason]. Nor is it the case that one whose defining characteristic is doubtful is a [valid] logical reason — so no logical reason would exist at all, i.e., there would be an absence of logical reasons — this supports the latter [alternative]. And consequently,
'fallacious reasons would follow from that too' —

children.text:
ity atrāpi yojitam iti |
  syān matam -- yasya pratiyogī dṛśyate tasyaiva pratihetubhāvāt ahetutvaṃ bhavatu, yasya tu pratiyogī hetur na dṛśyate sa vastuta evāsambhavat pratihetuḥ | na hi tatra vastutaḥ pratihetusambhavaḥ śaṅkyate, bādhakapratyayam antareṇa bādhāśaṅkāyā ayogāt | tad uktam --
children.translated_text:
this too has been connected [with the argument].
One might think: let there be non-reason-hood only for one whose counter-correlate is observed, since [only that] has counter-reason-hood. But for one whose counter-correlate reason is not observed — that is one whose counter-reason is actually impossible. For the possibility of a counter-reason is not suspected there, since the suspicion of invalidity is impossible without an invalidating cognition. As stated:
'But when an invalidating cognition has not arisen, the suspicion [of invalidity] is without <s>pramāṇa</s>.'

Thus.
Therefore he says:
'For when the defining characteristic is equal' —

children.text:
ityādi | śaṅyamānapratihetunā tulyaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ darśanādarśanamātranimittāvinābhāvarūpaṃ yasya tasmin dṛṣṭaḥ pratiyoginaḥ [T. 363b.] pratihetor bbādhakasya sambhava sa yeśām api tattulyalakṣaṇānāṃ pratiyogī na dṛśyate teṣv api śaṅkāṃ pratihetusambhavaviṣayām utpādayati | kiṃ kāraṇam? | adṛṣṭapratiyogino dṛṣṭapratiyogino viśeṣābhāvāt | na hi tasyetareṇa kaścidviśeṣo 'sti, yatas tatsambhavo na śaṅkyeta | puruṣaśaktivaikalyādinā tu tadadarśanaṃ[744]sambhāvyeteti kim ucyate `nāśaṅkā niḥpra(ṣpra)māṇikā` iti | atha viśeṣaḥ pratibandhalakṣaṇo 'vinābhāvaniścāyako dṛṣṭapratihetor adṛṣṭapratiyogina iṣyate yataḥ pratiyogisambhavāśaṅkā 'stam upaiti | [S. 204a.] tadā sati vā viśeṣe sa viśeṣo hetor lakṣaṇam | kiṃ kāraṇam? | yatas tato viśeṣād dhetur ekāntena niścayena nirastapratipakṣas tathāvidhe dharmiṇi pratihetvasambhavāt
svasādhyaṃ niścāyayatīti | yas tathāvidho na bhavati tadviśeṣavirahāt dṛṣṭapratihetuḥ so 'tallakṣaṇo na hetuḥ syāt | tathā ca yadi nāmā 'hetau pratihetur dṛṣṭo, hetoḥ kim āyātam, yena tannivṛttaye tatraikasaṃkhyāvivakśā kriyate, yathoktāvinābhāvavacanenaiva tannivṛtter ity āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. In one whose defining characteristic — of the form of invariable concomitance grounded merely in observation and non-observation — is equal to that of the suspected counter-reason, the observed possibility of a counter-correlate that invalidates [the reason] generates the suspicion regarding the possibility of a counter-reason even in those of equal defining characteristic whose counter-correlate is not observed. Why? Because of the absence of any distinction between one whose counter-correlate is unobserved and one whose counter-correlate is observed. For there is no distinction at all of it from the other, by which its [counter-reason] possibility would not be suspected. But one should consider that the non-observation of that [counter-correlate] is possible due to the deficiency of the person's power and the like — so what is [the point of] saying 'the suspicion is without <s>pramāṇa</s>'? But if a distinction characterized by necessary connection, which ascertains invariable concomitance, is accepted for one whose counter-reason is observed but whose counter-correlate is unobserved — by which the suspicion of the possibility of a counter-correlate ceases — then when that distinction is present, that distinction is the defining characteristic of a logical reason. Why? Because through that distinction, a logical reason establishes its own thesis with certainty, having definitively eliminated the opposing position, since a counter-reason is impossible in a property-bearer of that kind. And one which is not of that kind — which lacks that distinction — [even though] its counter-reason has been observed — would not have that defining characteristic and would not be a logical reason. And thus, even if a counter-reason has been observed for [something] that is not a reason, what has this to do with the [genuine] reason, such that in order to negate that [counter-reason], the intention of oneness of number should be applied there — since the negation of that [counter-reason] is [already accomplished] by the stated invariable-concomitance formula alone? — He says:
'And thus, in a reason' —
one that possesses that distinction,
'when a counter-reason is impossible' —
when [that] is the case,
'the intention of oneness of number is purposeless' —
is without use —
thus.

children.text:
| [T. 364a.] yathoktaviśeṣāṅgīkaraṇe tallakṣaṇasya pratihetor asambhavāt kasyaikasaṃkhyāvivakṣayā vyavacchedaḥ kriyate? yato 'sya kāryakatvaṃ syād iti |
  viruddhāvyabhicāriṇaś ca hetvābhāsasya vyavacchedārtham ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā hetulakṣaṇe kriyate | vastuto 'sambhavat pratihetutvasiddhye ca pratibandhalakṣaṇe viśeṣe hetāv iṣyamāṇe viruddhāvyabhicāry api hetvābhāso na [S. 204b.] bhavati | tato vyavacchedyābhāvāt kim ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣayā? iti darśayann āha --
children.translated_text:
Since, when the aforementioned distinction is accepted, a counter-reason having that defining characteristic is impossible — for what is the exclusion to be effected by the intention of oneness of number? — so that it would have causal-ground-status.
And the intention of oneness of number in the defining characteristic of a logical reason is applied for the purpose of excluding the fallacious reason [known as] the contradictory non-deviating (<s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s>). But when the distinction characterized by necessary connection is accepted as belonging to the reason, the contradictory non-deviating too does not become a fallacious reason. Therefore, since what is to be excluded does not exist, what [use is] the intention of oneness of number? — showing this, he says:
'Therefore' —
because of accepting the distinction characterized by necessary connection,
'the defining characteristic of the fallacious reason [known as] the contradictory non-deviating would be lost' —

children.text: na sambhavet | kiṃ punas tadviruddhāvyabhicāriṇo lakṣaṇam? ity āha --
children.translated_text: would not be possible. But what then is the defining characteristic of this contradictory non-deviating? He says:
'Its own defining characteristic' —

children.text:
ityādi | hetor yadātmīyaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ tadyuktayor hetvor {p. 216.1}ekatra dharmiṇi virodhena parasparaviruddhasādhyasādhakatvenopanipāte sati viruddhāvyabhicārīti viruddhāvyabhicāriṇo lakṣaṇam | na ca tat pratibandhāṅgīkaraṇe sati sambhavati | na hi tādātmyatadutpattibhyāṃ svasādhyapratibandhavaty ekatra hetau kvaciddharmiṇi saṃbhavati dvitīyas tallakṣaṇas tatraiva hetuḥ sambhavet,
[T. 364b.] bhāvānāṃ viruddhasvabhāvadvayāsambhavāt, viruddhadharmādhyāsasya bhedalakṣaṇatvāt | tadavyabhicāriṇo hetor dvitīyasya tatra kutaḥ sambhavāvakāśa iti |
  nanu yadi tathāvidhaviśeṣasambhave [S. 205a.] sati viruddhāvyabhicārilakṣaṇaṃ hīyate, ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā vā vyārthā, tathāpi naiva hetvabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ, tat kim uktaṃ hetvabhāvo vety ata āha --
children.translated_text:
and so forth. When two reasons, each possessing their own defining characteristic, impinge upon a single property-bearer with a mutual contradiction — i.e., with the capacity to prove mutually contradictory theses — [the fallacy is called] the contradictory non-deviating. This is the defining characteristic of the contradictory non-deviating. And that is not possible when necessary connection is accepted. For when one reason possessing necessary connection with its own thesis through identity and origination-from-that [is present] in a single property-bearer, no second reason having that same defining characteristic can be possible there, because entities cannot have two contradictory essential natures, and because the superimposition of contradictory properties is the mark of [conceptual] distinction. Whence then the possibility of a second reason that does not deviate from that [property-bearer] there?
But [the opponent argues]: if, when such a distinction is present, the defining characteristic of the contradictory non-deviating is lost, or the intention of oneness of number is purposeless, even so there is surely no consequence of the absence of logical reasons — so what [is the point of] saying 'the absence of logical reasons too'? To this he says:
'And not' —
'indeed not' —
'of that [distinction]' —

children.text: viśeṣasya pratibandhalakṣaṇasya, yato vastuto 'sambhavat pratihetutvaṃ niścīyate |
children.translated_text: of the distinction characterized by necessary connection, by which the counter-reason-hood that is actually impossible is ascertained —
'the essential form' —

children.text: tādātmyatadutpattilakṣaṇaṃ nirddeśyate bhavadbhiḥ yathā 'smābhir nirdiṣṭaṃ ydrūpaṃ
children.translated_text: characterized by identity and origination-from-that — is not described by you as it has been described by us, of what form —
'understanding [which]' —

children.text: pratipadya pratiyoginaḥ sambhavāsambhavāu utpaśyāmaḥ | yatra sa viśeṣo nāsti tatra pratiyoginaḥ sambhavaḥ kalpita āgamāśraye 'numāne | yatra tv asti sa viśeṣo vastubalapravṛtte 'numāne tatra pratiyogino 'sambhava iti yata evaṃ tasmān nāsty eva bhavatāṃ sa viśeṣaḥ -- bhavadbhir na jñāyata eva sa viśeṣa
children.translated_text: comprehending [which], we observe the possibility and impossibility of a counter-correlate. Where that distinction is absent, there the possibility of a counter-correlate is supposed — in inference based on scripture (<s>āgama</s>). But where that distinction exists — in inference operating by the force of reality — there, the impossibility of a counter-correlate [obtains]. Since this is so, therefore you do not at all have that distinction — you do not at all know that distinction —
thus —

children.text: -- tasmāt[745]sarvatra yatrāpi pratiyogī na dṛśyate tatrāpi ṣāṅkyā pratiyogiviṣayayā bhavitavyam | tām eva śaṅkhāṃ draḍhyann āha --
children.translated_text: therefore, everywhere — even where a counter-correlate is not observed — the suspicion regarding the counter-correlate must remain. Reinforcing that very suspicion, he says:
'Even of one whose counter-reason has been observed' —

children.text:
ityādi | yasyāpi [S. 205b.] hi pratihetur dṛṣṭas tasyāpi prāk pratiyogidarśanād itareṇa sarvakālam adṛṣṭapratiyoginā kaścid viśeṣo lakṣyate [T. 365a.] yaddarśanāj jñāyeta `atra pratiyogī sambhavati nyānyatra` iti darśanādarśanamātranibandhanayor anvayavyatirekayoḥ sarvatra samānatvāt | tathāpi paścāt tatra pratiyogī dṛṣṭa iti sarvatra tattulyalakṣaṇe pratiyogisadbhāvaśaṅkā na vivarttata iti |
  syān matam -- yeṣu pratiyogī sambhavati teṣvaśyam eva kadācid asāv upalabhyate | yeṣu tu puruṣāyuṣeṇāpi nopalabhyate trṣv asau {p. 217.1} nāsty eva | tataḥ sa tathāvidho hetur bhaviṣyati, tat kathaṃ hetvabhāvo 'smākam? ity ata āha --
children.translated_text:
and so forth. For even one whose counter-reason has been observed — prior to the observation of the counter-correlate, at all times when the counter-correlate was unobserved — is no distinction to be noted from the other [whose counter-correlate has never been observed], by observing which one would know 'here the counter-correlate is possible, but not elsewhere' — since the positive and negative correlations based merely on observation and non-observation are the same everywhere. Yet subsequently, the counter-correlate was observed there — therefore the suspicion of the existence of a counter-correlate does not cease in everything of equal defining characteristic.
One might think: in those for which a counter-correlate is possible, it is necessarily apprehended at some time. But in those for which [a counter-correlate] is not apprehended even in a person's lifetime — in those, it simply does not exist. Therefore, one of that kind will be a [valid] reason — so how is there an absence of reasons for us? To this he says:
'And not' —

children.text: ityādi | yeṣām api hi pratihetuḥ sambhavati teṣām api naiva sarvadā tasya pratihetor upalabdhiḥ pratipattṛṛṇām | na hy asarvadarśinām upalabdhiḥ sarvabhāvasattāṃ vyāpnoti, pratibandhavaikalyasadbhāvāt | nanu ca yatra sarvadaiva pratipatrā(ttrā) pratiyogī na dṛśyate tatra tadāśaṅkā [S. 206a.] kathaṃ kriyate? | tathā cāha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. For even for those for whom a counter-reason is possible, the apprehension of that counter-reason by cognizers is by no means [present] at all times. For the apprehension of those who do not see everything does not pervade the existence of all entities, because of the existence of deficiencies in the necessary connection [of cognition to its object]. But where a counter-correlate is never at all observed by a cognizer — how is the suspicion regarding that [counter-correlate] applied there? And thus he says:
'But when an invalidating cognition has not arisen, the suspicion [of invalidity] is without <s>pramāṇa</s>.'

children.text:
iti |
tathā 'param --
 śiṣyaparamparayākumārilotpādāt prāgdṛṣṭapratiyogiṣūpanyasteṣu, tenaiva prajñātiśayaśāktinā pratihetava utprekṣitāḥ tatas taddarśanāt yāvaj jīvaṃ adṛṣṭapratihetuṣv api tadāśaṅkā nivarttate |tataḥ katham āśaṅkā niṣpramāṇikocyate? |
children.translated_text: Thus. And moreover: through the succession of students, before the appearance of <s>Kumārila</s>, for [reasons] whose counter-correlates had been observed [and] presented [as examples], counter-reasons were conjectured by that very person of extraordinary intellectual power — therefore, from seeing that, even for those whose counter-reason was unobserved throughout one's lifetime, the suspicion regarding that ceases. So how is the suspicion said to be without <s>pramāṇa</s>?
'For when the defining characteristic is equal' —

children.text: ityādikam api pratiyogisambhavāśaṅkākāraṇam uktam eva | na ca pratiyogisambhavam āśaṅkamānas tannimittasaṃbhavāt `utprekṣeta hi` ityādyākrośamātrea nivarttayituṃ śakyate | tenāsya[747]pratiyogyāśaṅkāpanodakṣaṃ kiñcit kāraṇam abhidhānīyam yathā 'smābhir abhihitaṃ `svabhāvahetor viparyaye bādhakapramāṇavaśād ātmyaniścaye saty anvayavyatirekayos tatra nirṇaya; [S. 206b.] kāryahetau ca yathoktapratyakṣānupalambhataḥ kāryakāraṇasiddhes tanniścaya` iti | yata evaṃ sarvatra pratiyogyāśaṅkā na nivarttate bhavad darśane tena kāraṇāniścayaḥ pratiyoginaḥ sambhavayoḥ `iha pratiyogī sambhavati iha tu na sambhavati` ity evaṃrūpa
children.translated_text: and so forth — has also already been stated as a reason for the suspicion of the possibility of a counter-correlate. And one who suspects the possibility of a counter-correlate cannot be turned back merely by the rebuke 'one would conjecture indeed' and the like, since the possibility of that ground exists. Therefore, some reason capable of removing the suspicion regarding the counter-correlate must be stated — as we have stated: 'In the case of the essential-nature reason, when there is ascertainment of identity through the force of an invalidating <s>pramāṇa</s> regarding the contrary, there is the determination of positive and negative correlation there; and in the case of the causal-ground reason, the determination [is obtained] from the establishment of the cause-effect relation through direct perception and non-apprehension as stated.' Since this is so, the suspicion regarding the counter-correlate does not cease anywhere in your view — therefore, the non-ascertainment of the cause, regarding the possibility of the counter-correlate — 'here the counter-correlate is possible, but here it is not' — of such a form,
thus —

children.text:
-- tasmād[748]vastuto 'sambhavat pratihetutvaṃ {p. 218.1} yallakṣaṇam hetoḥ [T. 366a.] tasyāniścitatvād ekasaṃkhyāvivakśāv ādināṃ na kaściddhetuḥ syāt | na hy aniścitalakṣaṇo hetur bhavatīty upasaṃhāra iti |
  tad evaṃ `kiṃ yo vastuto 'sambhavatpratihetuḥ sa samyagjñānaviparyayahetur iṣṭaḥ` iti amuṃ vikalpaṃ nirākṛtya dvitīyaṃ vikalpaṃ nirācikīrṣur āha --
children.translated_text:
therefore, the defining characteristic of a logical reason — that the counter-reason-hood of which is actually impossible — since that is not ascertained, no reason whatsoever would exist under the intention of oneness of number and the like. For one whose defining characteristic is not ascertained is not a [valid] logical reason — this is the conclusion.
Having thus refuted the alternative 'is one whose counter-reason is actually impossible accepted as a cause of correct cognition and its contrary?' — wishing to refute the second alternative, he says:
'Or, one whose counter-reason has not been demonstrated' —

children.text: samyagjñānaviviparyayahetur iṣṭa iti sambandhaḥ | ayaṃ ca pakṣaḥ kiladiṅnāgācāryasyāpy abhimata iti para upadarśayann āha --
children.translated_text: is accepted as the cause of correct cognition and its contrary — this is the syntactic connection. And this position is also said to be the view of <s>Dignāga</s> himself — showing this, the opponent says:
'As <s>Dignāga</s> says' —
what does he say?
'When indeed' —
and so forth.
'For audibility (<s>śrāvaṇatva</s>) cannot in any way be a reason for exclusion' —
when this was stated by <s>Dignāga</s>, the opponent replied:

'When indeed the Grammarian (<s>Vaiyākaraṇa</s>) accepts sound-ness (<s>śabdatva</s>) — whether universal or particular — as permanent, then this logical reason characterized by audibility would indeed be a property of the subject. [The inference:] Sound is permanent, because of audibility, like sound-ness' —
when the opponent stated this, the master (<s>ācārya</s>) said:

'If, in the property-bearer called sound (<s>śabda</s>), anyone — a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> or the like — were not to demonstrate' a counter-reason (<s>pratihetu</s>) to the reason characterized as being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>), being-consequent-upon-effort (<s>prayatnānantarīyakatva</s>), and the like, for impermanence,
'then this would be a reason with an undemonstrated counter-reason — truly a reason' —

children.text:
iti |
  tad evamācāryāpadaiḥ[750]sākṣitve datte mujam utkṣipya śāstrakāraḥ pūtkurvann[751]āha --
children.translated_text: thus. | Having thus produced the testimony of the teacher (<s>ācārya</s>), the author of the treatise (<s>śāstrakāra</s>), tossing his fist and puffing, says:
'Now then, this' —
and so forth.

children.text: yadā hyācāryasyāpy[753]etad abhimatam iti [T. 366b.] kaiścidvyākhyāyate tadidaṃ[754]sumahadvyasanam āyatam -- gurubhir abhihitatvād aprakāśyam, na hi gurūṇāṃ doṣaḥ prakāśayituṃ yuktaḥ,
children.translated_text: When some [commentators] explain that this is indeed the view of the teacher (<s>ācārya</s>) himself, then this most grave calamity has arrived — because it was stated by the teachers, it should not be exposed, for it is not proper to expose the faults of teachers;
'but for those who uphold logic, it cannot be concealed' —
it cannot be covered up. So then, shall we fault the teachers, or
'shall we also disregard logic?' —
'both are impossible' —
how can this most painful calamity be endured?

children.text: | na kathaṃcid iti | kaḥ punar atra doṣo yenedaṃ kaṣṭataram ity āha --
children.translated_text: | It cannot [be endured] in any way. What then is the fault here, by which this is most painful? He says:
'That reason' —
characterized by audibility (<s>śrāvaṇatva</s>) —
'[applied to] real entities' —
sound and the like —
'making its own provable truth' — permanence —
'[those entities] having that nature' —
having that essence —
'having made' —
those persons — <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, grammarians, and the like — for whom the audibility of that is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, them — {p. 219.1}
'with prosperity' —
with heaven —
'with the highest good' —
with liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) —
'having conjoined' —

children.text: | tathā hi -- vastutattvaṃ yāvan kleśān na prajahāti tāvat svargamāsādayati, kleśāṃs tu prajahan nirvāṇaparāyaṇo bhavati | athavā śabdanityatvapratītau vedaprāmāṇyāt tadvahitāgnihotrānuṣṭhānāt[759]svarggo vedāntaniṣevaṇād apavarggaḥ | punar uttarakālaṃ
children.translated_text: | For thus: as long as [one apprehending] the true nature of reality does not abandon the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), one attains heaven; but abandoning the <s>kleśas</s>, one becomes devoted to <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Or alternatively: upon the apprehension of the permanence of sound, from the authoritativeness of the <s>Veda</s>, through the performance of <s>Agnihotra</s> and the like prescribed by it, [one attains] heaven; and from the practice of the <s>Vedānta</s>, [one attains] liberation. Then, at a later time,
'by a man of brilliance' —
by a person of the intelligence-type, a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> or the like —
'of another reason' —
of a counter-reason —
'by the demonstration' —
'whatever capacity of this' —
'to prove permanence' —
that existed when the counter-reason had not been demonstrated,
'that, by the demonstration thereof' —
'is uprooted' —

children.text:
apanītam iti | tāni vastūni nityatvasampadaḥ pracyāvya, tāṃś ca tatpramāṇakān[764]puruṣān svarggāpavarggasampadaḥ pracyāvya śrāvaṇatvalakṣaṇo hetuḥ śaktivaikalyāt paritrātum aśakto bhraṣṭarājya iva rājā tapovanaṃ gacchati
svair eva duścaritair[765]iti kim atra vayaṃ brūmaḥ? |
  tad evam upahasyaitasmin pakṣe [S. 208a.] doṣam upadarśayann āha --
children.translated_text: i.e., removed. Having dislodged those entities from their state of permanence, and having dislodged those persons — for whom that [audibility] is the <s>pramāṇa</s> — from their state of heaven and liberation, the reason characterized by audibility, unable to protect [them] because of the deficiency of its power — like a king whose kingdom has been lost — goes to the forest of austerities, driven out by its own misdeeds. What can we say here? | Thus, having ridiculed [this position] and demonstrated the fault in this view, he says:
'Human intuition (<s>puruṣapratibhā</s>)' —

children.text:
ityādi | yadā hy apradarśitapratihetur hetur iṣyate tadā puruṣapratibhākṛtaṃ sādhanatvam abhyupagataṃ bhavati | tataś ca vastuto na kiñcit sādhanam asādhanaṃ vā prāptam | tathā hi -- yadā pratihetur nopadarśyate tadā sādhanam, yadā tūpadarśyate tadā na sādhanam iti puruṣapratibhākṛtaṃ sādhanatvam āyātam iti |
  api ca -- apradarśitapratihetor hetor hetutve 'ṅgīkriyamāṇe vikalpadvayam -- kiṃ paramārthato hetus taddharmabhāvī, utā 'taddharmabhāvīti? | tatrādyaṃ vikalpam adhikṛtyāha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. For when a reason with an undemonstrated counter-reason is accepted [as valid], then the status of being a means of proof becomes a product of human intuition. And therefore, in reality, nothing is a means of proof or a non-means-of-proof. For thus: when the counter-reason is not demonstrated, [it is] a means of proof; but when [the counter-reason] is demonstrated, [it is] not a means of proof — thus the status of being a means of proof becomes a product of human intuition. | Moreover: when the reason-status of a reason with an undemonstrated counter-reason is accepted, there is a twofold alternative — is [that] reason, in ultimate reality, one that exists [only] in the property-possessor (<s>taddharmabhāvin</s>), or one that exists even in the non-property-possessor (<s>ataddharmabhāvin</s>)? Regarding the first alternative, he says:
'And that' —
the reason that is first taken up. That —
'if by its essential nature' —
'indeed' —
'in that' —
in the property to be proved —
'exists only [when that property] is present' —
if this is accepted through the acceptance of invariable concomitance (<s>pratibandha</s>) as described by us — of such a disposition,
'then how could it be made otherwise' —

children.text: hetvantareṇātaddharmabhāvī kathaṃ kriyate? | na kathañcit | kiṃ kāraṇam? | vastūnāṃ [S. 208b.] hetulakṣaṇānāṃ yaḥ svabhāvaḥ -- `saty eva sādhyadharme bhavanātmakaḥ` --
children.translated_text: how is it made into one that exists in the non-property-possessor through another reason? Not in any way. For what reason? The essential nature of real entities characterized as reasons — 'having the nature of existing only when the property to be proved is present' —
'of the otherwise-becoming of that' —
of the reversal of that —
'because of the absence' —

children.text: ubhayoś ca svasādhyadharmāvinābhāvitve {p. 220.1} svabhāvata eva dharmiṇy ekatra tayor bhāve viruddāv ubhau svabhāvāv ekasya syātām | na caikasya viruddhau svabhāvau sambhavataḥ, viruddhadharmādhyāsena tasyaikatvahāniprasaṅgāt | atha dvitīyo vikalpas tadā
children.translated_text: and because both [the reason and the counter-reason] have invariable concomitance with their respective properties to be proved, if both existed by their essential nature in one and the same property-bearer, there would be two contradictory essential natures of one [entity]. And two contradictory essential natures of one [entity] are impossible — because of the absurd consequence of the loss of its unity through the superimposition of contradictory properties. If the second alternative [is taken], then —
'and if it exists in the non-property-possessor' —
having the disposition of existing even when the property to be proved is absent, due to the non-acceptance of invariable concomitance —
'how could it be a means of proof even at other times' —
even in the state when the counter-reason has not been demonstrated —
'for anything?' —

children.text:
kasyacit? | naiva tadāpi sādhanam, na kevalaṃ pradarśitapratihetvavasthāyām iti |
  upasaṃharann āha --
children.translated_text: | It would not be a means of proof even then — not only in the state when the counter-reason has been demonstrated. | Concluding, he says:
'Therefore, by essential nature' —

children.text: ityādi | yata evaṃ bhāvānāṃ svabhāvo 'nyathā kartuṃ na śakyate, viruddhobhayasvabhāvaś caiko na sambhavati tasmāt paramārthataḥ svena svena [S. 209.1a.] sādhyenāvinābhāvinor yathoktalakṣaṇayoḥ [T. 368a.] kāryasvabhāvahetvoḥ tallakṣaṇasya kāryasvabhāvalakṣaṇasya pratihetor asambhavād
children.translated_text: and so forth. Since the essential nature of entities cannot be made otherwise, and since one [entity] with both contradictory essential natures is impossible — therefore, in ultimate reality, since a counter-reason of that defining characteristic — of the defining characteristic of the effect-nature reason — is impossible for the two types of reasons — the effect-reason and the essential-nature-reason — which are invariably concomitant each with its own property to be proved, as described,
'having the character of a single number (<s>ekasaṃkhyā</s>) is not a defining characteristic [of the reason]' —

children.text: vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvaṃ lakṣaṇam na bhavati | kiṃ kāraṇam? ity āha --
children.translated_text: the intended single-number-ness is not a defining characteristic. For what reason? He says:
'Because of the absence of that which is to be excluded.' —

children.text: | pratihetur hi vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvasya vyavacchedyo varṇyate | sa ca pratihetuḥ svalakṣaṇayuktayoḥ kāryasvabhāvayor na bhavaty eveti kathaṃ taddhetulakṣaṇaṃ syād iti | tad evam anayor dvayo rūpayor yaḥ sambhavo yathoktāvinābhāvā 'sambhave satīti rūpāntaropagame 'pi hetvābhāsataiveti
children.translated_text: | For the counter-reason is described as that which is to be excluded from the intended single-number-ness. And that counter-reason simply does not exist for the effect-reason and essential-nature-reason that possess their [proper] defining characteristics — so how could it be the defining characteristic of those reasons? | Thus, the possibility of these two forms — when, given the absence of invariable concomitance as described, even upon the acceptance of another form — is precisely pseudo-reason-hood. Thus
'the pseudo-reasons are those other [than the valid ones]' —
the meaning of this has been explained. | In order to refute being-known (<s>jñātatva</s>) [as a defining characteristic], he says:
'Cognition, moreover' —

children.text: ityādi | abādhitaviṣayatvaṃ vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvaṃ ca kāryasvabhāvahetvor evāvinābhāve sati bādhāpratihetvor asambhavāt vyavacchedyābhāvatvena saty api liṅgadharmatve tallakṣaṇaṃ na bhavatīty uktam | jñānaṃ tu jñātatvam, tasyaiva [S. 209.1b.] bhāvapratyayenābhidhānāt | tathā hi -- jñānaśabdapravṛttinimittaṃ jñātatvam ucyate, tac ca jñānam eva, tadutpāde sati jñāta iti vyavahārāt | na ca tat liṅgasyātmarūpam iti [T. 368b.] kathaṃ liṅgalakṣaṇaṃ bhaviṣyati? | yady api vikalpapratibhāsī sāmanyākāro liṅgatayā 'vasthāpyate tathāpi na jñānasya liṅgadharmatā | na hy asau svatantra eva liṅgam | yad āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. Having-an-uncontradicted-object and intended-single-number-ness — since, given the invariable concomitance of the effect-reason and essential-nature-reason alone, a contradicting counter-reason is impossible, these [features], being [equivalent to] the absence of that which is to be excluded, do not constitute defining characteristics even when the property-of-the-mark (<s>liṅgadharmatā</s>) obtains — this has been stated. But cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) means being-known (<s>jñātatva</s>), since the same thing is denoted by the nominal suffix. For thus: what is called the ground for the application of the word 'cognition' is being-known, and that is cognition itself, since the designation 'known' [arises] upon its production. And that is not the self-form of the inferential mark — so how could it be a defining characteristic of the mark? Even though a universal form (<s>sāmānyākāra</s>) appearing in a concept is posited as the inferential mark, still cognition does not have the property-of-the-mark (<s>liṅgadharmatā</s>). For it is not an inferential mark independently. As [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:
'Since the distinctions of concepts,' —
'which are independent, [each] taking up [only] their own meaning — from an object constructed by them,' —
'in the apprehension of the object' —
'there would be only the apprehension of a non-object.' —

children.text:
iti | tamād bāhyavastūpādānasyaivāsya liṅgatā 'vasthāpyate | sādhyasādhanasaṃkalpe
vastudarśanahāneḥ[768]svalakṣaṇasya kvacidananvayāc ca taddharmatām eva tv anusmaranto vikalpā nānaikavyatirekān[769]saṃdarśayanto vastuni paramparayā pratibandhād avisaṃvādakāḥ kāryādiliṅgavyapadeśanibandhanaṃ cety uktaprāyam |
  na ca tasya kāryāder ātmarūpaṃ [S. 209.2a.] jñātam | vikalpāvabhāsī ca sāmānyākāro naiva vikalpasyātmabhūtaḥ, tasya nīrūpasya vasturūpavirodhāt | tadrūpasya ca vikalpapratibimbacakrasya sāmānyātmatāvirahāt | yasmād abāhyāsyāpi bāhyatayā vyavasitasyānanuyāyino 'py anuyāyitayā sāmānyāmakatvaṃ tathātve cāsya vikalparūpatayā kutaḥ? yadā ''ha --
children.translated_text: Thus. Therefore, the mark-status of this [inferential mark] is established only with respect to the external object-substrate. Since in the intention regarding the provable and the means of proof, the perception of the real entity is abandoned, and since the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) does not have co-presence (<s>anvaya</s>) anywhere — the concepts, however, while recollecting precisely the property-of-the-mark, displaying the non-single exclusions [of the particular], are non-deceptive with respect to the real entity through mediate invariable concomitance, and this is the basis for the designation as effect-reason and the like — [all] this has been mostly stated. | And being-known is not the self-form of that — the effect and the like. And the universal form appearing in a concept is not at all the self of the concept, because of the contradiction of a form possessing real-entity-form with the formless [concept]. And because the circle of reflections-in-concepts that have that form lacks universal-selfhood. Since even what is non-external is determined as external, and even what does not follow [the particular] is [determined] as following — [if] it has universality [under those conditions], then since it [would thereby have] the nature of a concept, how [could it be a universal]? As [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:
'And how could what is non-distinct from cognition go to another object?' ||
'Therefore, this apprehension of single-selfhood in objects is a false appearance.' |

children.text: iti | na jñānasya liṅgadharmatā | etad eva sādhayann āha --
children.translated_text: Thus. There is no property-of-the-mark for cognition. Establishing this very [point], he says:
'From what form' —
and so forth. 'From a reason of what nature' —
'the object to be inferred is to be known' — when this is the inquiry,
'that is being undertaken' —
'of the apprehender' —

children.text:
puṃso yad avisaṃvādakaṃ liṅgaṃ tasya svarūpam abhidhīyate śāstrakāraiḥ [T. 369a.] yasya rūpasya darśanādayaṃ pratipattā ôyatra tadrūpasambhavaḥ tat sādhanam tadrūpavikalam asādhanamô iti pravibhāgena vyavasthāpya yat tatra sādhanatvena vyavasthāpitaṃ tasyeṣṭārthasannidhānasampratyayāt pravṛttim avalambate | tathā, etasmiṃś ca nyāye [S. 209.2b.] vyavasthite yad asya liṅgasyātmarūpaṃ tal lakṣaṇaṃ bhavitum arhati pakṣadharmādivat na tu yat pararūpam |
  syād etad -- jñātasya liṅgasya sādhakatvād yuktaiva sādhyasiddhyupayogino jñānasya liṅgalakṣaṇatety ata āha --
children.translated_text: of the person — the self-form of the non-deceptive inferential mark is stated by the authors of treatises, who, having established by classification — 'from seeing what form, where there is the possibility of that form, that is a means of proof; what is deficient in that form is a non-means-of-proof' — [the apprehender,] relying on what is established therein as being a means of proof, undertakes activity because of confidence in the proximity of the desired object. And when this principle is established, what is the self-form of this inferential mark — that is fit to be its defining characteristic, like being a property of the thesis and the like, but not what is of another's form.
'In the birth of apprehension' —

children.text: ityādi | yady anumeyapratītijanmany upayujyate jñānam iti tanmātreṇa liṅgasya lakṣaṇam iṣyate tadā 'tiprasaṅgaḥ prāpnoti | tam evāha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. If cognition is useful in the birth of the apprehension of the object to be inferred, and if by that mere [usefulness] it is accepted as a defining characteristic of the inferential mark — then over-extension would follow. He states that very [over-extension]:
'Thus, if [something is] a defining characteristic of the inferential mark merely by its usefulness in the birth of apprehension — of the provable' —
'of the object' —
'of the person' —
{p. 222.1} 'of the one who cognizes' —
'and the like' —

children.text: śabdāt saṃyogasamavāyādīnām ālokamanaskārādīnāṃ liṅgalakṣaṇatvaṃ bhavet | atra kāraṇam āha --
children.translated_text: by the word 'and the like,' conjunction, inherence, and the like, illumination, mental attention, and the like — would [all] have the status of defining characteristics of the inferential mark. He states the reason here:
'For even in the absence of those' —

children.text: prameyādiṣu asatsu liṅgini jñānaṃ bhavatīti kṛtvā | atra paro 'niṣṭam āpādayann āha --
children.translated_text: the provable and the like — when the mark-bearer is absent, cognition does not arise. Here the opponent, pressing an undesired consequence, says:
'Then the mention of 'ascertained'' —

children.text: ityādi | yadi pararūpatvāj jñānaṃ liṅgalakṣaṇaṃ na bhavati tadā ca yad etadācāryeṇa --
children.translated_text: and so forth. If cognition is not a defining characteristic of the inferential mark because of being of another's form, then the mention of 'ascertained' (<s>niścita</s>) that was made by the teacher (<s>ācārya</s>) —
'In the object to be inferred and what is equal to it, the existence; in what is not [equal], the non-existence;' |
'when ascertained' —

children.text:
ti --
niścitagrahaṇaṃ kṛtaṃ bhavataś cābhimataṃ [T. 369b.] tan na karttavyam | tathā hi -- niścayo hi liṅgasya pararūpam eva | sa cet tallakṣaṇam, jñānaṃ kim iti neśyate yato niścayo vijñānam eva tadviśeṣatvād asyeti |
  siddhāntavāy āha --
children.translated_text: — this mention of 'ascertained,' which is accepted by you, should not be made. For thus: ascertainment is indeed of another's form with respect to the mark. If that is [accepted as] its defining characteristic, why is cognition not accepted [as such], since ascertainment is precisely a form of cognition, being a specific form of it? | The <s>Siddhāntavādin</s> says:
'It is not the case that it should not be made' —

children.text: kintu kartavyam eva tasya [S. 210a.] niścitagrahaṇasya liṅgarūpapratipādanād anyārthatvāt | tām evānyārthatāṃ darśayann āha --
children.translated_text: rather, it must indeed be made — because the mention of 'ascertained' has a different purpose from demonstrating the form of the inferential mark. Showing that very different purpose, he says:
'In the similar and dissimilar instances' —

children.text:
ityādi | pare hi sapakṣe darśanamātreṇāsapakṣe cādarśanamātrato gamakaṃ hetum icchanti | teṣāṃ naiva darśanamātreṇa sādhyasiddhau samartho hetur bhavatīti jñāpanārthaṃ niścitagrahaṇaṃ kṛtam | yataḥ sator vidyamānayor api darśanādarśanayor agamakatvaṃ hetor dṛśyate `sa śyamaḥ, tatputratvāt` ityādau | yata evaṃ tena kāraṇena sapakṣe bhāvena vipakṣe sarvatrābhāvaviśiṣṭenā 'sapakṣe ca sarvatrābhāvena sapakṣe tādātmyatadutpattilakṣaṇabhāvaviśiṣṭena gamako hetur ity asyārthasya jñāpanārthaṃ lakṣaṇavākye niścitagrahaṇaṃ kṛtaṃ boddhavyam | etad uktaṃ bhavati -- yāv eva sapakṣavipakṣayoḥ bhāvābhāvau pratibandhasādhakapramāṇavṛttyā niścitau tābhyām
eva hetur gamako bhavati, na tu yathākathañciddarśanamātreṇety asyārthasya [S. 210b.] jñāpanāya niścitagrahaṇaṃ kṛtam iti |
  prakṛtam upasaṃharann āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. For the opponents hold that a reason is indicative merely by being seen in the similar instance and merely by not being seen in the dissimilar instance. [To show] that for them, a reason is not capable of establishing the provable by mere seeing, the mention of 'ascertained' was made. For the non-indicativeness of a reason is seen even when seeing and not-seeing are present, as in 'he is dark, because of being a son of that [dark man].' Since this is so, by that reason, the mention of 'ascertained' in the defining statement should be understood as made for the purpose of making known the following meaning: a reason is indicative [when qualified] by existence in the similar instance qualified by the absence [of the reason] everywhere in the dissimilar instance, and by absence everywhere in the non-similar-instance qualified by existence in the similar instance characterized by identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and origination-from-that (<s>tadutpatti</s>). This is what is stated: the very co-presence and co-absence in the similar and dissimilar instances that are ascertained through the operation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> establishing invariable concomitance (<s>pratibandha</s>) — by those alone is the reason indicative, not by mere seeing in any manner whatsoever — for making known this meaning, the mention of 'ascertained' was made. | Concluding the main topic, he says:
'Therefore' —

children.text:
ityādi | yena viśiṣṭayor bhāvābhāvayor eva khyāpanāya niścitagrahaṇaṃ kṛtam, na rūpāntarābhidhānāya, anātmarūpasya [T. 370a.] ca lakṣaṇatā na yujyate, tena pararūpaṃ liṅgasya lakṣaṇaṃ na bhavati | yataḥ tena jñānādinā pararūpeṇa liṅgasya na kiñcid rūpaviśeṣo 'bhidhīyata iti |
  {p. 223.1} nanu ca pare 'pi sapakṣavipakṣayor bhāvābhāvābhyāṃ gamakaṃ hetum icchanti, darśanādarśane tu tayor eva sādhake, tat kim arthaṃ niścitagrahaṇam? iti, ata āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. Because the word 'ascertained' (<s>niścita</s>) was used for the purpose of indicating qualified presence and absence only, not for stating another form, and because it is not reasonable that what is not of the self's form should be a defining characteristic — therefore, a form belonging to another is not a defining characteristic of the mark (<s>liṅga</s>). Because by that [extraneous form] such as cognition and the like — which is of another's form — no specific form of the mark is stated. But others too accept that the indicative reason is [characterized] by presence in the similar class (<s>sapakṣa</s>) and absence in the dissimilar class (<s>asapakṣa</s>), and [they hold that] mere observation and non-observation alone are what prove those [presence and absence] — so for what purpose is the word 'ascertained' used? — to this he says —
'For those two' —

children.text:
ityādi | yady api pare bhāvābhāvābhyām eva gamakaṃ hetum icchanti tathāpi sapakṣa eva bhāvo 'sapakṣe cābhāva eveti bhāvābhāvau darśanādarśanamātrato vyavasthāpayanti | na ca tatas tau tathāvidhāu sidhyataḥ, pratibandhavikalānām apy athānāṃ kvacid bhāvābhāvayoḥ kathañciddarśanādarśanasambhavāt | tasmād [S. 211a.] yau `hetoḥ sapakṣe eva bhāvo 'sapakṣe cābhāva eva` ity evam ātmakau bhāvābhāvau tau tadbhāvasya sādhakaṃ yat pramāṇaṇ tādātmyatadutpattisādhanaviṣayaṃ tadvṛttyā boddhavyau | kutaḥ? upāyāntarasyābhāvāt | tadanabhyupagame hi hetoḥ sapakṣa eva bhāvaḥ sarveśāṃ hetumatāṃ bhāvānāṃ sādhyenānugamadarśane sati vipakṣe cābhāva eva sādhyavikalānāṃ sarvārthānāṃ
hetuviviktānāṃ upalambhe sati syāt | na caitad asarvadarśinaḥ sambhavatīti | yata upayāntaraṃ nāsti tena kāraṇena tayor viśiṣṭayor bhāvābhāvayoḥ pratipādanāya niścitaśabdaḥ prayukto lakṣāṇe lakṣaṇakāeṇeti |
  nanu ca bhāvābhāvavacanamātrād eva pramāṇato niścayo labhyate anyathā tayor eva sattā na prasidhyed iti, ata āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. Even though others accept that the indicative reason is [characterized] by presence and absence only, nevertheless they establish presence in the similar class alone and absence in the dissimilar class alone — these presence and absence — from mere observation and non-observation. But those two [presence and absence] are not established as being of that qualified kind from that [mere observation and non-observation], because even for things whose essential natures are not invariably connected, some kind of presence and absence can somehow be observed somewhere. Therefore, the presence and absence that are of the kind 'the reason exists only in the similar class and is absent only in the dissimilar class' — those are to be understood through the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves their being-so, whose object is [establishing] identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) or arising-from (<s>tadutpatti</s>). Why? Because of the absence of another means. For without accepting that, presence of the reason only in the similar class would [have to] obtain when the accompaniment of all entities that possess reasons with the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) has been observed; and absence only in the dissimilar class would [have to] obtain when the apprehension of all objects devoid of the <s>sādhya</s> as devoid of the reason has been made. And this is not possible for one who does not see everything. Because there is no other means, for the purpose of communicating those qualified presence and absence, the word 'ascertained' was employed in the definition by the master, and is accepted by us. But if there were no disagreement from the other side, then it would not be employed at all.
'Even though' —
and so forth.
'In what is to be inferred, an entity has similar existence; in what is not, non-existence.' —

children.text: ity anenaiva sapakṣāsapakṣayoḥ [T. 370b.] bhāvābhāvavacanamātreṇa niścitagrahaṇanirapekṣeṇa tayor bhāvābhāvayor yat sādhanaṃ pramāṇaṃ tasya vṛttir yady apy ākṣipyate | kathaṃ punar niścitagrahaṇam antareṇa bhāvābhāvavacanamātratas tadvṛtteḥ ākṣepaḥ? ity āha --
children.translated_text: By this [verse] alone, merely by stating presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar classes, without depending on the word 'ascertained' — even though the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves those presence and absence is implied. But how is the operation of the proving <s>pramāṇa</s> implied merely from the statement of presence and absence, without the word 'ascertained'? — he says —
'Otherwise' —
if the operation of the proving <s>pramāṇa</s> were not implied, then
'of those very two' —

children.text: sapakṣavipakṣayor eva bhāvābhāvayor yā sattā svarūpavyavasthā tasyā
children.translated_text: of the presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar classes only — their reality, i.e., the establishment of their own form,
'would not be established.' —
Why would it not be established? — he says —
'Of cognition' —

children.text: upalabdher yā sattā utpattiḥ tannibandhanatvāj jñeyasya bhāvābhāvalakṣaṇasya sattāvyavasthāyāḥ svarūpavyavasthiteḥ | na hy upalambham antareṇa svata evārthāḥ {p. 224.1} sidhyanti, sarvasya sarvasiddhiprasaṅgāt | tasmād idam evaṃrūpaṃ naivaṃrūpam iti tadākārajñānodayād eva vyavasthāpyate | yata evaṃ tasmāt sarvatra śāstre loke vā jñeyasattāvyavasthaiva niścitagrahaṇaṃ vinā 'pi
children.translated_text: because the establishment of the reality of the knowable — characterized as presence and absence — is grounded in the reality, i.e., the arising, of cognition, i.e., of apprehension. For objects are not established by themselves without apprehension, because of the absurd consequence that everything would be established for everyone. Therefore, [things] are established as 'being of this form' or 'not being of this form' only from the arising of cognition having that form. Since this is so, therefore everywhere — in treatises or in the world — the establishment of the reality of the knowable, even without the word 'ascertained,'
'attracts the [pramāṇa] that proves that' —
the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves that reality,
'attracts' —

children.text: ākṣipatīti | kiñ ca, parārthatvāc ca śāstrapraṇayanasya tatsādhanapramāṇavṛttir ākṣipyata iti sambandhaḥ | kīdṛśaṃ punas tacchāstrapraṇayanaṃ yat parārtharūpatayā svavyavasthāpitajñeyasattāsādhanaṃ pramāṇam ākṣipati? ity āha --
children.translated_text: i.e., implies. Moreover, because the composition of the treatise is for the sake of others, the operation of the proving <s>pramāṇa</s> is implied — this is the connection. But what kind of treatise-composition is it that, being for the sake of others, implies the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves the establishment of the reality of the knowable established by oneself? — he says —
'The three-formed mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is for you the one that conveys, that leads to' —
the desired object. Even if the treatise-composition for the sake of others is of such a form, how does it imply the operation of the proving <s>pramāṇa</s>? — he says —

children.text: vāñcitasyārthasyeti | yadi nāmaivaṃrūpaṃ parārthaṃ śāstrapraṇayanaṃ tathāpi kathaṃ tat sādhanapramāṇavṛttim ākṣipatīty āha --

children.translated_text: 'The form of that' —

children.text: tasya liṅgasya trirūpasya rūpaṃ svabhāvaṃ śāstroktaṃ ye pratipattāro na vidanti, na teśāṃ tatas trirūpāl liṅgāc chāstroktād vāñcite 'rthe pravṛttir bhavati, ajñātasyārthasya [S. 212a.] jñāpakasya svasattāmātreṇa pravartakatvābhāvāt | yata evam
children.translated_text: the form, i.e., the essential nature, of that three-formed mark — as stated in the treatise — those recipients who do not know [it], for them there is no operation from that three-formed mark stated in the treatise with respect to the desired object, because what merely exists by its own reality cannot motivate [action] when the object [it signifies] is unknown. Since this is so,
'therefore' —

children.text:
tasmāt paropalakṣaṇatvād eva pareṣāṃ jñāpakatvād eva pravarttake trirūpaliṅge jñānaṃ siddham iti yady api niścitagrahaṇam atiricyate tathāpi tāv eva
liṅgasya sapakṣāsapakṣayor bhāvābhāvau viśiṣṭau śastroktau `sapakṣa eva bhāvo 'sapakṣe cābhāva eva` ity evaṃrūpau kecinnaiyāyika prabhṛtayaḥ, pare darśanādarśanamātreṇa -- ye darśanādarśane pratibandhasādhake na bhavataḥ -- tanmātreṇa vyavasthāpayanti
children.translated_text: precisely because of being the indicator for others — because of being the informer for others — knowledge is established in the motivating three-formed mark. Therefore, even though the word 'ascertained' is redundant, nevertheless those very presence and absence of the mark in the similar and dissimilar classes — qualified, as stated in the treatise — of the kind 'presence only in the similar class and absence only in the dissimilar class' — certain [logicians], the <s>Naiyāyika</s> and others, establish these by mere observation and non-observation — [observation and non-observation] that do not serve to prove invariable connection — by that alone [they establish them].
'For precisely this reason' —
'therefore' —

children.text:
tasmāt teṣāṃ vādināṃ niśedhārtho 'yaṃ lakṣaṇe niścitaśabdaḥ prayuktaācāryeṇāsmābhiś cābhyupagata iti | yadi tu paravipratipattiḥ na syāt tadā naivāsau prayujyeteti |
  kim iti punar darśanādarśanābhyāṃ bhāvābhāvaviśayābhyāṃ sapakṣā[sa]pakśayoḥ viśiṣṭau bhāvābhāvāv anvayavyatirekātmakau [T. 371b.] neṣyeta ity āha --
children.translated_text: for the purpose of refuting those disputants, this word 'ascertained' was employed in the definition by the master, and is accepted by us. But if there were no disagreement from the other side, then it would not be employed at all. Now, why are qualified presence and absence — having the nature of positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s>) — in the similar and dissimilar classes not accepted [as established] from observation and non-observation that have presence and absence as their objects? — he says —
'Even when there exist' —

children.text:
ityādi saty api kvacit sapakṣe bhāvadarśane hetoḥ kvacic cāsapakṣe 'bhāvadarśane `sa śyamaḥ, tatputratvāt` ityādāv anvayavyatirekayoḥ saṃśayāt | tathā hi -- anvayo nāma sarvatra saty eva sādhye hetor {p. 225.1} bhāvo vyāptyā cāsati sādhye hetor abhāvo vyatirekaḥ | na ca kvacit sati sādhye [S. 212b.] hetor bhāvadarśane 'pi tanmātreṇa tathābhāvaḥ sarvatra bhavati, apratibaddhasvabhāvānāṃ sahabhāvaniyamā 'bhāvāt | tathā kvacit sādhyābhimatasyābhāve saty abhāvadarśane 'pi hetoḥ sarvatra tadabhāve 'vaśyam abhāvaḥ, tadanāyat tasya tannivṛttau niyamena nivṛttyabhāvāt | tasmāt pratibandhaprasādhakapramāṇavṛttyaiva yathoktau sapakṣāsapakṣayoḥ bhāvābhāvau sidhyataḥ nānyatheti vipratipattinirāsārtham eva niścitagrahaṇaṃ
kṛtam ity upadarśayann āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. Even when there is observation of the presence of the reason in some similar class, and observation of its absence in some dissimilar class — as in [the inference] 'he is dark-complexioned, because he is his son' and the like — because of doubt regarding the positive and negative concomitance. For thus: positive concomitance means the presence of the reason wherever the <s>sādhya</s> is present — through pervasion — and its absence wherever the <s>sādhya</s> is absent is negative concomitance. And even when the presence of the reason is observed when the <s>sādhya</s> is present in some [instance], from that alone such [universal] presence does not obtain everywhere, because of the absence of a rule of co-existence for things whose essential natures are not invariably connected. Likewise, even when the absence of the reason is observed when what is regarded as the <s>sādhya</s> is absent in some [instance], [it does not follow that] in every case of absence of that [<s>sādhya</s>] there is necessarily absence [of the reason], because for what is not dependent on that [<s>sādhya</s>], there is no rule of cessation when that ceases. Therefore, the presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar classes, as described, are established only through the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves invariable connection — not otherwise. Showing that the word 'ascertained' was used precisely for the purpose of removing this disagreement, he says —
'Therefore' —
and so forth.
'By us' —
because the word 'ascertained' in the master's work is accepted by us elsewhere,
'by us' —

children.text:
ity āha |
  tad evaṃ vipratipattinirāsārthaṃ niścitagrahaṇam, asatyāṃ tu vipratipattau tan na kartavyam eveti pratipādya ata eva nyāyāt jñātatvaṃ rūpāntaraṃ na bhāvatīti [T. 372a.] darśayann āha --
children.translated_text: he says. Thus, the word 'ascertained' is for the purpose of removing disagreement; but when there is no disagreement, it need not be used at all — having demonstrated this, and thereby showing that 'being-known' (<s>jñātatva</s>) is not another form [i.e., a fourth characteristic], he says —
'Moreover' —
and so forth.
'Separately from this' —
from the three characteristics beginning with being the property of the thesis. Why?
'By that very' —
by the very statement of the three characteristics, through the implication of the proving <s>pramāṇa</s>,
'because of being known' —
because of being understood. Like what?
'Like the meaning of the <s>upanaya</s> (application), [which is implied] from the property-of-the-thesis' —

children.text:
iti | yathā pakṣadharmatvavacanenaiva hetor upanayasyārtho 'vagatas tasya dharmiṇi hetoḥ sadbhāvapradarśanātmakatvāt, pakṣadharmavacanasya ca tadrūpatvāt tataḥ pṛthagupanayo [S. 213a.] rūpāntaraṃ na bhavati; tathā trairūpyāt jñānaṃ, tadvacanenaivāvagatatvād iti |
  atra paro 'niṣṭam āpādayann āha --
children.translated_text: Just as the meaning of the <s>upanaya</s> — the application of the reason — is understood from the very statement of the property-of-the-thesis, because its nature is the demonstration of the existence of the reason in the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), and because the statement of the property-of-the-thesis has that form — therefore, the <s>upanaya</s> as a separate additional form does not exist; likewise, knowledge [is understood] from the three characteristics, because it is understood by the very statement of those.
'Of positive and negative concomitance too' —

children.text: ityādi | yadi trairūpyavacanenaiva sāmarthyāj jñānaṃ labhyata iti tat tataḥ pṛthag na vaktavyam
children.translated_text: and so forth. If knowledge is obtained by the power of the very statement of the three characteristics, and therefore need not be stated separately from those —
'well then' —

children.text:
tarhi anvayāt pṛthag vyatireko na vaktavyaḥ vyatirekāc ca pṛthaganvayaḥ | kiṃ kāraṇam? | ekasyānvayasya vyatirekasya vā prayogād ubhayasya gateḥ | kṛtaṃ ca tayoḥ pṛthagvacanaṃ, tathā jñātatvasyāpi trairūpyād gamyamānasyāpi pṛthagvacanaṃ karttavyam iti |
  siddhāntavādy āha --
children.translated_text: negative concomitance need not be stated separately from positive concomitance, and positive concomitance separately from negative concomitance. What is the reason? Because from the formulation of a single one — positive or negative concomitance — both are understood. And since separate statement has been made for those two, so too for being-known, even though it is understood from the three characteristics, separate statement should be made. The proponent says —
'No — of the reason' —

children.text:
ityādi | nānvayavyatirekayor na pṛthaktvaṃ kintu bhinnarūpataiva | tathā hi -- anvayo hetoḥ {p. 226.1} sapakṣe bhāva ucyate, vyatirekaḥ punar abhāvo 'sapakṣe | na ca tau parasparam ākṣipataḥ [T. 372b.] parasparam antarbhavato vidhipratiṣedharūpayor bhinnasvabhāvatvāt | na ca yo yato bhinnasvabhāvaḥ sa tatrāntarbhūto yuktaḥ | nanu ca yady anvayavyatirekayor bhinnarūpatā kathaṃ tarhi trairūpaṃ liṅgam ucyate? | na hi parasparabhinnāv ātmānāv evāsya yujyate, svabhāvabhedalakṣaṇatvād vastubhedasya | naiṣa doṣaḥ, yato yathā 'nvayavyatirekau [S. 213b.] vyavasthāpyete na vā nayo(-pyete tathā tayo)r anantarbhāva ucyate nānyathā | kathaṃ caitau vavasthāpyete? | vyāvṛttikṛtaṃ bhedam upādāya | tathā cānayor bhinnarūpataiva | vyāvṛttibhede 'pi ca paramārthato bhedo nāstīty ekaṃ liṅgaṃ trirūpam ity ucyata iti |
  kathaṃ tarhi prāguktam[771]`nānayor arthaḥ kaścid bhedaḥ, anyatra prayogabhedād` iti? ata āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. Positive and negative concomitance are not non-separate; rather, they have distinct forms indeed. For thus: positive concomitance is stated as the presence of the reason in the similar class; but negative concomitance is the absence in the dissimilar class. And those two do not mutually imply each other or include each other, because affirmation and negation have different essential natures. And it is not reasonable that what has a different essential nature from something should be included in it. But if positive and negative concomitance have different forms, how then is the mark called three-formed? For it is not reasonable that two mutually different selves should be [forms] of it, because a real difference is characterized by difference of essential nature. This is not a fault, because just as positive and negative concomitance are established or not established, so their non-inclusion [in each other] is stated — not otherwise. And how are these two established? By taking into account the difference produced by exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>). And thus these two have distinct forms indeed. But even though there is difference in exclusion, since in ultimate reality there is no difference, the mark is called one [with] three forms.
'But how then was it stated earlier: 'There is no meaning or difference between these two, apart from the difference of formulation'? — to this he says: 'A single statement' —

children.text:
ityādi | anvayamukhena vyatirekamukheṇa vā prayuktam ekaṃ vākyam ubhayam anvayaṃ vyatirekaṃ ca bhinnalakṣaṇam eva gamayatīty ucyate 'smābhir naiko 'rthaḥ svabhāvo dvitīyasyocyate, parasparabhinnayor evaikavākyārtharūpatvāt |
  atra para āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. A single statement, formulated through the medium of positive concomitance or through the medium of negative concomitance, conveys both — positive concomitance and negative concomitance — which have distinct characteristics. We say this; we do not say that one has the nature of the second, because the two, though mutually distinct, have the form of the meaning of a single statement.
'But in that very [statement]' —

children.text:
ityādi | ayam abhiprāyaḥ -- lakṣaṇavākyapratipāditāv anvayavyatirekāv āśritya parasparāntarbhāvaścodyate | sa ca vidyata[772]eva | tathā hi -- `tatraiva bhāvaḥ` ity atra lakṣaṇavākye tadarthatayā[773]tadabhāve 'bhāvo gamyate; `atadabhāve 'vaśyam abhāvaḥ` iti [T. 373a.] cātra `tadbhāve bhāvaḥ` | na hy asati pratibandha ekābhāve 'parasyābhāvaḥ | pratibandhaś ca tādātmyatadutpattibhyāṃ tadbhāve bhāvarūpa eva | tataś caikenaiva sapakṣāsapakṣyor bhāvābhāvapratipādakena [S. 214a.] prativiśiṣṭena lakṣaṇavākyenobhayagater dvitīyavacanaṃ na karttavyam iti | tathā caikavākyārthāntarbhāvād bhinnasvabhāvatā 'py anayor durllabhā | tataś ca yaduktam `anvayavyatirekayor api tarhi na pṛthaktvam iti` tat tadavastham eveti |
  {p. 227.1} siddhāntavādy āha --
children.translated_text: and so forth. The purport is: the mutual inclusion of positive and negative concomitance is objected to on the basis of the defining statement. And that [inclusion] indeed exists. For thus: in the defining statement 'presence precisely there,' the absence in the absence of that is understood as its meaning; and in 'necessarily absence in the absence of that,' the presence when that is present [is understood]. For without invariable connection, when one is absent the absence of the other would not [follow]. And invariable connection, through identity and arising-from, has precisely the form of presence when there is presence [of the other]. Therefore, since both are understood from a single defining statement that communicates presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar classes — each being qualified — the second statement need not be made. And thus, because of inclusion in the meaning of a single statement, the distinct nature of these two is also hard to obtain. And therefore what was said — 'of positive and negative concomitance too, then, there would be no separateness' — that remains just as it is. The proponent says —
'This statement' —
of the form 'presence precisely there' and the like,
'implies both' —
communicates [both]. Why? From the capacity, the power to communicate both?
'The restriction of the pervader' —

children.text: `sapakṣa eva bhāvo 'sapakṣe cābhāva eva` iti sāvadhāraṇasya
children.translated_text: 'presence only in the similar class and absence only in the dissimilar class' — with the restrictive particle,
'because of being an inevitable implication of the second' —
because of being an inevitable communication of the second.
But the single essential nature of the two is not [established] merely by being communicated by a single statement.
